The tale fuses a household brownie tradition with the memory of a real accidental death, two strands of local history and folklore knotted together so tightly that even Surtees, writing two centuries closer to events, could only partly pull them apart.
earliest_record: Robert Surtees, The History and Antiquities of the County Palatine of Durham, Vol. III, 1820.
historical_setting: Local tradition links the ghost to Roger Skelton, a stable boy killed at Hylton Castle on 3 July 1609, accidentally struck by a scythe wielded by Sir Robert Hylton, 13th Baron of Hylton, while mowing; an inquest ruled it 'accident of misfortune' and Hylton received a pardon from Bishop James, recorded 6 September 1609. Surtees himself, in 1820, treated the Cauld Lad primarily as an older brownie/household-spirit tradition and noted that some accounts had merged it with the Skelton death as 'an admixture of English superstition.'

name: Ceridwen
summary: The Welsh enchantress who brewed the cauldron of inspiration and knowledge, Awen. When her servant Gwion Bach accidentally tasted three drops, she pursued him through a cycle of transformations before swallowing him whole and giving birth to the great poet Taliesin.
detail:
Ceridwen is the great enchantress of Welsh legend, a sorceress of Penllyn dwelling beside Llyn Tegid (Bala Lake) whose story survives in the medieval Tale of Taliesin. She had a son, Morfran (also called Afagddu), so monstrously ugly that she resolved to compensate him with wisdom, and set about brewing a magical draught in her great cauldron, a potion of inspiration and knowledge the Welsh called Awen. It had to be boiled for a year and a day, and only the first three drops would carry the gift; all the rest was deadly poison.

She set a blind man to tend the fire and a boy, Gwion Bach, to stir the cauldron. But when the year was almost up, three scalding drops leapt out onto Gwion's thumb, and sucking it to ease the burn he swallowed the very essence meant for Morfran. In that instant the boy knew all things, including that Ceridwen's fury would fall upon him, and he fled. What followed is one of the most vivid shape-shifting chases in Celtic myth: Gwion became a hare and Ceridwen a greyhound; he a fish and she an otter; he a bird and she a hawk. At last he turned into a single grain of wheat, and she, becoming a black hen, scratched through the heap and swallowed him whole.

Made pregnant by the grain, Ceridwen bore the child nine months later, and finding him too beautiful to kill, she sewed him into a leather bag and cast him into the sea. He was drawn from the water by a prince and grew into Taliesin, the greatest of the early Welsh poets, so that Ceridwen's cauldron, brewed for one son, in the end gave Wales its bard. She endures as a potent emblem of poetic inspiration, transformation and the dangerous, generative magic of the cauldron.
earliest_record: Elis Gruffydd's mid-16th-century 'Ystoria Taliesin' (part of his Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World, National Library of Wales MS 5276) is the earliest complete surviving text of the Ceridwen/Taliesin tale, though Gruffydd's own account points to earlier sources, possibly as old as the 9th century. Some of the 56 poems in the related, older 14th-century Book of Taliesin are considered by scholars to originate in the 10th century or earlier
period: Early Modern Wales (earliest complete surviving text); the tradition itself is judged considerably older

name: Cerne Abbas Giant
summary: A 55-metre chalk giant cut into the hillside above Cerne Abbas in Dorset, naked, ithyphallic, and carrying a great club. His age is debated, his identity disputed, and his connection to fertility rites very much alive.
detail:
The Cerne Abbas Giant dominates the hillside above the village of Cerne Abbas in Dorset: a 55-metre figure cut in chalk, male, naked, and unmistakably aroused, wielding a knotted club in his right hand. He is one of the most startling prehistoric figures in Britain, and one of the most mysterious, because unlike the Uffington White Horse, no medieval or earlier documentary record of him has yet been found.

The silence of the medieval record has led some historians to suggest he was cut relatively recently, perhaps in the seventeenth century as a political satire. Others maintain his origins are genuinely ancient, pointing to parallels with the Roman Hercules (club, nakedness, heroic scale) and suggesting he was created or adapted during the Roman period. A 2021 optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) study by the National Trust, University of Gloucestershire, and Cerne Historical Society dated sediment in the chalk outline to 700-1100 AD, with a mid-point in the late 10th century, around the time nearby Cerne Abbey was founded, overturning both the prehistoric/Roman theory and the 17th-century Cromwell-mocking theory. The National Trust now owns and maintains him.

Whatever his origin, the fertility tradition attached to him has been persistent and energetic. Women wishing to conceive were said to sleep on the figure, and particularly within the outline of his most prominent feature. The Maypole at Cerne Abbas was historically erected just above the giant's head. The tradition has been documented from the eighteenth century and continues informally today.
earliest_record: A 2021 optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) study by the National Trust, University of Gloucestershire, and Cerne Historical Society dated sediment in the chalk outline to 700-1100 AD, with a mid-point in the late 10th century, around the time nearby Cerne Abbey was founded. This overturned earlier theories of a prehistoric/Roman (Hercules) origin and a 17th-century Cromwell-mocking origin
period: Late Anglo-Saxon England

name: Cernunnos
summary: The antlered Celtic god associated with wild nature, animals, fertility, and the deep green world. His image appears on ancient objects, a horned figure seated among beasts and mystery.
detail:
Cernunnos is the antlered god of the ancient Celts, a deity of wild nature, beasts, fertility and abundance whose image is far better attested than his myth. He is depicted as a mature, often cross-legged figure crowned with the antlers of a stag, frequently holding or wearing the torc, the sacred neck-ring of Celtic nobility, and accompanied by animals, above all the stag and the ram-horned serpent, a strange composite creature that recurs in his iconography. The name itself, 'the horned one', survives on only a single inscription: the Pillar of the Boatmen, raised in Roman Lutetia (Paris) between 14 and 37 AD by a guild of river boatmen, and rediscovered by chance in 1710 during building work beneath Notre-Dame Cathedral. Uninscribed images of a horned or antlered god appear far more widely across the Celtic world, including in Britain, possibly as early as the Iron Age rock carvings of Val Camonica in northern Italy, dated to around 400 BC, though these earlier images cannot be certainly tied to the name Cernunnos itself.

As a horned lord seated in mastery among the creatures of the forest, Cernunnos seems to embody the meeting of the human and animal worlds, the generative power of wild life, and the wealth that flows from it, the torcs and coins shown spilling from his presence on some monuments suggesting a god of plenty as well as of beasts. The most famous depiction, on the great silver Gundestrup cauldron, shows him antlered and cross-legged, grasping a torc and a horned serpent, surrounded by animals.

Because almost no narrative about him survives, Cernunnos remains a figure of suggestion and mystery, reconstructed from sculpture and symbol rather than story. Modern Pagan and folkloric traditions have embraced him as the archetypal Horned God of the greenwood, and he is often linked in the popular imagination with later figures of the wild, the Green Man, Herne the Hunter, and the leaf-crowned spirits of the British woods.
origin_date: 14-37 AD (named inscription); iconographic antlered-figure depictions possibly as early as c. 400 BC
earliest_record: The Pillar of the Boatmen, erected in Lutetia (Roman Paris) by the Parisii boatmen's guild between 14-37 AD, is the only surviving inscription naming 'Cernunnos', rediscovered in 1710 during work beneath Notre-Dame de Paris. Earlier, uninscribed antlered-figure iconography appears in Iron Age rock carvings at Val Camonica, Italy (from c. 400 BC) and on the 1st-century BC Gundestrup Cauldron, though these can't be certainly linked to this specific name
period: Roman Gaul (named attestation); presumed pre-Roman Iron Age in iconographic origin

name: Chanctonbury Ring
summary: An Iron Age hillfort ringed with beech trees on the South Downs. Walk seven times around it at midnight and the Devil will appear with a bowl of soup. Roman offerings were found buried within. The trees were blown down in 1987, and something changed.
detail:
Chanctonbury Ring is a prehistoric hillfort high on the South Downs of West Sussex, made unmistakable by the ring of beech trees planted within its ramparts in 1760 by Charles Goring. Beneath the trees lie far older remains: Iron Age earthworks, the foundations of Romano-British temples, and Roman votive offerings found buried inside. The brooding crown of beeches has made it one of the most legend-haunted spots in southern England.

The best-known tradition concerns the Devil. It is said that if you run (or walk backwards) seven times around the Ring at midnight, in some versions on Midsummer Eve or Halloween, the Devil himself will appear and offer you a bowl of soup, porridge or milk, in exchange for your soul. A related belief holds that the trees of the Ring can never be accurately counted. The place gathered a dark reputation for ghosts and apparitions, from a phantom white-bearded treasure-seeker to spectral riders, and in the 20th century it became notorious in accounts of the uncanny, including reports of strange experiences among those who dared to sleep there.

The Ring's mood changed dramatically in the Great Storm of October 1987, when the hurricane-force winds tore down most of the ancient beeches in a single night. The clump has since been replanted and is slowly regrowing, but to many who knew it the old enchantment of the place was bound up with those vanished trees, and the legends of the Devil's circuit endure on the bare, wind-scoured down.
earliest_record: The Devil-summoning story's earliest recorded instance is in Arthur Beckett's 'The Spirit of the Downs' (1909); folklorists classify these stories as post-medieval inventions. Separately, the hillfort itself is a slight univallate earthwork, generally dated late Bronze Age/early Iron Age (assessments range from c. 7th century BC to 400-300 BC); a 1987-91 excavation (prompted by storm damage in 1987) confirmed two Romano-Celtic temples within the earthworks, dating from the mid-1st century AD, with evidence of a boar/pig cult
period: Iron Age (hillfort); Roman Britain (temples); early 20th century (the specific Devil legend, as recorded)

name: Cheesewring
summary: A strange granite tor on Bodmin Moor, said in local legend to have been formed during a stone-throwing contest between a giant and a saint. The impossible stack looks less built than argued into being.
detail:
The Cheesewring is a dramatic natural tor on Bodmin Moor in Cornwall, a precarious stack of great granite slabs, broad above and narrow below, that looks so improbable it seems impossible it was not built or balanced by some deliberate hand. Its name comes from its resemblance to a 'cheesewring', the old apparatus used to press cheese, but Cornish legend gives the strange pile a far better origin, a contest between a giant and a saint.

In the tale, the giants of the moor were affronted by the coming of the Christian saints and the loss of their old dominion, and one great giant, Uther, challenged a saint, usually named as St Tue (Saint Tew), to a trial of strength in rock-throwing, the loser to submit to the other's faith. The two hurled great stones, piling them up, and the contest seemed to favour the giant by sheer brawn until the saint, aided by an angel or by divine power, was able to cast or catch the heaviest rocks with miraculous ease, building the impossible balanced stack that is the Cheesewring and winning the day for the new faith.

The Cheesewring is also linked to other moorland lore, a golden goblet said to have been offered to a thirsty druid or hidden in the rocks, and the general belief that Bodmin Moor's tors and stone-piles were the work or the playthings of giants. As a place where an extraordinary natural form is explained by a saint-and-giant legend, the Cheesewring is a classic of Cornish folklore, the landscape itself read as the frozen record of a contest between the old powers and the new.
cultural_tradition: Cornish giant-versus-saint contest motif, a recurring type in Cornish folklore (cf. Cormoran, other Bodmin/West Penwith giant tales)
historical_setting: Stowe's Hill, Bodmin Moor, Cornwall. The Cheesewring rock stack sits beside Stowe's Pound, a scheduled prehistoric hillfort with Bronze Age cairns and hut circles (Historic England list entry 1012352), so the landscape itself is securely dated even though the giant legend attached to it is not
period: No dated written source for the giant-and-saint (Uter and St Tue) legend could be located. Wikipedia's own citation for the tale is a 2008 popular book (Chapman & Chapman, Iconic Cornwall), not an earlier folklore collection; searches of Robert Hunt's Popular Romances of the West of England (1865) and William Bottrell's collections did not turn up a Cheesewring-specific version

name: Cheetham Close
summary: A Bronze Age stone circle on the Lancashire moors, once imagined as a druidical temple where bards performed rites. Its destruction was sealed by a Victorian farmer who sledgehammered the stones to keep visitors away.
detail:
Cheetham Close sits at around 1,060 feet on exposed moorland near Turton, on the old boundary between Lancashire and Greater Manchester. The stone circle originally comprised eleven uprights arranged in a ring roughly fifteen metres across, with a substantial ring-bank cairn nearby, a second, larger enclosure measuring twenty-four yards across with carefully revetted walls four feet thick. Together, the complex testifies to sustained Bronze Age ceremonial activity in these Pennine uplands.

Nineteenth-century antiquarians saw the site through a romantic lens. One writer imagined 'bards in their different orders' conducting 'rites and mysteries' before assembled crowds, and the site was characterised as a 'bardic temple.' A Roman road passed within two hundred yards, prompting speculation that the monument was already ancient when Rome came through. Archaeological finds, including a Bronze Age saddle quern, a British copper axe-head discovered around 1819, and a Celtic bronze tool, lent substance to the antiquarians' sense of deep time, even if their druidical interpretations owed more to imagination than evidence.

The circle's destruction came not from time but from deliberate vandalism. A farmer employed by the nineteenth-century landowner James Kay sledgehammered the stones 'to prevent people visiting the situation.' By 1871 two stones had been broken almost to fragments, and today only two of the original stones remain standing, according to a 1983 survey.
earliest_record: M. Fletcher's Bronze Age Complex survey (Greater Manchester Archaeological Unit) dates the monument to the Early Bronze Age; the ring cairn was first excavated in 1893, and the site is scheduled by Historic England (list entry 1009121)
period: Early Bronze Age Britain
historical_setting: The stone circle's destruction is separately and precisely dated: a farmer employed by landowner James Kay sledgehammered the stones in the 1870s, with only two of the original stones still in place by an 1871 record

name: Church Grim
summary: A guardian spirit said to haunt churchyards, often appearing as a black dog. Folklore claims an animal was sometimes buried first in a new graveyard so its ghost would protect the dead.
detail:
The Church Grim is a guardian spirit of the churchyard in English and Scandinavian folklore, a being whose duty is to watch over the dead and protect the sacred ground from those who would defile it, thieves, witches, and above all the Devil. It most often appears as a large black dog, though it could take other forms, prowling the graveyard especially in foul weather and at night, and tolling the church bell at a death.

Behind the Church Grim lies a dark old belief about consecration. It was held that the first body buried in a new churchyard must stand guard over all the rest, and so be doomed to a restless vigil instead of peaceful rest. To spare a human soul this fate, the custom arose of burying an animal, most commonly a black dog, alive in the foundations or the north side of a new graveyard when it was first consecrated, so that the beast's spirit, rather than a Christian's, would become the protecting Grim. The same grim logic of the foundation-sacrifice attached to churches themselves and to other buildings.

The Church Grim is closely related to the wider British family of spectral black dogs (the Barghest, Black Shuck, Padfoot and their kin) but differs in its essentially protective role: where many phantom hounds are omens of doom, the Grim is a warden, a fierce but rightful keeper of holy ground. Sightings of a black dog about a church porch, or the sense of being watched among the graves, were long laid at its door.
earliest_record: The protective animal-burial custom believed to generate the Church Grim is documented from the 18th century onward in both England and Scandinavia; no earlier firm written record was found
period: England and Scandinavia, oral tradition of uncertain age

name: Chûn Quoit
summary: Cornwall's best-preserved Neolithic burial chamber, named from the Cornish for 'House on the Downs'. Folklore says giants hurled its massive capstone into place during a game of quoits.
detail:
Chûn Quoit stands on the wild granite moorland between Morvah and Madron in west Cornwall, a striking monument of four inward-leaning stone slabs supporting a massive convex capstone nearly four metres square. Dating to around 2400 BC, it is the best-preserved of Cornwall's Neolithic quoits, the local name for portal dolmens, and its silhouette against the sky has inspired stories for millennia. The name derives from the Cornish 'Chy Woone', meaning 'the house on the downs'.

The most enduring legend explains how such impossibly heavy capstones came to rest atop their pillars: giants, the stories say, hurled them into place while playing a game of quoits, much as humans might toss horseshoes. The giant of Chûn Quoit, known in one tradition as Old Denbras the Hurler, was said to guard the surrounding moor and ensure no one disturbed the sacred ground. Cornish folklore warns that any stones removed from a quoit will magically return to their original positions, and that whoever tampers with them will suffer a curse.

Archaeologists believe the chamber originally served as a place of excarnation, where the dead were laid upon the capstone for carrion birds to strip the flesh from their bones before the remains were gathered for communal burial. In Cornish tradition, quoits are regarded as liminal spaces, thresholds where the veil between the physical and spirit worlds grows thin. Local belief held that shamans visited such places to commune with ancestral spirits through trance and altered states of consciousness.
earliest_record: Scheduled by Historic England as part of the Chun Downs prehistoric landscape complex (list entry 1007264, covering Chûn Quoit, Chun Castle, and a nearby barrow)
period: Neolithic Cornwall
historical_setting: The giant-hurler folk explanation for the capstone's placement (and its associated taboo against moving the stones) has no independently dateable origin distinct from the monument itself

name: Cock Lane ghost
summary: A sensational 1762 haunting in London's Smithfield (scratching sounds, a ghostly presence, and accusations of murder) drew crowds, fascinated Dr Johnson, and ended with the exposure of a twelve-year-old girl producing the knockings with a piece of wood hidden in her stays.
detail:
The Cock Lane ghost was the great supernatural scandal of Georgian London. In 1762, a lodging house off Smithfield market became the centre of a haunting: scratching and knocking sounds that seemed to emanate from within the walls, reportedly making accusations against a William Kent, a lodger who had recently left, of poisoning his common-law wife, Fanny. The sounds could apparently answer yes-or-no questions by knocking.

The case drew enormous public attention. Crowds packed the narrow street; society figures and clergymen held vigils; Dr Johnson attended and took the matter seriously enough to write a report when the ghost failed to perform on command. The 'ghost' was ultimately identified as the twelve-year-old daughter of the house's owner, Richard Parsons, who was found to have hidden a piece of wood in her stays and was making the scratching sounds herself.

Parsons was convicted of conspiracy and sentenced to stand in the pillory. The affair became a byword for credulity and fraud, satirised by Hogarth in his print Credulity, Superstition, and Fanaticism. It remains one of the best-documented cases in the history of poltergeist claims: a complete record from first report to exposure, with named witnesses on every side, including several who never quite lost their unease about what they had heard.
earliest_record: A well-documented historical hoax centred on 12-year-old Elizabeth Parsons of Cock Lane, near Smithfield in London; investigated by a commission including Samuel Johnson, who concluded the scratching noises were faked by the girl. The perpetrators, including her father Richard Parsons, were convicted at Guildhall on 10 July 1762
period: Georgian London

name: Coventina
summary: A Romano-British goddess of wells and springs, especially associated with Coventina's Well near Carrawburgh on Hadrian's Wall. Offerings to her were dropped into sacred water.
detail:
Coventina was a Romano-British goddess of wells and springs, whose worship is known above all from a single remarkable site: Coventina's Well at Carrawburgh (Brocolitia), a fort on Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland. There a walled basin enclosed a natural spring sacred to her, and into its waters generations of worshippers cast their offerings. When the antiquarian John Clayton excavated the well in October 1876, it yielded an extraordinary treasure: more than twenty altars, roughly 16,000 coins, along with brooches, rings, glass, pottery, carved stones and other votive gifts, dropped into the spring as offerings to the goddess over centuries of Roman occupation.

She is shown on carved reliefs from the site as a water-nymph: a reclining female figure pouring water from a vessel, or three nymphs together, holding cups and water-plants, the imagery of a deity of flowing, life-giving and perhaps healing water. Inscriptions from the well name her and record the vows of her devotees, including soldiers of the Wall garrison drawn from across the Empire, showing how a local British spring-goddess gathered worshippers from many lands.

Coventina is one of the best examples of the intensely local water-cults of Roman Britain, deities tied not to a pantheon or a grand temple but to a single sacred spring, honoured by the simple, ancient act of casting an offering into the water. Worship at the well continued for some two centuries before it was ritually sealed and decommissioned around 388 AD, and the great hoard recovered from it nearly fifteen centuries later gives an unusually vivid picture of personal religion at the very frontier of the Roman world.
earliest_record: Coventina's Well shrine was excavated by antiquarian John Clayton in October 1876 at Carrawburgh (Brocolitia) on Hadrian's Wall, yielding over 20 altars, roughly 16,000 coins, and other votive offerings attesting continuous worship from the 2nd to 4th centuries AD. The well was ritually sealed and decommissioned c. 388 AD
period: Roman Britain

name: Craddock Moor stone circle
summary: Overgrown and reduced to sixteen fallen stones near Bodmin Moor's Hurlers, Craddock Moor may carry the name of Caradoc, a British king folded into Arthurian legend.
detail:
Half a mile north-west of the better-known Hurlers, on Bodmin Moor near Minions, lies a stone circle far less visited and far harder to find. Craddock Moor's circle has fallen entirely: sixteen stones now lie flat in the moor grass, with perhaps one broken stump still upright, the whole site so overgrown that it ranks among the trickiest on the moor to locate.

Its name may preserve an older story than its ruined state suggests. Some antiquarians have argued that "Craddock" derives from Caradoc, a British king folded into the wider cycle of Arthurian legend, though no local tale about the circle itself survives to confirm the connection. Archaeologist John Barnatt has proposed a more measurable link to the landscape: the circle appears to have been positioned so that the summit of Brown Willy, Cornwall's highest point, lines up with the sunset at midsummer.

Unusually for a Bronze Age circle, every one of Craddock Moor's stones lies flat rather than a mix of standing and fallen, a state some read as evidence the monument was pulled down deliberately or never finished. The archaeologist Christopher Tilley has argued that the circle, a nearby stone row and an embanked enclosure form what he called a "possible axis of movement" running toward the Hurlers, an alignment he considered too consistent to be chance, even though none of the sites can actually be seen from any of the others.
earliest_record: An Early-to-Middle Bronze Age stone circle, unusual among Cornish circles for having all sixteen stones recumbent; part of a wider ritual landscape with a nearby stone row and embanked enclosure, possibly aligned with the Hurlers circles and Brown Willy's midsummer sunset. Scheduled by Historic England (list entry 1010329)
period: Bronze Age Britain

name: Cŵn Annwn
summary: The spectral hounds of Annwn, the Welsh Otherworld. Their baying grows quieter as they draw nearer. Silence means they are upon you.
detail:
The Cŵn Annwn, the 'Hounds of Annwn', are the spectral hunting dogs of the Welsh Otherworld, the pack of Arawn, king of Annwn, and later in folk tradition of Gwyn ap Nudd. In the medieval texts they are creatures of fearful beauty: shining white with blood-red ears, the traditional colouring of Otherworld animals in Celtic myth, glimpsed coursing a stag through the forest in the opening of the First Branch of the Mabinogi, where their master and Pwyll first meet.

In later Welsh folklore they became darker and more dreadful, the hounds of the Wild Hunt, sweeping across the night sky and the wild uplands of Wales, especially around the Brecon Beacons and Cadair Idris, as a portent of death. To hear them was to know that a soul was soon to be gathered. Their most uncanny trait is the way their cry behaves: the baying of the Cŵn Annwn sounds loudest when the pack is far off and grows fainter as they draw near, so that a distant howl is the true warning and a near-silent whisper means they are almost upon you.

They belong to the wide British and European family of phantom hunting hounds (kin to the Gabriel Hounds, the Wisht Hounds of Dartmoor and Dando's Dogs) but keep their distinctly Welsh character as the hounds of Annwn, escorting the dead to the Otherworld. With the coming of Christianity they were sometimes recast as hell-hounds, but their oldest role is gentler and stranger: the psychopomp pack of a king of the dead.
earliest_record: First Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed', composed c.1060-1120; earliest surviving manuscripts are the White Book of Rhydderch (c.1350) and Red Book of Hergest (c.1382-c.1410).
period: Medieval Wales (Mabinogi composition, 11th-12th century)

name: Dando's Dogs
summary: A spectral hunt led by the wicked priest Dando, doomed to ride forever with infernal hounds after refusing to give up his game to the Devil.
detail:
Dando and his dogs are a Cornish form of the Wild Hunt, a cautionary tale of a worldly, hard-hunting priest of the parish of St Germans who cared more for the chase and his pleasures than for his calling. Hunting one Sunday and crying that he would go to hell itself for a drink if none could be found on earth, Dando was answered: a dark stranger appeared, handed him a draught, and when the priest's hounds turned snarling on the newcomer, the stranger swept up Dando and his whole pack onto his black horse and plunged with them into the river and away.

Ever since, the country folk said, Dando and his dogs may be heard on stormy nights sweeping across the Cornish sky and moors in a spectral hunt, the baying of the hounds carrying on the wind. Collected by the Cornish folklorist Robert Hunt in his 'Popular Romances of the West of England' (1865), Dando's Dogs is Cornwall's own telling of the demon huntsman carried off for his impiety, a local strand of the great European Wild Hunt tradition.
earliest_record: Robert Hunt, 'Popular Romances of the West of England' (Second Series, 1865).
period: Recorded in the Victorian Cornish folklore revival; narrative setting is unspecified but implicitly pre-modern (a hunting parish priest)

name: Devil's Arrows
summary: Three great standing stones near Boroughbridge, said to have been hurled by the Devil at the town of Aldborough. He missed, which is exactly the kind of thing folklore remembers forever.
detail:
The Devil's Arrows are a row of three huge prehistoric standing stones near Boroughbridge in North Yorkshire, gritstone monoliths up to some seven metres tall and deeply weathered into long vertical grooves at their tops, among the most impressive Bronze Age monuments in the north of England. The stones were quarried from Plumpton Rocks, some fifteen kilometres away, and may originally have formed part of a larger alignment of as many as five stones, of which two are now lost. Their great size and the strange fluting of their summits invited explanation, and folklore supplied it in the figure of the Devil.

The legend tells that the Devil, in a fury against the nearby town (usually the old Roman settlement of Aldborough), hurled these great stones at it to destroy it, launching them like arrows or bolts from a hill some miles off (in some versions How Hill or Howe Hill). But his aim was poor: the mighty missiles fell short and stuck fast in the ground where they now stand, missing the town entirely. The deep grooves down the stones are pointed to as the very marks of the Devil's fingers, scored into the rock as he gripped and flung them.

Such 'the Devil threw it' tales cluster around great prehistoric stones across Britain, where the medieval and later imagination, unable to credit human hands with raising such monuments, attributed them to giants or to the Devil, and explained any oddity of form as the mark of his touch. The Devil's Arrows, with their fingered grooves and their story of a misjudged throw at Aldborough, are among the finest examples of the type, folklore growing up to account for stones whose true makers had been forgotten.
earliest_record: The stones are scheduled and recorded by Historic England (list entry 1014705); archaeological dating places stone alignments of this type between the Late Neolithic and Middle Bronze Age (c.2500-1000 BC)
period: Late Neolithic to Bronze Age Britain (monument construction). The 'Devil's throw' folk explanation has no independently dateable origin of its own
historical_setting: The stones were quarried from Plumpton Rocks approximately 15km away, and may originally have formed part of a larger alignment of up to five stones

name: Ding Dong mines
summary: An ancient Cornish mining landscape with traditions connecting it to Joseph of Arimathea and old tin-working lore. Mine country often births knockers, hidden spirits, and stories of wealth beneath the hill.
detail:
The Ding Dong mines lie in the high granite moorland of West Penwith near Madron, in the far west of Cornwall, an ancient and atmospheric tin-mining landscape dominated by the ruined engine houses of the old workings. Reputed to be among the very oldest mines in Cornwall, worked (it was said) since prehistoric times, the antiquity of Ding Dong gathered to it one of the most remarkable legends in Cornish tradition: that it was visited by Jesus Christ himself.

The legend grows from the real ancient trade in Cornish tin, which reached the Mediterranean world long before the Roman conquest. Folk tradition held that Joseph of Arimathea (the wealthy man of the Gospels, here imagined as a tin-merchant trading with Cornwall) came to these mines, and that on one voyage he brought with him the boy Jesus, who walked among the tinners and spoke to them. Cornish miners of the Victorian age still repeated the belief in the mine's fabulous age; one old miner declared that only Dolcoath was older than Ding Dong, 'which was worked before the time of Jesus Christ'.

Like all Cornish mines, Ding Dong was also the domain of the Knockers, the small mine-spirits whose tapping in the workings might warn of danger or lead to rich lodes, and who expected their due of respect. Between the Knockers in the dark below and the wondrous tale of Joseph and the young Jesus above, the Ding Dong mines hold a special place in Cornish folklore, their great age made the seedbed of a legend that reached all the way to the Holy Land.
earliest_record: Sources disagree on the mine's own earliest documentary reference, one attributing it to the Elizabethan surveyor John Norden (active c.1584-1600), another placing the earliest reference at 'the beginning of the 18th century'. The two accounts have not been reconciled.
period: The Joseph of Arimathea/young Jesus tradition attached to the mine is not independently dated by any source found; it likely belongs to the wider 19th-century 'Jesus in Britain' mystical tradition associated with Glastonbury and popularised alongside William Blake's 'Jerusalem' (1804-08), though this specific Ding Dong telling was not traced to a first written appearance

name: Doom Bar
summary: A dangerous sandbar at the mouth of the River Camel, linked to the Mermaid of Padstow. In legend, a dying mermaid cursed the harbour after being shot, raising the bar to wreck ships forever.
detail:
The Doom Bar is a treacherous bank of sand stretching across the mouth of the Camel estuary near Padstow in north Cornwall, a real and deadly hazard that has wrecked countless ships over the centuries, and Cornish legend explains its existence as a mermaid's dying curse. In the story a local man, out shooting near Hawker's Cove, saw a beautiful young woman in the water and either fell to talking with her or, in the harsher versions, shot her, only to discover too late that she was a mermaid of Padstow, the guardian spirit of the harbour, whose presence had kept its waters deep and safe.

Mortally wounded and enraged at the betrayal, the dying mermaid pronounced a curse upon the harbour she had once protected: she swore that Padstow should have a bar of doom, a barren bank of sand that would choke the river-mouth and bring death and ruin to its shipping. As she sank beneath the waves a great storm rose, and when it cleared the Doom Bar had appeared across the estuary, where it has lain ever since, shifting and lethal, ending the days when great ships could ride safely into the once-prosperous port.

The legend is a classic example of folklore grown up to account for a genuine and dangerous feature of the landscape, the sandbar's grim toll of shipwrecks given a tragic supernatural cause. The Doom Bar remains a byword on the Cornish coast, its name now also carried far and wide by a popular ale, though its origin lies in a drowned mermaid's last, vengeful breath.
earliest_record: Enys Tregarthen's 1906 published version is the earliest specifically dated written source located; Robert Hunt's 'Popular Romances of the West of England' (1865) covers extensive Padstow-area mermaid and Doom Bar folklore and likely predates it, though the mermaid-curse telling given here has not been confirmed in Hunt's text
period: Recorded in the Victorian and Edwardian Cornish folklore-collecting tradition (1865-1906)

name: Dozmary Pool
summary: A lonely pool on Bodmin Moor, often named as one of the places where Arthur's sword Excalibur was returned to the Lady of the Lake. It is also tied to ghostly and infernal stories.
detail:
Dozmary Pool is a lonely, reed-fringed lake high on Bodmin Moor in Cornwall, a still sheet of water in a bare and windswept landscape that has drawn legend to it for centuries. Its most famous association is Arthurian: Dozmary is one of the waters claimed as the home of the Lady of the Lake, and the place where, after the last battle, the dying Arthur commanded Sir Bedivere to cast away the sword Excalibur, where a hand rose from the pool to catch the blade, brandish it, and draw it under. The pool was long reputed to be bottomless, which suited its role as a doorway to the Otherworld.

Dozmary's other great legend is darker. It is bound to the ghost of Jan Tregeagle, a wicked 17th-century steward and magistrate of fearsome local memory, whose soul was conjured back from the dead to give evidence in a lawsuit and then could not be got rid of. To keep him from Hell and out of mischief, Tregeagle was set an impossible, eternal penance at Dozmary Pool: to empty the bottomless lake using only a leaking limpet shell. There he labours still, in the telling, until the howling of the moorland storms, when the demons come for him and he flees across the moor with the hounds of Hell at his heels, his shrieks heard on the wind.

In reality the pool is not bottomless (it has been known to dry out in times of drought), but its bleak isolation and its double burden of legend, Arthurian and infernal, have made it one of the most atmospheric and storied spots on Bodmin Moor.
earliest_record: Robert Hunt's 'Popular Romances of the West of England' (First Series, 1865) contains dedicated sections on 'The Demon Tregeagle', 'Jan Tregeagle the Steward', and 'Dozmary Pool', making it the earliest firmly confirmed written source for this specific legend pairing
period: The historical Jan Tregeagle was a real 17th-century steward to Lord Robartes of Lanhydrock, later a magistrate; the supernatural legend was well established in Cornish oral tradition by the time Hunt recorded it in 1865
historical_setting: The Arthurian Excalibur association is a separate and undateable strand. Dozmary is one of several Bodmin Moor and Welsh/English lakes claimed as the sword's resting place, with no specific first record for this particular attribution found

name: Dragon Hill, Uffington
summary: A low chalk hill below the Uffington White Horse, said to be where Saint George slew the dragon. The bare chalk patch on top marks where the dragon's blood poisoned the grass.
detail:
Dragon Hill is a curious flat-topped natural knoll standing just below the great prehistoric chalk figure of the Uffington White Horse, on the Berkshire Downs in Oxfordshire. Its most striking feature is a bare patch of white chalk on its summit where, despite the surrounding turf, no grass will grow, and folklore has long fixed on this barren scar with a famous explanation: it is the place where Saint George slew the dragon, and where the dragon's poisonous blood, spilling out as it died, soured the ground forever so that nothing green can cover it. The hill's earliest written mention is John Aubrey's Monumenta Britannica (1670), which discusses the mound as a possible burial site rather than confirming the dragon legend, and the specific story of St George cannot itself predate his adoption as England's patron saint in the 14th century.

The legend ties England's patron saint and his dragon-slaying directly into this ancient ritual landscape, recasting the prehistoric monuments around it as the setting for the saint's great deed. The nearby White Horse, itself thousands of years old and of uncertain original meaning, was sometimes reinterpreted not as a horse at all but as the very dragon St George fought, or as a memorial of the victory, folklore weaving the older pagan figures into the Christian story.

Dragon Hill sits within one of the richest concentrations of legend-laden monuments in England, alongside the White Horse, the Iron Age hillfort of Uffington Castle, and the Neolithic tomb of Wayland's Smithy a little along the ridge. Together they form a landscape where prehistoric earthwork, pagan tradition and Christian saint-legend overlap, and the bald chalk crown of Dragon Hill keeps the memory of St George's dragon pinned to the Oxfordshire downs.
period: The St George legend attached to this hill cannot predate George's adoption as England's patron saint in the 14th century; John Aubrey's 'Monumenta Britannica' (1670) is the earliest written reference to Dragon Hill located, though it discusses the mound as a possible burial site rather than confirming the dragon-slaying legend specifically
historical_setting: The hill itself is a natural chalk knoll, its summit artificially flattened at an unknown date, possibly during the Iron Age contemporary with the nearby Uffington White Horse (c.1000 BC)

name: Dragon of Mordiford
summary: A girl named Maud is said to have found a tiny serpent and raised it in secret until it grew into a dragon. It took to the hills above Mordiford, feeding on livestock and men while sparing only her.
detail:
The Dragon of Mordiford is one of the best-known of the English dragon legends, attached to the Herefordshire village of Mordiford where the River Lugg meets the Wye. The story begins tenderly: a young girl named Maud found a beautiful little creature in the woods, no bigger than a cucumber, brilliantly coloured, and took it home as a pet and hid it. Despite her family's alarm she fed and cared for it, and the creature thrived, and grew, and kept growing, until it was a full-sized dragon that could no longer be hidden and took itself off to live in the wooded hills above the village, on Mordiford's 'Dragon's Walk'.

As it grew the dragon turned to preying on the countryside, devouring cattle and sheep and at last human victims, terrorising the whole district, yet it never harmed Maud, the girl who had raised it, sparing her alone out of its old affection. The villagers lived in dread until a champion came forward to destroy the beast. In the most popular version the dragon-slayer (sometimes named as a condemned criminal promised his freedom, sometimes as a member of the local Garston family) hid inside a cider barrel set by the river where the dragon came to drink, and shot or speared it through the bung-hole as it approached, killing the monster, though in some tellings he too died from its venomous dying breath.

For centuries a great painted image of a green dragon adorned the west end of Mordiford church, said to commemorate the legend, until it was removed in the early 19th century. The tale, with its poignant detail of the girl whose pet outgrew all bounds and the dragon that spared only her, remains among the most vivid of Britain's dragon stories.
earliest_record: Thomas Blount observed the dragon/serpent image on Mordiford church's west wall in 1670; contemporaries Thomas Dingley and John Aubrey independently described the same feature around the same time. Earlier partial mentions of the folktale appear in Samuel Ireland (1797) and George Lipscomb (1799); the first full written narrative is James Dacre Devlin's account of 1848
period: Attested in print from 1670 (the church image) through to 1848 (the full narrative); the image itself was destroyed in an 1811 church renovation

name: Dragon of Wantley
summary: A comic Yorkshire dragon from ballad tradition, slain by More of More Hall after being kicked in its vulnerable backside. It is dragon-slaying with muddy boots and tavern laughter.
detail:
The Dragon of Wantley is a Yorkshire dragon-legend best remembered through a rollicking seventeenth-century comic ballad. A fearsome winged, many-toothed beast, it terrorises the district of Wantley (Wharncliffe, near Sheffield), devouring trees, cattle, children and buildings alike, until the desperate people beg the help of a hard-drinking local champion, More of More Hall.

More has a special suit of spiked armour made and lies in wait; in the ballad's famously irreverent climax he despatches the dragon not with sword or lance but with a well-aimed kick to its one vulnerable spot, its backside, whereupon the beast spins round and dies. The story first appeared as an anonymous comic broadside ballad in 1685, was republished in Bishop Thomas Percy's 'Reliques of Ancient English Poetry' (1765), and was turned into a hit comic opera in 1737. It was widely read as a satire on a real local lawsuit over tithes, the 'dragon' standing in for a grasping landlord. Mock-heroic and merry, the Dragon of Wantley is the great comic counterpoint to Britain's many solemn dragon-slayings.
earliest_record: An anonymous comic broadside ballad of 1685 is the original form of the story, later republished in Bishop Thomas Percy's 'Reliques of Ancient English Poetry' (1765) and adapted into a comic opera in 1737
period: Restoration England (1685); popularised in the 18th century via opera and Percy's anthology

name: The Dullahan
summary: A headless horseman carrying his own severed head, which glows like a lantern. Where the Dullahan stops and calls your name, you die. No lock or gate can bar his passage.
detail:
The Dullahan rides the night roads of Ireland as a harbinger of death, a headless horseman carrying his own severed head, which he holds aloft or sets upon his saddle, a head with a hideous grinning face the colour and texture of mouldy cheese, and eyes that dart about ceaselessly, glowing with an unearthly light by which the rider sees his way, sometimes said to be used as a lantern. Few figures in Irish folklore are as feared. In many tellings he drives a black coach, the cóiste bodhar or 'death coach', drawn by black horses, its trappings made from grisly materials (a spine for a whip, human bones, a shroud-cloth).

Where the Dullahan halts his ride and calls out a name, the person named will die; for the calling of the name is itself the summons of death, and no door, lock or gate can bar the Dullahan's way, and all fly open before him. He is implacable and not to be watched: those who spy on his passage may be lashed blind by his bone whip or have a basin of blood flung over them, marking them as the next to die. Only one thing is said to give him pause: gold. A piece of gold, even a small one, will frighten the Dullahan away, the single weakness in an otherwise unstoppable terror.

The Dullahan belongs to the same family of death-omens as the banshee in Irish tradition, an embodiment of death come riding rather than wailing. Popularised in the 19th-century folklore collections, he has ridden on into modern imagination, and stands behind many a later headless-horseman tale.
earliest_record: The earliest substantial written documentation is in Thomas Crofton Croker's Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland, Part II (1828; Part I published 1825), which devotes a chapter to the Dullahan containing four stories and a ballad, with Croker's own commentary on the name's etymology (from Irish dubh, 'black/dark').
period: Attested in print from the early-to-mid 19th century; believed to reflect older Irish oral tradition
cultural_tradition: Irish folklore

name: Dunnie
summary: A shape-shifting Northumbrian spirit that often appears as a horse or donkey. It delights in tricks, carrying riders only to vanish and dump them into mud or water.
detail:
The Hazelrigg Dunnie is a shape-shifting bogle of Northumberland, haunting the country around Belford and the crags near Hazelrigg. Like the Border bogles generally, it was a creature of mischief rather than real malice, but its favourite trick was a cruel one. It would take the shape of a horse and offer itself to be saddled; the moment the rider or ploughman mounted, the Dunnie would vanish, dropping its victim into the mud or the burn and braying with laughter from a safe distance.

The folklorist William Henderson, drawing on an account from a clergyman who knew the area, recorded two particular tricks that became attached to the Dunnie's name. In one, a farmer saddling up to fetch the midwife found his horse carried both riders safely to their errand, only to vanish in the mire on the way home, leaving them stranded in the dark. In the other, a ploughman who thought he had caught his own horse got only as far as buckling on the harness before it slapped to the ground and the Dunnie bolted off laughing, transformed back to its true shape.

It was blamed for leading travellers astray, miscalling the hours, and meddling with the farm work. Tradition tied it especially to a cave in the Hazelrigg crags, where it was said to wander chanting a mournful, half-nonsensical verse about a lost key and hidden treasure: 'Cocken heugh there's gear enough, / Collier heugh there's mair, / For I've lost the key o' the Bounders, / An' I'm ruined for evermair.' Henderson read this as the ghost of a Border reiver mourning plunder he buried and died before he could recover, the Dunnie's endless haunting explained as a dead man's grief rather than simple mischief. The Dunnie is a fine example of the trickster-spirit of the Anglo-Scottish border, half practical joker, half ghost.
earliest_record: The Denham Tracts, a collection of pamphlets published by Michael Aislabie Denham between 1846 and 1859, and William Henderson's 'Notes on the Folk-lore of the Northern Counties of England and the Borders' both document the Hazelrigg Dunnie
period: Recorded in the mid-19th-century Northumbrian folklore-collecting tradition (1846-1859)
cultural_tradition: The reiver-ghost strand of the legend (Dunnie as the restless spirit of a Border reiver who died before recovering hidden plunder) is a distinct localising addition on top of the more general shape-shifting-horse bogle motif

name: Dunstan and the Devil
summary: Saint Dunstan was said to have seized the Devil by the nose with blacksmith's tongs. The tale explains horseshoes as protection and gives English folklore one of its best infernal workplace accidents.
detail:
Saint Dunstan (c. 909-988) was one of the towering figures of Anglo-Saxon England: Abbot of Glastonbury, Archbishop of Canterbury, reformer of the English Church and adviser to kings. But in folk memory he is best remembered for a homely and comic legend in which he got the better of the Devil himself. Before his rise to high office Dunstan was a skilled craftsman and metalworker, and folklore made him a blacksmith, working at his forge, and it is at the forge that his famous encounter takes place.

The story tells that the Devil came to tempt the saint, in some versions disguised, in others openly, or even (in a bawdier telling) appearing as a beautiful woman whose cloven hoof gave the game away. Dunstan, seeing through the disguise, seized the Devil's nose in a pair of red-hot blacksmith's tongs straight from the fire and held him fast, twisting and burning, while the Devil roared and begged for release. Only when the Devil promised never to enter a place where a horseshoe was hung did Dunstan let him go.

This is the folk-explanation for one of the most enduring of English superstitions: the horseshoe nailed above the door for luck and protection, said to keep the Devil out because of the bargain wrung from him by Dunstan's tongs. The tale, gleefully retold for a thousand years, gives English folklore one of its finest images (the saintly smith catching the Devil by the nose) and a domestic charm still seen on doorways across the country. Dunstan's chief seat at Glastonbury anchors the legend in Somerset.
earliest_record: Osbern of Canterbury's 'Vita S. Dunstani' (c.1090) is the first surviving text to tell the tongs-and-nose story, roughly a century after Dunstan's own death in 988; two earlier Lives of Dunstan existed but did not include this episode
period: Anglo-Norman England (hagiography composition, late 11th century); Dunstan's own lifetime was 909-988

name: Enfield Poltergeist
summary: Britain's most famous modern haunting: flying furniture, ghostly knockings, and a gruff old man's voice issuing from eleven-year-old Janet Hodgson at an Enfield council house, 1977-79.
detail:
The Enfield poltergeist is the most famous British haunting of the twentieth century, reported between 1977 and 1979 at a council house at 284 Green Street in Enfield, north London. The Hodgson family (a single mother and her four children) described knockings, furniture that slid and overturned, objects that flew across rooms, and above all phenomena centred on eleven-year-old Janet: levitations, and a gruff old man's voice said to issue from her.

The case drew investigators from the Society for Psychical Research, notably Maurice Grosse and Guy Lyon Playfair, whose long vigils produced photographs and tape recordings that believers held to be compelling and sceptics dismissed as a mixture of trickery by the children and the suggestibility of the watchers. Playfair set down the fullest account in his 1980 book 'This House Is Haunted', drawing on Grosse's contemporaneous case notes and roughly 600 pages of tape transcripts made during the investigation itself, still the primary published record of what the family, Grosse and Playfair say took place at Green Street.

Never resolved either way, Enfield became a touchstone in the British argument over the reality of poltergeists, and its fame has only grown through books, documentaries and films that have made the Green Street house a modern legend.
earliest_record: Guy Lyon Playfair's 'This House Is Haunted' (1980, Stein and Day/Scarborough House) is the primary published account, drawing on Maurice Grosse's contemporaneous investigation notes and roughly 600 pages of tape transcripts made during the case itself
period: Late-1970s London; the case remains a touchstone in British parapsychology discourse to the present

name: Epona
summary: A Celtic horse goddess worshipped across the Roman world, including Britain. She protected horses, riders, cavalry, and journeys, often shown with mares, foals, or a cornucopia.
detail:
Epona was the great horse-goddess of the Celtic world, and one of the very few Celtic deities to be taken up so warmly by the Romans that her worship spread right across the Empire, carried above all by the cavalry, who honoured her as the protector of horses, mules and the men who rode and tended them. Her name derives from the Gaulish word for horse, and she is almost always shown in her company: seated side-saddle on a mare, flanked by horses or by foals, or feeding them from a dish, and frequently holding a cornucopia or basket of fruit, marking her also as a goddess of plenty, fertility and abundance.

In Roman Britain Epona was honoured at cavalry forts and stables, with dedications known from key bases including Chester and Caerleon, wherever mounted units were stationed. Uniquely among Celtic deities she was even given a feast day in the Roman calendar, a measure of how thoroughly her cult was embraced. Her care extended beyond the living horse to the journey of the soul, and some evidence links her with guiding and protecting the dead on their final ride.

Epona's deep importance to a horse-keeping people carried into the insular Celtic traditions: scholars have long seen her shadow behind the Welsh Rhiannon, who appears riding an unovertakable horse and is bound up with sovereignty and with horses, and behind the Irish horse-and-sovereignty goddesses. As the divine guardian of the horse, an animal central to war, travel, farming and status in the ancient world, Epona was among the most beloved and far-travelled of all the Celtic gods.
earliest_record: A lead tablet from Rom (Deux-Sèvres, France), dated to the late 1st century BC, is the oldest known Epona inscription, recording a bilingual Gaulish-Latin ritual sacrifice invoking her alongside other deities
period: Late Iron Age Gaul (earliest attestation); peak Roman-era cult activity 1st-3rd century AD, with literary references persisting to around 525 AD
historical_setting: In Britain, inscriptions are known from key cavalry bases including Chester and Caerleon

name: Fairy Bridge
summary: A small Isle of Man bridge where travellers traditionally greet the fairies as they pass. Failing to acknowledge the Little People is considered unlucky, especially on journeys across the island.
detail:
The Fairy Bridge is a small, unremarkable-looking road bridge on the Isle of Man, crossing the Santon Burn on the main road between Douglas and Castletown, and yet it is one of the most observed sites of living folk custom in the British Isles. Manx tradition holds that the bridge is a haunt of the Themselves (the fairies, or 'Little People', whom the islanders have always been careful never to name directly or offend) and that anyone crossing it should greet them politely to ensure good luck and a safe journey.

The custom is remarkably persistent. To this day many Manx people, and visitors who have learned the tradition, will offer a greeting as they pass over the bridge: 'Laa mie' (good day) in Manx Gaelic, or simply 'Hello, fairies'. It is widely held that to cross without acknowledging the Little People risks bad luck, a spoilt journey, or worse.

The custom reflects the deep and characteristic Manx attitude to the fairies: a careful, respectful wariness toward an unseen people who must be placated rather than provoked, neither openly named nor lightly mocked. (Folklorists note that the modern roadside bridge may not be the 'true' original fairy bridge, an older crossing lying elsewhere, but it is here that the tradition has fixed itself.) The Fairy Bridge is a rare case of a folk custom still practised daily, a courtesy to the Little People exchanged on a busy island road.
period: No written record of the fairy-greeting custom at this specific bridge predates 1800. John Bullock's 'A History of the Isle of Man' (1816) describes the nearby crossing as the 'Devil's Bridge', a place of ill-omen to be avoided. That is the opposite valence from the modern fairy-greeting custom, and not the same tradition. According to Yvonne Cresswell, former social history curator at Manx National Heritage, the greeting custom in its now-familiar form appears to date from around 1997-98, coinciding with a documented sharp increase in visitor awareness of it, with wider promotion during the island's tourism boom in the 20th century

name: Fat Lips
summary: Fat Lips is the guardian spirit of Dryburgh Abbey's ruins in the Scottish Borders, said to keep the vaults dry by treading the floors in heavy iron shoes.
detail:
Fat Lips was the guardian spirit, or brownie, of the romantic ruins of Dryburgh Abbey in Berwickshire, in the Scottish Borders, a curious and rather melancholy figure recorded by Sir Walter Scott, who knew the Borders and its lore intimately and lies buried at Dryburgh himself. The spirit took its odd name from its appearance, and was bound to the abbey ruins as their resident sprite, a lingering supernatural presence among the broken arches and old graves.

The tale Scott preserved gives Fat Lips a poignant human dimension. The 'spirit' was, in the telling, associated with a real recluse, a woman who, having lost her lover, withdrew from the world and lived for many years hidden among the vaults and ruins of Dryburgh Abbey, emerging only by night and shunning all human company. To the local people, her shadowy night-time figure flitting among the ruins became the abbey's resident brownie or bogle, and the name Fat Lips attached to the spirit said to haunt the place. It was said that Fat Lips kept the vaults dry by treading the damp floors with heavy iron shoes.

Fat Lips is a small but characteristic piece of Border folklore, blending the widespread belief in a guardian brownie attached to an old or holy site with the local memory of a real, tragic hermit. It is the kind of story in which a flesh-and-blood recluse fades, over the retellings, into the resident ghost or fairy of a ruin. Set among the beautiful, ivied ruins of Dryburgh, it gives the abbey a wistful spirit of its own.
earliest_record: The earliest reported sighting comes from a widow sheltering in the abbey vaults in the aftermath of the 1745 Jacobite Rising; Sir Walter Scott recorded the legend in 'Ballads and Lyrical Pieces' (1806)
period: 18th-century Scottish Borders (first sighting); recorded in print during the early-19th-century Romantic antiquarian revival (1806)

name: Finfolk
summary: Powerful sea-sorcerers of Orcadian folklore who move between the underwater realm of Finfolkaheem and the vanishing island of Hildaland. They steal mortals for spouses and servants.
detail:
The Finfolk are the dark sorcerers of the sea in Orcadian folklore, a mysterious, amphibious race of powerful and sinister beings who dwell beneath the waves and come ashore to work their will on the islanders. Gloomy, grasping and skilled in magic, they were among the most feared of all the supernatural peoples of Orkney, for their great vice was the abduction of mortals: a Finman or Finwife would carry off a human husband, wife or servant to live with them beneath the sea, and many an Orkney tale tells of a young person snatched from the shore or the boat by the Finfolk and lost to their kin forever.

The Finfolk lived between two homes. In winter they dwelt in Finfolkaheem, their splendid city on the sea-bed, a place of crystal halls and gardens of waving sea-plants lit by the glimmer of the deep. In summer they came up to Hildaland (or Hether Blether), a magical vanishing island (one of the enchanted 'disappearing isles' of Orkney lore) which could be seen on the horizon but never reached, fading away as a boat approached. A famous tale tells how the island was at last won from the Finfolk and made fast by a determined farmer, becoming the island of Eynhallow, the 'holy isle', from which the Finfolk were driven by salt and faith.

The Finwife, in particular, was dreaded: a Finman's wife was said to lose her beauty as she aged and was set to drudgery, and was always seeking mortal gold, for a Finwife who could win a human husband would keep her beauty. Distinct from the gentler selkies and the mermaids, the Finfolk are the malign magicians of the Orkney sea, proud, covetous and dangerous, a whole hidden civilisation beneath the northern waters.
earliest_record: Walter Traill Dennison's 'The Orcadian Sketch-Book' (1880), written partly in Orkney dialect, is the earliest substantial written collection of Finfolk lore located
period: Recorded in the late-Victorian Orcadian folklore-collecting tradition (1880)

name: Fingal
summary: Under his Scottish name, Fionn mac Cumhaill built a causeway to Ireland to fight his rival, then tore it apart in fright. Fingal's Cave and the Giant's Causeway are what's left of it.
detail:
Fingal is the name under which the great Gaelic hero Fionn mac Cumhaill passes into Scottish tradition, especially in the western Highlands and Islands, popularised across Europe by James Macpherson's 1762 epic poem 'Fingal', part of his controversial Ossian cycle, which made 'Fingal' a king of Morven. In the older folk legend he is a giant, and to him is credited the building of the Giant's Causeway, the great colonnade of basalt that runs out into the sea off Antrim.

The famous tale tells how Fingal built the causeway to cross to Scotland and fight his rival, the giant Benandonner; but seeing how huge his enemy was, he let his wife disguise him as a baby in a cradle. When Benandonner saw the size of the 'infant', he fled in terror at the thought of its father, tearing up the causeway behind him so the two could never meet, which is why only its ends remain, at the Antrim shore and at the island of Staffa, where the matching basalt columns frame Fingal's Cave. The cave's strange natural acoustics and grandeur later inspired Mendelssohn's celebrated overture.
earliest_record: James Macpherson's 'Fingal, an Ancient Epic Poem, in Six Books' (London, 1762), part of his controversial Ossian cycle, is the text that popularised the Scottish name 'Fingal' and its associated Giant's Causeway/Fingal's Cave legend across Europe
period: 18th-century Scottish literary revival (1760-63, the main Ossian publications)

name: Fintan's Grave
summary: The Arra Mountains near Lough Derg hold Fintan's Grave, resting place of Ireland's oldest witness, who outlived the Flood as a salmon, an eagle, and a hawk before living on for millennia.
detail:
Fintan's Grave is a mythological cave or site on the mountain of Tul Tuinde ('the hill of the wave') in the Arra Mountains near Lough Derg, associated with Fintan mac Bóchra, one of the most extraordinary figures of Irish legendary history. Fintan is the great survivor of Irish myth: he is said to have come to Ireland before the Biblical Flood, with the company of Cessair, the very first settlers, and to have lived on, alone or transformed, through all the ages that followed.

When the Flood came and drowned all the rest, Fintan survived. In the tradition he was changed into a salmon, and later an eagle and a hawk, before regaining human form, and so lived for thousands of years through every successive invasion and settlement of Ireland, from the days before the Deluge down to the coming of Christianity. Because he had seen it all, Fintan became the supreme witness and rememberer, the living repository of the whole history and lore of Ireland, summoned in legend to recount the events of the ages no other living being could recall.

The place named as his grave, where the ancient witness at last lay down, fixes this vast mythological figure to the landscape near Lough Derg. Fintan belongs to the same family of Irish 'oldest beings' as the ancient animals questioned in other tales, and embodies a profound theme of Irish myth: the unbroken memory of the land, carried through flood and ages by a single deathless witness, so that nothing of the old knowledge should ever be wholly lost.
earliest_record: Fintan mac Bóchra's story belongs to the Lebor Gabála Érenn tradition, with the earliest manuscript witness in Lebor na hUidre (c.1100) and the fuller recension in the Book of Leinster (c.1160)
period: Early Medieval Ireland (manuscript compilation, late 11th-12th century)

name: Folkestone White Horse
summary: England's youngest white horse was cut into the Kent chalk in 2003 by Gurkha soldiers and volunteers, a millennium landmark inspired by the ancient Uffington Horse and the fort on Horse Hill below.
detail:
The Folkestone White Horse stretches ninety metres across Cheriton Hill, overlooking the English terminal of the Channel Tunnel. Designed by local artist Charlie Newington and inspired by both the ancient White Horse of Uffington and a nearby Iron Age fort on a ridge known as Horse Hill, it is the youngest hill figure in England, completed in June 2003 as a millennium landmark intended to regenerate the Folkestone area.

The project was born in controversy. Planning permission was first sought in April 1998, but English Nature, the Green Party, and Friends of the Earth opposed it: the hillside was protected under the European Habitats Directive as a Site of Special Scientific Interest. The horse was finally approved in March 2002 by the Secretary of State, who ruled that its ‘emotional and symbolic value’ outweighed the possible environmental damage. Construction was completed entirely by hand: volunteers staked out a canvas template directed by the artist via radio, dug shallow trenches into the topsoil, and filled them with limestone slabs.

A team of locally based Gurkha soldiers spent seven days cutting and positioning the stones. A time capsule containing the names and remarks of supporters was buried at the point marking the horse’s heart. In 2004, the Friends of the Folkestone White Horse was formed to maintain the figure, which requires periodic weeding to keep the chalk visible against the advancing grass.
earliest_record: Planning permission first sought April 1998; approved by the Secretary of State March 2002; construction completed June 2003
period: Contemporary Britain (millennium-landmark project, 1998-2003)

name: Glastonbury Tor
summary: The sacred hill rising from the Somerset Levels, said to be the Isle of Avalon where Arthur was carried after his final battle. Beneath it lies the entrance to Annwn, the Celtic otherworld, ruled by Gwyn ap Nudd.
detail:
Glastonbury Tor rises 158 metres from the flat expanse of the Somerset Levels, a terraced conical hill crowned by the roofless tower of the medieval Church of St Michael. A millennium ago, when the water table was higher and the surrounding marshes flooded regularly, the Tor would have appeared as an island, and it is this island character that anchors its identification with Avalon, the place where King Arthur was carried after his mortal wounding at the Battle of Camlann. Geoffrey of Monmouth named Avalon the ‘Isle of Apples’ and described it as a place of healing presided over by Morgan le Fay; later writers, including the monks of Glastonbury Abbey, cemented the connection by claiming to have discovered Arthur’s grave in the abbey grounds in 1191.

But the Tor’s mythology runs deeper than Arthur. In Welsh tradition it is the palace of Gwyn ap Nudd, Lord of Annwn, the Celtic otherworld, a realm parallel to the living world where the dead and the fair folk coexist. A hidden cave beneath the hill is said to open into Annwn, and those who enter may find the Cauldron of Rebirth but will struggle to return. St Collen, a sixth-century Welsh saint, is said to have descended into the Tor and confronted Gwyn ap Nudd in his fairy court, flinging holy water at the assembled spirits until they vanished and left him standing alone on the bare hillside.

The terraces that spiral around the Tor’s slopes have been interpreted by some researchers as the remains of a Neolithic processional labyrinth, a ceremonial path winding seven times around the hill to the summit. Whether this interpretation is correct or the terraces are simply medieval strip lynchets, they give the Tor an unmistakable sense of deliberate shaping. The ruined tower of St Michael’s at the summit dates from the fourteenth century, built to replace an earlier church destroyed by earthquake in 1275. The National Trust, which manages the site, records that Glastonbury Tor remains one of the most visited sacred landscapes in Britain.
origin_date: 1135-1139 (Geoffrey of Monmouth names Avalon); 1191 (Glastonbury Abbey monks' claimed discovery of Arthur's grave, the event that cemented the Tor/Avalon identification specifically)
earliest_record: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1135-1139) is the earliest text to name and describe Avalon; the 1191 grave discovery at Glastonbury Abbey is the earliest firm link of that Avalon to this specific site
period: High Medieval England (literary naming of Avalon, 1135-39; site identification confirmed 1191)
historical_setting: The St Collen/Gwyn ap Nudd episode is a separate Welsh tradition whose own earliest written record has not been confirmed

name: Gogmagog
summary: The last of the giants of Albion, said to have roamed Cornwall before being cast into the sea by the Trojan hero Corineus. Effigies of Gog and Magog still march in the Lord Mayor's Show, ancient guardians of the City of London.
detail:
Gogmagog is the last and greatest of the giants of Albion in the legendary history of Britain set down by Geoffrey of Monmouth. Before the coming of Brutus and his Trojans, the island was said to be held by a race of giants, of whom Gogmagog, twelve cubits tall and able to uproot oaks as though they were hazel wands, was the champion. When the Trojans landed in the west and the giants fell upon them, it was the Trojan Corineus, who delighted in wrestling giants, who took up the challenge of their leader.

The two grappled on the cliffs above the sea near Plymouth in a terrible bout; Gogmagog crushed three of Corineus's ribs, but the enraged Trojan heaved the giant onto his shoulders and hurled him from the heights to be dashed to pieces on the rocks below, at a place long remembered as 'Gogmagog's Leap'. The tale was set down by Geoffrey of Monmouth in his 'Historia Regum Britanniae', composed around 1135 to 1139; one of its many surviving medieval copies is held today by Cambridge University Library. The giant's name lived on across the country, in the Gogmagog Hills near Cambridge, and in the pair of giant effigies, Gog and Magog, that have been carried in the Lord Mayor's Show and stood in London's Guildhall for centuries as the city's mythic guardians.
earliest_record: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1135-1139) is the original source for the Corineus/Gogmagog wrestling match and the giant's fatal fall from the Plymouth cliffs
period: High Medieval Britain (literary composition)

name: Granny Kempock Stone
summary: A hooded standing stone above Gourock harbour, walked round seven times by newlyweds and sailors for luck, and, in 1662, the alleged target of a witch coven who tried to topple it into the sea.
detail:
On a low cliff behind Kempock Street in Gourock stands a six-foot block of mica schist, weathered into a shape that locals have long read as a hooded old woman bent over, hence "Granny" Kempock. Its origins are unknown: suggestions over the years have ranged from a prehistoric standing stone or altar to a memorial marking an ancient battle, but no record explains who first gave it its name or its grandmotherly nickname.

For generations the stone was treated as a source of luck for anyone setting out on a journey by sea or into marriage. Fishermen about to sail, and couples newly wed, would carry a bucket of sand up from the shore and walk around the stone seven times against the sun (withershins) while chanting, in the belief that this secured Granny Kempock's blessing for a safe voyage or a fortunate marriage, and a wedding in the district was said to be unlucky if the couple skipped the circuit.

The stone's reputation took a darker turn in 1662, during one of Scotland's many witch-hunts. Mary Lamont, a teenage servant from nearby Innerkip, confessed, after questioning, to having met with a coven of local women who danced around the Kempock Stone on the sabbath and plotted to drag it into the Firth of Clyde, believing this would raise a storm to wreck ships and ruin the local fishing fleet. Lamont and several of her co-accused were burned for witchcraft later that year, a real and brutal episode that has since become inseparable from the stone's folklore, turning a stone for blessing sailors into one supposedly capable, in the wrong hands, of sinking them.
earliest_record: Marie Lamont's 'Note of the Voluntary Confession', a thirteen-article document held at the National Records of Scotland, records her confession before Archibald Stewart and the minister of Inverkip; she was tried 7 May 1662 alongside five other accused women and executed the same year
period: Restoration-era Scotland (witch trial, 1662)
historical_setting: The stone's own age and original purpose remain undated and disputed (prehistoric standing stone, altar, or battle memorial have all been suggested)

name: Green Children of Woolpit
summary: In the 12th century, two children with green skin emerged from pits near Woolpit, speaking an unknown tongue. The girl survived and spoke of an underground land called St Martin's Land.
detail:
In 12th-century Woolpit, Suffolk, harvesters in the fields came upon two children, a boy and a girl, standing bewildered by the wolf-pits that gave the village its name. Two chroniclers of the period, Ralph of Coggeshall and William of Newburgh, separately recorded what happened next: the children were ordinary in every way but one: their skin was entirely green. They wore clothes of an unfamiliar material, spoke no language anyone could understand, and at first would eat nothing but raw broad beans.

Taken in by the villagers and by the local knight, the boy sickened and died, but the girl survived. As she learned to eat ordinary food her green colour gradually faded, she was baptised, and in time she learned to speak English. When she could be understood, she told an extraordinary story of where they had come from: a twilit underground country she called Saint Martin's Land, where everything and everyone was green, lit by no bright sun but a perpetual gloaming. She and her brother had been minding their father's flocks, she said, when they followed the sound of bells into a cavern and emerged, dazzled, into the fields of Woolpit, unable to find their way back.

What lies behind the account has been argued over for centuries. Suggestions include a folk memory of fairy-folk emerging from the Otherworld; a garbled tale of lost or migrant children, perhaps Flemish, suffering from the greenish pallor of malnutrition (chlorosis, the 'green sickness'); or a pure marvel-story of the kind medieval chroniclers loved to collect. The girl, in some versions, grew up, married and settled in the area. Whatever its origin, the legend has kept Woolpit on the map of the uncanny, and the village sign today proudly bears the two green children.
origin_date: 1135-1154 (narrative setting, the reign of King Stephen, per William of Newburgh's own dating)
earliest_record: William of Newburgh's Historia rerum Anglicarum (written c.1198) and Ralph of Coggeshall's Chronicon Anglicanum (early 13th century) are the two independent medieval chronicle sources; William explicitly places the events during the reign of King Stephen (1135-1154), the period of the Anarchy
period: High Medieval England; chronicled roughly half a century to a century after the events they describe

name: The Green Knight
summary: A huge green challenger enters Arthur's court carrying a holly branch and an axe. His beheading game with Gawain tests courage, courtesy, truth, and the strangeness of winter.
detail:
The Green Knight is the eerie supernatural challenger of the great 14th-century English poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, one of the masterpieces of medieval literature. He bursts into King Arthur's Christmas feast at Camelot, an enormous man, entirely green from his skin to his clothes to his horse, bearing a holly branch in one hand and a great axe in the other. He issues a strange and terrible 'beheading game': he will allow any knight to strike him a single blow with the axe, on condition that the same knight seek him out a year and a day later to receive a blow in return.

Gawain takes up the challenge and strikes the Green Knight's head clean from his shoulders, whereupon the giant simply picks up his own severed head, which speaks, reminding Gawain of his bargain and naming the Green Chapel as the trysting place, before riding away. The rest of the poem follows Gawain's honour-bound winter journey to keep his appointment and meet what seems certain death, and the subtler test of his virtue that awaits him at the castle of a hospitable lord along the way.
