summary: A clan piper led companions into this sea cave to test his skill against its monstrous cave-dwelling ogress. His pipes still seem to echo from the rock when the wind is right.
detail:
On the wild west coast of Mull near Gribun lies a cave so deep that, by tradition, no one has ever reached its end. Samuel Johnson and James Boswell tried to measure it themselves during their tour of the Hebrides in 1773, an expedition Boswell recorded in his journal, though even they turned back before finding an end to it.

According to the older story, twelve men of Clan Fingon (MacKinnon) once set out to explore its full length, led by a piper, while a second party walked the cliffs above, following the sound of his pipes to mark how far the cave ran.

Deep in the dark, the explorers came upon a fearsome being, in most versions a monstrous female ogre, in others a fairy woman of the cave, who attacked the party and killed them one by one. Only the piper was spared, on condition that he keep playing for her; his music was said to be so charming that she let him live as long as the tune continued. When his strength finally failed and the music stopped, she killed him too.

Above ground, the search party heard the piping falter through the rock and rushed to the cave mouth, arriving just as the last note died away. They found the piper's mangled body, with the remains of his companions beyond him in the dark. The fullest surviving telling of the story appears in J. P. MacLean's History of the Island of Mull (1923), and locals still say that on certain days, when the wind is right, the cave breathes out the ghost of a tune, the last performance of Mull's most famous piper.
earliest_record: Samuel Johnson and James Boswell measured the cave during their 1773 tour of the Hebrides (recorded in Boswell's journal); the fullest surviving telling of the piper-and-fairy legend appears in J. P. MacLean's History of the Island of Mull, Vol. 1 (1923)
period: In oral circulation by the 18th century; first substantial written record 1773, fullest narrative account 1923
historical_setting: Isle of Mull, Highland Scotland, clan-era Highlands (legend told of Clan Fingan/Clan MacKinnon)
cultural_tradition: Scottish Highland fairy-legend tradition (piper-challenges-fairies motif)

name: Windhouse
summary: Reputedly Shetland's most haunted house: a 'Lady in Silk' glides the stairs, a phantom dog roams the halls, and a shipwrecked sailor's troll-fight became local legend.
detail:
Standing isolated above Whale Firth on the island of Yell, the roofless shell of Windhouse has long been called the most haunted building in Shetland. The house was built in 1707 on the site of an older dwelling and extended in 1885; it is said to be troubled by several spirits: a man in a top hat, a phantom dog, a servant girl, and most famously the 'Lady in Silk', a woman believed to have been a housekeeper or mistress of the house who fell down the stairs and broke her neck. She is said to walk in a circle at the top of the staircase before vanishing with a sigh.

The haunting gained an eerie corroboration during nineteenth-century renovations, when workers digging beneath the main staircase uncovered a skeleton (by some accounts that of a large man), lending grim substance to the old stories of violent deaths at the house.

A separate strand of local folklore tells of a shipwrecked sailor who came ashore one Christmas Eve and took shelter at Windhouse, ignoring the family's warnings as they fled the house for the night. Left alone, he was confronted by a monstrous troll, which he fought and killed with an axe before dawn, a tale that fused the house's reputation for hauntings with older Shetland troll-lore.
period: laird's house built 1707, remodelled/extended 1885; site includes an unmarked burial ground dated to the 13th-14th century
historical_setting: Mid Yell, Shetland; Category B listed ruin (HES ref LB45326)

name: White Lady of Tattershall Castle
summary: A glimmering woman in a medieval headdress has paced the battlements of Tattershall Castle for centuries, forever waiting for a lost love who never returns.
detail:
Tattershall Castle is the great brick tower house raised in the 1430s and 1440s for Ralph Cromwell, Treasurer of England under Henry VI, one of the earliest and finest surviving brick buildings in the country. It is here, on the battlements and in a private upper chamber, that a 'White Lady' is said to walk: a glimmering figure in a flowing white gown and a French-style medieval headdress. No record survives of who she might have been; tradition holds only that she walks in search of a lost love who never comes.

Visitors and staff over the years have reported more than the apparition itself. Unexplained taps and bangs echo through the floors, disembodied voices seem to murmur in empty rooms, and leaflets left in a turret room have reportedly been found scattered about after the castle was locked for the night.

The castle itself narrowly escaped a stranger fate than haunting. Its four great carved chimneypieces were sold and nearly shipped to America in 1911 before the peer Lord Curzon bought the castle to save them, restoring the building and gifting it to the National Trust in 1925. Under the Trust's care today, Tattershall leans into its reputation each Halloween with ghost-story evenings, though the White Lady herself is said to need no special occasion, having reputedly paced the ramparts on quiet nights for centuries.

name: Old Man of Storr
summary: A 55-metre pinnacle on the Trotternish Ridge is said to be the petrified thumb of a buried giant, left jutting from the earth when the rest of him was laid to rest.
detail:
On the Trotternish Ridge above Loch Leathan stands a 55-metre pinnacle of black basalt, the Old Man of Storr, said in Skye tradition to be the petrified thumb of a giant. According to the story, when the giant died and was buried in the hillside, his thumb was left protruding above the ground, and there it has stood ever since, weathering into the jagged spire seen today.

A second version of the tale gives the giant a more dramatic end. He was said to have been chasing a fairy across the ridge when he made the fatal mistake of looking back over his shoulder, and was turned to stone on the spot, along with his pursued quarry nearby.

The pinnacle stands among a cluster of rock towers known as the Sanctuary, on the flank of the Storr itself, which at 719 metres is the high point of the Trotternish Ridge. Geologists explain the whole formation as the product of the Trotternish landslip, the longest such landslip in Britain: around 60 million years ago a vast slice of the escarpment sheared away from the main ridge and slumped downhill, leaving isolated towers of dolerite and basalt standing free where the ground beneath them had given way. The site is also the type locality for the mineral gyrolite, first identified here.

For generations of islanders the simpler and more memorable explanation was a buried giant, his thumb still reaching for the sky. The pinnacle has since found a very different kind of fame: it stood in for an alien world in Ridley Scott's 2012 film Prometheus, and a photograph of the formation won the Landscape Photographer of the Year award in 2009. A well-built path now carries a steady stream of walkers up from the A855 to stand among the pinnacles, most day-trippers content to reach the Sanctuary without pushing on to the summit.
period: No earliest written record of the petrified-giant's-thumb tale itself was pinned down with certainty; the earliest print appearance located in search is Otta Swire's 'Skye: the Island and its Legends' (1952, reprinted 1961), a mid-20th-century collection of oral tales she heard from her mother and grandmother, so the tale's oral pedigree is likely much older than its first printing but cannot be dated further back with the sources available in this pass
cultural_tradition: Scottish Highland petrified-giant/buried-giant motif, the same type as other Skye and Highland stone-giant tales

name: Gunby Hall Ghost Walk
summary: A jealous squire shot his daughter's lover dead and dumped his body in the pond, the murdered postillion still walks 'Ghost Walk' awaiting his love.
detail:
Gunby Hall, a red-brick house of 1700 near Spilsby, carries one of Lincolnshire's grimmer ghost stories. Tradition holds that Sir William Massingberd discovered his daughter was planning to elope with a postillion in his service. On the night the couple intended to flee, Sir William lay in wait, shot the servant dead, and had the body dragged through the grounds and thrown into the pond; some versions of the story add that, in his rage, he shot his own daughter too.

Word of the killing spread despite efforts to keep it quiet, and locals began to whisper that Gunby was cursed: no male heir of the Massingberd line, it was said, would ever again inherit the house in the direct line, a 'curse' that some later genealogists noted did indeed seem to play out in the family's history.

The path beside the pond where the postillion's body was dumped became known as 'Ghost Walk', and is said to be haunted by his spectre still, pacing the route forever, waiting for a lover who can never return. The Massingberd family gave Gunby Hall to the National Trust in 1944, and the Trust now occasionally opens the house for Halloween events that draw on this and other tales of its haunted past.
period: Late 17th - early 18th century (Gunby Hall was built c.1699-1700 for Sir William Massingberd, 2nd Baronet, 1650-1719, and the legend is traditionally set within his residency)
historical_setting: Gunby Hall, Lincolnshire, built c.1699-1700 for Sir William Massingberd, 2nd Baronet; remained in Massingberd family ownership until gifted to the National Trust in 1944

name: The Curse of the Campbells of Jura
summary: A witch evicted by the grasping Campbells of Jura cursed their last laird to be one-eyed and leave the island by horse-cart, fulfilled to the letter in 1938.
detail:
When Clan Campbell took control of Jura in 1661, their factor Duncan Campbell began steadily raising rents on the island's crofters, driving many families to emigrate to America rather than face ruin. According to island tradition, one of the women evicted in this process, remembered simply as an old witch, turned on the Campbells with a curse before she left: that the last of the Campbell line on Jura would be one-eyed, and would leave the island for good carried to the shore in a cart drawn by a white horse.

The prophecy passed into local legend and was retold for generations as the Campbells' fortunes on the island slowly declined through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, their estate gradually sold off piece by piece.

Remarkably, islanders point to 1938 as the moment the curse came true. Charles Campbell, who had lost an eye fighting in the First World War, sold the last of the family's Jura estate, and, as the old story demanded, his belongings were carried down to the boat in a cart drawn by a white horse. The tale is often told alongside Jura's other great legend, the roaring tidal whirlpool of Corryvreckan off its northern tip, as part of the island's reputation for uncanny goings-on.
period: Curse traditionally said to date to the early 18th century; its supposed fulfilment is dated to 1938
historical_setting: The eviction of an elderly seer by the Campbell landlords who then dominated Jura, and the departure of Charles Campbell from the island in 1938
cultural_tradition: Highland second sight, in the same tradition as the Brahan Seer and the Seaforth prophecy
origin_date: The prophecy is attributed to the early eighteenth century, and its reported fulfilment is dated to 1938

name: Hard Apple Blyth, the Smuggler of Paglesham
summary: Paglesham's churchwarden, grocer and parish constable William 'Hard Apple' Blyth ran a smuggling operation under the noses of the very authorities he was sworn to serve.
detail:
The twin hamlets of Paglesham, tucked among the creeks of the Essex coast near Rochford, were for generations one of the county's busiest smuggling centres, and their most celebrated smuggler was, by the standards of the trade, a deeply respectable man. William Blyth (1753-1830), known to everyone as 'Hard Apple', was at various times the village's churchwarden, its grocer, a parish councillor, and, improbably, its local constable.

That last role gave him an unrivalled vantage point from which to run his real business: moving contraband brandy, tobacco and other goods past the very excise men he was nominally employed to assist. Local tradition remembers him less as a criminal than as a folk hero, a cheerfully two-faced figure who embodied the way an entire Essex coastal community quietly lived off the smuggling trade for over a century.

Blyth is buried in the north churchyard of St Peter's Church, Paglesham, alongside his wife and two sons, and his grave remains a minor point of interest for those exploring the village's smuggling past, a past so embedded in local identity that Paglesham's old inns still trade on the same seafaring, smuggling heritage today.
period: Georgian to early Victorian Essex; Paglesham's documented smuggling heyday ran from roughly 1750 to 1840

name: The Pump Hill Smuggler
summary: A headless, legless smuggler, his head dangling loose between his shoulders, still drags a sack of plunder up from Cart Gap through Happisburgh, groaning from an old well whenever a storm is coming.
detail:
One of the grimmest ghost stories on the Norfolk coast belongs to the village of Happisburgh, where eighteenth-century farmers returning home late at night told of a terrible figure coming up the main street from the direction of Cart Gap. He was a headless, legless man in a sailor's dark coat and leather belt, a pistol thrust through it, his pigtailed hair so long it trailed on the ground from a head that hung down between his shoulder blades.

The story behind the apparition traced back to a violent falling-out among Dutch smugglers on the beach at Cart Gap, which ended in gunfire and at least one death. Two men were said to have waylaid the wandering ghost and followed it to a well at the top of Pump Hill, where they dropped a bundle down the shaft, then threw the ghost in after it.

After that, the well became the focus of the haunting. Whenever a storm was brewing, low groans were said to rise from it, as if the dead smuggler were still trying to warn the village. The well and its pump have long since gone, but for years afterwards people refused to have the pump removed, fearing that without it the groaning, and whatever it warned of, would return.
earliest_record: Ernest R. Suffling, 'History and Legends of the Broad District [Norfolk]; with a glance at its folk lore, ghosts, churches, etc.' (Jarrold & Sons, 1891), pp.107-111
period: The haunting is set among 18th-century smuggling on the Norfolk coast; the earliest known published record of the ghost story itself is 1891

name: Lough Ree Monster
summary: Three priests fishing near Glasson in 1960 watched a 20-foot serpentine creature glide across Lough Ree, the latest in centuries of sightings on Ireland's 'monster lake'.
detail:
Lough Ree, the long lake on the River Shannon where counties Longford, Westmeath and Roscommon meet, has its own resident monster, a creature reported, in one form or another, for centuries by people living along its shores. The earliest hint may go back to the medieval Life of St Mochua of Balla, a hagiography that describes a fierce monster in the lake deterring hunters from an island refuge. Descriptions since have varied, but the most consistent picture is of a long, dark, serpent-like animal with a small head, moving slowly through the water with little more than its neck and head breaking the surface.

The most celebrated sighting came in 1960, when three Catholic priests on a fishing trip near Glasson, close to Athlone, watched what they described as a strange object moving slowly across the calm water about eighty yards away. They reported a serpent-like head tapering to a point, and estimated the creature's length at over twenty feet, an account that, coming from clergymen rather than tourists, gave the story unusual credibility at the time.

Sceptics have suggested more mundane explanations, from large eels to floating debris, and one self-styled monster-hunter has claimed the Lough Ree creature is simply an oversized lamprey. But the lake's reputation has endured regardless, kept alive by centuries of reported sightings and that one well-attested afternoon in 1960.
earliest_record: A medieval hagiographic reference (the Life of St Mochua of Balla) to a fierce monster in Lough Ree deterring hunters from an island refuge; the best-documented modern account is the July 1960 sighting by three Catholic priests near Glasson
period: Medieval monastic tradition (precise date of the saint's life text uncertain) revived as a well-documented 20th-century cryptid tradition
cultural_tradition: Irish lake-monster tradition, comparable to other Irish loughs' cryptid legends

name: Denbigh Dragon
summary: A giant knight with eight fingers and two thumbs on each hand slew the dragon nesting in Denbigh Castle's great hall, and the townsfolk's cry of 'Dim bych!' (No dragon!) is said to have given the town its name.
detail:
According to the folklore attached to Denbigh Castle, the great hall of the castle was once the lair of a dragon that had put the town under siege, dropping from the sky to prey on livestock and people alike. The task of dealing with the beast fell to a knight remembered in some versions as John Salusbury of Lleweni, a documented Denbighshire gentry figure, but in the oldest form of the tale as Sion y Bodiau ('John of the Thumbs'), a giant of a man said to have eight fingers and two thumbs on each hand. The nickname actually belonged to two Salusburys, an uncle who died in 1547 or 1549 and his nephew who died in 1578, and the dragon story has been told of both, so which Sion is meant depends on which telling is followed.

Sion rode to the castle in full armour on a great shire horse, carrying a broadsword built for a giant's grip. Onlookers were said to have heard the awful sounds of battle and seen sparks and arcs of fire thrown off by the dragon's breath as the fight dragged on for hours, sword against claw and scale, neither side giving ground. The turning point came when Sion spotted two bare patches of unscaled skin at the base of the dragon's wings; waiting for the creature to rear up and spread its wings to attack, he drove his broadsword into one of the unprotected spots and, after several more blows, cut off its head.

Riding back into the town with the dragon's severed head held aloft on his sword, Sion was met by townsfolk who had been hiding from the beast. Their relieved cry, 'Dim bych!', Welsh for 'No dragon!', is said in this telling to be the origin of the town's name, Dinbych (Denbigh), a folk etymology that has helped keep the story, and the dragon, alive in local memory for centuries. No early written text for the dragon tale itself has been located; it appears to be a folk giant-slayer motif that became attached, at some later point, to the real Salusbury family name.
period: Some tellings attach the giant-slayer to John Salusbury of Lleweni (d. 1578), though the 'oldest form' of the tale, which names the giant Sion y Bodiau, cannot itself be firmly dated
earliest_record: No early written text for the dragon tale itself is known; the tale is a folk giant/dragon-slayer motif that became locally attached to the historical Salusbury family of Lleweni, specifically John Salusbury ('Sion y Bodiau', d. 1547/49), a documented 16th-century Denbighshire gentry figure (see History of Parliament Online and the Dictionary of Welsh Biography)
historical_setting: The Dictionary of Welsh Biography notes that two Salusbury family members of Lleweni were nicknamed 'Sion y Bodiau': an uncle, John Salusbury I (d. 1547/49), and his nephew John Salusbury II (d. 1578). The dragon-slaying tale has historically been attached to both, and the two are easily confused.

name: Witch of Slieu Whallian
summary: Suspected witches were sealed into spiked barrels and rolled down Slieau Whallian. The bare scar of 'the Witch's Way' still marks where one woman's screams are said to echo every year.
detail:
Slieau Whallian, a hill above St John's in the Isle of Man, was traditionally used as the site of a brutal ordeal for people accused of witchcraft. According to the story collected by folklorist Sophia Morrison in her Manx Fairy Tales (1911), a suspected witch would be sealed inside a barrel lined on the inside with sharp iron spikes, and the barrel would then be sent rolling from the summit to the bottom of the hill.

If the accused survived the descent, torn by the spikes and battered by the fall, they were put to death anyway, the ordeal serving only to 'confirm' their guilt rather than offer any real chance of escape. The same source records that this method was used on 'many other persons of both sexes' at this spot, not only women.

For generations afterwards, islanders pointed to a bare scar running down the steep slope of Slieau Whallian where, it was said, grass would never grow again, known locally as 'the Witch's Way'. Local tradition added a final, eerie detail: that on the anniversary of her death, the screams of one executed witch could still be heard carried on the wind down the hillside. The historian Ronald Hutton has traced the tale's likely lineage back through an earlier Scottish retelling to a German legend, suggesting it was imported to the island and given a local setting sometime in the 1840s rather than recording any actual Manx execution, a reminder that even the island's most vivid folk-memories can turn out to be borrowed stories, wearing local scars.
earliest_record: A.W. Moore, 'Folk-lore of the Isle of Man' (1891); Sophia Morrison, 'Manx Fairy Tales' (1911)
period: first attested in print in the 1890s-1910s; folklorist Ronald Hutton has argued the tale itself is a 19th-century import (via a Scottish version) of an earlier German legend, first appearing in the 1840s
cultural_tradition: Manx witch-persecution folklore, associated with Slieau Whallian near Peel/Tynwald Mount

name: Marshal Brain of Clongowes Wood
summary: In 1757, the ghost of an Austrian-army officer appeared to two sisters at Clongowes Wood, describing his uniform in perfect detail. He came to announce, at the very hour, their brother's death in battle at Prague.
detail:
Clongowes Wood, near Clane in County Kildare, was the seat of the Wogan-Browne family before it became a Jesuit school in the nineteenth century, and one of the most discussed ghost stories of eighteenth-century Ireland is set there. In 1757, two sisters living at the house are said to have seen the apparition of an officer in the uniform of the Austrian army, his chest streaming with blood.

At the time, the sisters' brother was serving abroad as an officer in Austrian service, far from any news the family could quickly receive. They identified the ghostly visitor as their brother, and within days, before any letter could plausibly have reached them, word arrived that he had indeed been killed in action at the Battle of Prague that same year, at almost exactly the time of the vision.

What made the case unusual, and kept it circulating in accounts of Irish ghost-lore for generations afterwards, was a further detail: local people with no knowledge of foreign military dress were said to have been able to describe the Austrian officer's uniform precisely as the sisters had seen it. The episode is still cited today as one of Ireland's best-documented 'crisis apparitions', a vision of a death occurring at the moment it happened, far away.
earliest_record: The apparition is traditionally tied to the 1757 death of Marshal Wogan-Browne, an officer in Austrian service killed at the Battle of Prague, as recorded in Turtle Bunbury's genealogical history of the Wogan-Browne family of Clongowes Wood
period: Mid-18th century (1757), Seven Years' War
historical_setting: Clongowes Wood (then Castle Browne), County Kildare, seat of the Wogan-Browne family; the Battle of Prague was fought 6 May 1757 during the Seven Years' War, between Prussia and Habsburg Austria
cultural_tradition: Irish death-omen/warning-apparition legend tied to a specific historical family

name: Canthrig Bwt
summary: Beneath a stone by Pont-y-Cromlech in the Llanberis Pass lay Canthrig Bwt, a devil-bargained giantess with a taste for children's brains, until a length of iron found her neck.
detail:
In the folklore of the Llanberis Pass, Canthrig Bwt was a giantess who was also a witch, feared throughout the district around Nant Peris for her taste for children. Tradition places her lair beneath a great stone close to Pont-y-Cromlech, the old bridge partway along the pass, where she was said to lie in wait for unwary youngsters after selling her soul to the devil for a permanent appetite for their brains.

The tale survives in at least two distinct tellings. The version recorded by the Welsh-American folklorist Wirt Sykes in his influential 1881 collection British Goblins names her Canrig Bwt and gives her killer as a condemned criminal, offered his freedom in exchange for ridding the district of her. He found her mid-meal, and she told him to wait "till I have finished eating the brains in this sweet little skull" before he cut off her head at a single blow. A separate, more elaborated local telling instead gives a young avenger who arms himself with an iron sword and first secures the blessing of both a Christian monk and a benevolent 'white witch' before confronting her; in this version she is seized by the arm and beheaded with a sickle, then buried near a place called Tir Coch outside Llanberis.

Sykes recorded that the legend was still doing its job as a cautionary tale in his own day: "to this day they scare children thereabout with the name of Canrig Bwt." Some storytellers date the killing as far back as the fourth century, and Pont-y-Cromlech is still pointed out to walkers in the pass as her former haunt.
origin_date: Uncertain oral origin; earliest known written record is 1880
earliest_record: Wirt Sikes, British Goblins: Welsh Folk-lore, Fairy Mythology, Legends and Traditions (1880)
period: In print by 1880
cultural_tradition: North Wales (Gwynedd) child-eating giantess/witch folklore attached to the Cromlech Boulders (Creigiau'r Gromlech), Nant Peris, Llanberis Pass

name: Isobel Gowdie
summary: In 1662 a Highland cottar's wife gave four unforced confessions of riding with the Queen of Elfhame, shape-shifting into a hare, and turning sticks into horses, the richest witch-lore ever recorded in Scotland.
detail:
Isobel Gowdie was a young farmer's wife living near Auldearn, close to Nairn, when in the spring of 1662 she made a series of four remarkable confessions to witchcraft over six weeks. What sets her case apart is that the testimony appears to have been given freely, without the violent torture usual to such trials, and that it is soaked in the imagery of older Highland fairy belief rather than the imported demonology of the courts.

Gowdie described slipping out of her own body to fly through the night air, feasting with the fairy folk beneath the hills, and riding with the Queen of Elfhame. She chanted rhymes that turned straws and beanstalks into horses, that let her vanish from sight, and that transformed her into a hare, a cat or a crow and back again, echoes of the Highland *fith-fath*, the charm of shape-changing. Her coven, she said, met to work their magic and to trouble their neighbours' crops and cattle.

It is uncertain whether Gowdie was executed in the usual way or simply allowed to slip back into obscurity, for the records fall silent after her confessions. The confessions themselves came close to vanishing too. The original documents were long thought lost, until the historian Emma Wilby rediscovered them in an uncatalogued box of papers at the National Records of Scotland, work she set out fully in The Visions of Isobel Gowdie (2010). What survives, now that the papers have resurfaced, is one of the most vivid windows ever opened onto the folk belief of seventeenth-century Scotland, where witchcraft, fairy lore and the charms of the cunning folk were tangled inseparably together.
earliest_record: Original confession records, now held at the National Records of Scotland (rediscovered by historian Emma Wilby in an uncatalogued box of papers after long being thought lost)
period: Restoration-era Scotland (confessions given over six weeks in spring 1662)
historical_setting: Emma Wilby's 'The Visions of Isobel Gowdie: Magic, Witchcraft and Dark Shamanism in Seventeenth-Century Scotland' (Sussex Academic Press, 2010) is the leading modern academic analysis, built directly on the rediscovered original confession documents

name: Major Thomas Weir
summary: A respected Covenanter soldier stunned Edinburgh by confessing to witchcraft and was strangled in 1670; his shunned house on the West Bow stood empty for a century, lit at night by phantom revels.
detail:
Major Thomas Weir was a pillar of Presbyterian Edinburgh, a Covenanting officer and captain of the Town Guard, so austere in his piety that locals called him the 'West Bow Saint'. He shared a narrow flat on the West Bow with his spinster sister Grizel. Then, around 1670, while leading a prayer meeting, the elderly major astonished the company by confessing unbidden to a lifetime of secret crimes and to commerce with the Devil.

Weir was strangled and burned, often named as the last man executed for witchcraft in Scotland, and his sister was hanged soon after. But it was his house that fixed him in the city's folklore. For more than a century the dwelling on the West Bow stood empty, for no one would live in it. Passers-by reported lights moving in the windows of the deserted rooms, the sound of music and laughter, and the shapes of enormous women behind the glass.

When an old soldier named William Patullo at last took the cheap house around 1780, he and his wife are said to have fled after a single night, driven out when a spectral calf appeared at the foot of their bed and rested its forelegs on the frame to stare at them in the dark.
period: Restoration-era Scotland; often cited as among the last people executed for witchcraft in Scotland
historical_setting: The house on the West Bow stood empty for over a century afterward, until William Patullo's brief and frightened tenancy around 1780

name: Bessie Dunlop
summary: A Dalry healer tried in 1576 said her cures came from Tom Reid, a ghostly man slain at Pinkie who led her among the 'gude wichtis' of the Court of Elfame. She was strangled and burned in Edinburgh.
detail:
Bessie Dunlop was a farmer's wife, midwife and healer from Lynn near Dalry in Ayrshire, brought to trial on 8 November 1576 for sorcery and witchcraft. Her defence, extraordinary in its detail, was that her gift for healing and for finding lost goods came not from the Devil but from a spirit named Tom Reid, an honest-looking old man in a grey coat and black bonnet who carried a white wand.

Reid, she said, had been killed at the Battle of Pinkie Cleugh in 1547, and now moved between the living world and the 'Court of Elfame', the fairy realm. He acted as her intermediary with the *gude wichtis*, the good wights or fairies, bringing her the knowledge of herbs and charms by which she helped her neighbours. Her testimony is one of the clearest surviving accounts of how Scottish folk healing and fairy belief became fatally entangled with the legal idea of witchcraft.

Reported by a neighbour, Dunlop was taken to Edinburgh, and despite a defence rooted entirely in the older fairy faith she was found guilty, strangled and burned on Castle Hill. In 2022 her home community of Dalry gathered to remember her among the many ordinary women caught up in Scotland's witch trials.
earliest_record: Surviving Scottish court trial record, dated 8 November 1576
period: Early Modern Scotland

name: Biddy Early
summary: The Wise Woman of Clare read a magic blue bottle said to be a gift of the fairies, healing thousands for a glass of whiskey until priests and landlords cried witchcraft. The bottle lies lost in her lake.
detail:
Biddy Early (c.1798-1874) was a *bean feasa*, a wise woman or seer, who lived in a small mud cottage above Kilbarron Lake near Feakle in County Clare. People walked for days to reach her door, seeking cures for themselves and their animals, and she is said to have turned no one away, taking no money, only a measure of poitín or whiskey in return.

The heart of her legend is the blue bottle into which she would gaze, like a clairvoyant with a crystal ball, to see the cause of an affliction or the face of an enemy. Every account agrees that the bottle came from the fairies, and that her uncanny knowledge of things she could not have known by ordinary means set her apart and frightened those in power. When her cures crossed the wishes of the landlords and the Catholic clergy she was denounced and even charged with witchcraft, though no conviction held.

When Biddy died, the famous blue bottle was thrown into the lake below her cottage, and though it has been searched for many times it has never been found, the Good People, it is said, took it back. W. B. Yeats and Lady Gregory gathered stories of her in the early 1900s, not long after her death, and she remains one of Ireland's most beloved and ambiguous figures, hovering forever between witch and healer.
earliest_record: A real, documented historical figure (baptised Bridget Connors, 1798-1874) who was tried for witchcraft at Ennis in 1865 but not convicted; the first substantial published life-and-legend account followed not long after Lady Augusta Gregory began collecting stories about her, in the early 1900s
period: 19th-century Ireland

name: The Bargarran Witches
summary: In 1697 eleven-year-old Christian Shaw of Bargarran accused her neighbours of bewitching her; seven were hanged and burned on Paisley's Gallow Green, the last mass execution for witchcraft in western Europe.
detail:
The affair began at Bargarran House in Renfrewshire in 1696, when eleven-year-old Christian Shaw, daughter of the laird, fell into violent fits after a quarrel with a servant, Katherine Campbell, whom she had reported for stealing a drink of milk. The girl complained of being tormented by unseen tormentors and named a growing list of her neighbours as the witches responsible. The case was set down at length the following year in Francis Grant, Lord Cullen's Sadducismus Debellatus, a full contemporary narrative of the 'sorceries and witchcrafts' supposedly exercised on the child.

A commission was appointed, opening on 5 February 1697 under Lord Blantyre. One of the accused, John Reid, was found dead in his cell on 22 May 1697 before he could be tried, in circumstances never fully explained. Seven others, Margaret Lang, Katherine Campbell, Agnes Naismith, Margaret Fulton, John Lindsay, James Lindsay and John Lindsay of Barloch, were found guilty of bewitching the child. On 10 June 1697 they were hanged and then burned on the Gallow Green in Paisley, the last mass execution for witchcraft in western Europe. As she went to her death, Agnes Naismith was said to have laid a dying curse on all present and their descendants, and for generations afterward every misfortune in Paisley was blamed on it.

The accuser, Christian Shaw, lived on to become a successful businesswoman and a pioneer of the Paisley thread industry. The case has fascinated and troubled historians ever since, read variously as mass hysteria, a child's malice, and a community's readiness to kill on the word of an eleven-year-old.
earliest_record: Francis Grant, Lord Cullen, Sadducismus Debellatus: or, A True Narrative of the Sorceries and Witchcrafts Exercis'd by the Devil and His Instruments upon Mrs. Christian Shaw...from Aug. 1696 to Apr. 1697, London: D. Newman and A. Ball, 1698.
historical_setting: Christian Shaw's fits began 22 August 1696 after she witnessed Katherine Campbell stealing milk on 17 August 1696; the special Commission opened 5 February 1697 under Lord Blantyre; suspect John Reid was found dead in his cell 22 May 1697; seven of the accused were hanged and burned on Paisley's Gallow Green on 10 June 1697

name: Isaac Gulliver
summary: Dorset's 'gentle smuggler who never killed a man' ran gin, tea and lace with a livery of powder-haired 'White Wigs', and once escaped the excise by lying powdered in a coffin as though dead.
detail:
Isaac Gulliver (c.1745-1822) was the most successful smuggler of the Dorset coast, styled the 'King of the Smugglers' yet remembered in local tradition as the gentle smuggler who never killed a man. At his height he controlled the shore from Lymington in Hampshire through Dorset to the edge of Devon, running a fleet of luggers laden with gin, brandy, tea, silk and lace from the Continent into Poole Bay.

His gang of forty or fifty men wore a kind of livery (smocks and powdered hair) which earned them the nickname the 'White Wigs'. The most famous tale told of him is that, with the revenue men closing in, Gulliver faked his own death, lying in an open coffin with his face powdered white so that the excise officers, filing past to confirm the body, went away believing the smuggler king was gone.

Gulliver was never hanged. He used his vast wealth to buy estates and farms, turned respectable banker and citizen, and died peacefully at Wimborne in 1822 leaving a fortune of some sixty thousand pounds. He lies buried at St Andrew's, Kinson, where the church tower is said to bear the marks of ropes used to haul contraband.
period: Georgian to Regency England; his smuggling career is generally placed in the 1770s-1800s, before his transition to respectable banking and landownership

name: The Hawkhurst Gang
summary: From the Mermaid Inn at Rye, this ruthless smuggling syndicate terrorised the south-east in the 1740s, raiding the Poole Custom House until the Goudhurst militia broke them in a pitched battle.
detail:
The Hawkhurst Gang was the most feared smuggling organisation in England, operating from the Kentish village of Hawkhurst on the Sussex border between about 1735 and 1749. At their peak they could muster hundreds of armed men and ran contraband from the Channel coast across Kent and Sussex and up to London, openly drinking and firing their guns at inns such as the Mermaid at Rye.

Their power rested on terror. They tortured informers, extorted whole villages, and in their most notorious exploit broke into the Custom House at Poole in 1747 to recover a seized cargo of tea. When a witness, the shoemaker Daniel Chater, and a customs officer, William Galley, threatened to expose them, the gang murdered both with appalling cruelty, an outrage that finally turned the country against them.

The villagers of Goudhurst, drilled into a militia by a former soldier, William Sturt, beat off a gang assault in a pitched battle on 21 April 1747, in which the gang leader Thomas Kingsmill's own brother George was among the dead. Within two years the ringleaders had gone to the gallows: Arthur Gray was executed in 1748, and Kingsmill himself was hanged at Tyburn in April 1749 alongside William Fairall, another of the gang's leaders. Kingsmill's body was afterwards gibbeted at Goudhurst and Fairall's at Horsmonden, a grim public warning that closed the affair, and the Hawkhurst Gang passed into folklore as the byword for the violent golden age of English smuggling.
period: Active c. 1735-1749
historical_setting: 18th-century organised smuggling in south-east England (Kent and Sussex), driven by high import duties on tea, spirits, and other goods. First documented reference to the gang dates to c. 1735. The Battle of Goudhurst, in which the Goudhurst militia defeated the gang in a pitched fight around St Mary's Church, took place on 21 April 1747, killing gang leader Thomas Kingsmill's brother George and two other smugglers. The retaliatory raid on Poole Custom House took place on the night of 6-7 October 1747, after the gang's tea cargo (seized by the revenue vessel Swift on 22 September 1747) was stored there. Gang leader Arthur Gray was executed in 1748. Thomas Kingsmill and William Fairall were convicted at the Old Bailey and hanged at Tyburn on 26 April 1749; Kingsmill's body was gibbeted at Goudhurst and Fairall's at Horsmonden.

name: The Wherwell Cockatrice
summary: A toad hatched a cock's egg in the priory cellars, loosing a cockatrice on Wherwell until a man named Green lowered a mirror and let the beast battle its own reflection to death.
detail:
The Hampshire village of Wherwell, once home to a great Benedictine nunnery founded around 986 AD by Queen Ælfthryth, widow of King Edgar, keeps the legend of the cockatrice, a serpent with a cockerel's head, hatched, as the old belief held, when a toad broods a cock's egg. The monstrous creature is said to have been born in the cellars beneath Wherwell Priory and to have grown until it terrified the whole village.

Unable to slay it by force, the people drove the cockatrice into the dungeons below the priory and sealed it in, offering a prize of land to anyone who could kill it. At last a man named Green hit upon a cunning plan: he lowered a polished steel mirror into the vault. Believing its own reflection to be a rival, the cockatrice fought itself furiously against the glass until it dropped exhausted, and Green climbed down to dispatch it.

For his courage Green was rewarded with an estate near the village still remembered as Green's Acres. A weathervane in the shape of the cockatrice once turned above the village church and is now preserved in Andover Museum, keeping the tale fixed to its place long after the priory itself was dissolved in 1538.
period: medieval, before 1538
historical_setting: Wherwell Priory (a Benedictine nunnery founded c.986 AD by Queen Ælfthryth/Elfrida, widow of King Edgar), Hampshire, on the River Test. The legend is set before the priory's dissolution in 1538

name: Jimmy Squarefoot
summary: A bipedal, boar-tusked creature once ridden by a stone-throwing giant, Jimmy Squarefoot haunts the Grenaby river as a great white pig, feared for carrying the unwary off to his cave.
detail:
Jimmy Squarefoot belongs to the older, stranger corners of Manx folklore. He is described as a creature that walks upright with two great tusks like a boar's, and whose broad, squarish feet, swaddled in calico bands, give him his name. For the most part he is a harmless wanderer of the southern hills of the Isle of Man.

In his more menacing aspect, however, Jimmy Squarefoot is counted a kind of buggane, a phantom haunting the river and bridge at Grenaby, where he appears as a huge white boar. In that shape he is greatly feared, for he is said to be able to seize mortals and carry them off up the river and through a cave somewhere near the slopes of Barrule.

His origin story is stranger still. He was once, the tale runs, the mount of one of the Foawr, the race of stone-throwing giants of Manx legend, and a hurler of stones himself, whose favourite target was his own wife. When at last she left him, he is said to have taken on his semi-human form and wandered the island alone, a melancholy and grotesque relic of the giants' age.

The fullest early account of him appears in Walter Gill's 'A Manx Scrapbook' (1929); a possible still earlier mention surfaces in the Folk-lore Society's Jubilee Congress proceedings of September 1928, likely by the same author, suggesting Gill was chiefly responsible for setting the tale down in writing at all.
earliest_record: Walter Gill's 'A Manx Scrapbook' (1929), which also documents the Glashtyn, contains the most substantial early description; a possible earlier reference appears in the Proceedings of the Folk-lore Society's Jubilee Congress (September 1928), possibly also authored by Gill
period: Recorded in the late-1920s Manx folklore-collecting tradition

name: Peg Powler
summary: A green-haired hag of the River Tees who drags the young and unwary under to drown and devour them; the river's drifting froth is still called 'Peg Powler's Suds'.
detail:
Peg Powler is the water-hag of the River Tees, a bogey invoked across the dales to keep children back from the dangerous banks. She is pictured as a woman crowned with long green tresses, the green hair that marks a river spirit in English folklore, with, in the words of the Victorian folklorist William Henderson, writing in 1866, 'an insatiable desire for human life'.

Like her sisters Jenny Greenteeth and Nelly Longarms, Peg Powler lurks at the water's edge and seizes those who stray too close, dragging them down to drown or be devoured. In some tellings she lures men and boys by pretending to be a beautiful young woman in difficulty, so that her would-be rescuers wade in to their doom.

Her presence is written into the river itself. The masses of foam that gather on the higher reaches of the Tees are called 'Peg Powler's Suds', and the thinner scum that rides the surface is 'Peg Powler's Cream', everyday names that kept the old warning alive long after anyone truly feared the green hag beneath the current.
earliest_record: William Henderson's 'Notes on the Folk-Lore of the Northern Counties of England and the Borders' (1866), which describes 'an insatiable desire for human life', the same source that documents the Duergar, the Dunnie and Jenny Greenteeth
period: Recorded in the mid-19th-century English folklore-collecting tradition (1866)

name: The Hedley Kow
summary: A shape-shifting Northumberland bogie that turned itself into straw, cattle or a pot of changing treasure to bamboozle country folk, then vanished with a snickering, horse-like laugh.
detail:
The Hedley Kow was the mischievous bogie of Hedley on the Hill, a village near Ebchester in Northumberland. Unlike the malevolent water-hags or the spectral hounds, the Kow was a trickster whose pranks ended in laughter rather than harm, a shape-shifter who could take not only the forms of animals but of ordinary inanimate things.

In one well-loved tale, recorded by the folklorist Joseph Jacobs in More English Fairy Tales (1894), an old woman finds a pot of gold by the roadside; but each time she glances down the treasure has changed, gold to silver, silver to iron, iron at last to a plain stone, which then springs up, reveals itself as the Kow, and capers off. In another, the creature disguises itself as a bundle of straw that grows impossibly heavy in a woman's arms before standing up and shuffling away with a snickering, horse-like laugh.

The Kow delighted in such deceptions: overturning milk pails, frightening farm servants, leading travellers astray and imitating their sweethearts' voices, always melting away with its braying laugh once the trick was sprung. It belongs to the great family of British hobgoblins and bogies, household spirits who are tolerated, even half-affectionately remembered, for the chaos they cause.
earliest_record: Joseph Jacobs, More English Fairy Tales (London: David Nutt, 1894), story XI, 'The Hedley Kow' -- the standard printed source for this tale, specific to the village of Hedley on the Hill, Northumberland.
cultural_tradition: Northumberland rural bogie/shapeshifter folklore

name: Petticoat Loose
summary: Damned for killing an unbaptised child, the ghost Petticoat Loose was banished to Bay Lough in the Knockmealdowns to twist ropes of sand forever; parents still warn children she will get them.
detail:
Petticoat Loose is a malevolent Irish ghost known across the south from Waterford into Tipperary, called Moll Shaughnessy in Cork and Sprid na Bearnan in Limerick. In life, the stories say, she was a woman who murdered an unbaptised child, and for that crime her soul was denied rest.

She is best remembered haunting the mountain road above Bay Lough in the Knockmealdowns, where riders travelling by night told of their horses breaking into a foaming, uncontrollable bolt the moment her spirit drew near. One well-told tale has a man riding through the dark to fetch a priest, set upon along that same road until words of holy scripture drive her off; a priest is needed to lay her properly, and he banishes her, in some versions to the Red Sea, in others to Bay Lough itself, to an impossible, endless task: twisting ropes of sand, or baling out the lough with a thimble, so that she can never finish and return.

Bay Lough itself has a matching reputation. Local tradition holds it fills the crater of an extinct volcano, a small dark tarn with no visible outlet cut into the mountainside, and that when the people of nearby Clogheen once tried to drain it, they looked down and saw their own town apparently ablaze, and abandoned the work rather than test whether the vision was true.

Her name became a household warning long before that. From Cork to Waterford, parents still tell wilful children to behave or 'Petticoat Loose will get you', and the lonely waters of Bay Lough keep their reputation as a haunted place where her restless spirit is said to linger yet.
earliest_record: Recorded by schoolchildren across several Cahir/Clogheen-area schools in the National Folklore Collection's Schools' Collection (1937-1939), reflecting oral tradition locals already described at the time as generations old
period: Oral tradition documented in the 1930s Schools' Collection; the legend is locally said to be at least two centuries old, but no earlier fixed written record was found
cultural_tradition: South Tipperary/West Waterford witch-ghost tradition of the Knockmealdown Mountains

name: The Nine Witches of Gloucester
summary: The Gwiddonod Caerloyw, nine warrior-sorceresses of the 'Shining Fortress', ravaged kingdoms in the tale of Peredur until the young hero rode against them and broke their reign of terror.
detail:
In the medieval Welsh romance of Peredur son of Efrawg, one of the tales gathered into the Mabinogion, the hero's true enemies are at last revealed to be the Gwiddonod Caerloyw, the Nine Witches of Caer Lloyw, the 'Castle of Glow' or Shining Fortress later identified with Gloucester. Far from helpless hags, they are fearsome mistresses of warfare and magic who ravage kingdoms and whose deeds have laid waste the land of Peredur's own kinsmen.

The witches first take Peredur in, training him in arms and horsemanship over three weeks before he rides on. Only later does he learn that the severed head borne bleeding through his uncle's hall belonged to a cousin the Nine Witches had slain. In a story that elsewhere shadows the Grail quest, Peredur's task becomes not the finding of a sacred vessel but the destroying of the witches who plague Britain, and with Arthur and his men he returns to put them to the sword.

The episode seems to reach back into an older stratum of Celtic narrative, in which troops of nine supernatural women, echoed in the nine maidens of Avalon and the nine sorceresses of Geoffrey of Monmouth, guard, teach and destroy. Peredur's own text survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch, a Welsh manuscript of around 1350 and, alongside the later Red Book of Hergest, one of the two great sources for everything now gathered under the modern name Mabinogion. Their fixing to Gloucester gives this archaic motif a local habitation, and the Nine Witches survive in the county's storytelling today, retold in collections such as Anthony Nanson's Gloucestershire Folk Tales.
earliest_record: Peredur son of Efrawg, composed 12th-13th century (scholarly dating debated); earliest surviving manuscript witness MS Peniarth 7 (early 14th century), with the fullest text in the White Book of Rhydderch (MS Peniarth 4, mid-14th century, c.1325-1350) and Red Book of Hergest (late 14th century, c.1382-1400)
period: Medieval Wales, 14th-century manuscript attestation of a 12th/13th-century tale
cultural_tradition: Welsh Arthurian romance / Mabinogion tradition

name: Crazy Kate, the Witch of Swineshead
summary: A reclusive fenland woman with three cats for familiars was said to summon the Devil at the Manwar Rings earthwork, until a mob who came to spy on her found only her cats and broom, and her curse.
detail:
Crazy Kate is the witch of Swineshead in the Lincolnshire fens, a figure of the kind that gathered around any solitary, unliked woman in a superstitious age. She was said to keep three cats as her familiars and, by night, to make her way to the Manwar Rings, earthworks east of the village long held in local tradition to date from the time of Canute and to be a place where witches met to take their instruction from the Devil. Historic England schedules the site as the remains of a 12th-century motte-and-bailey castle raised by the Norman de Gresley family, the same lords of the manor who founded Swineshead Abbey, centuries later than the Danish-era origin the legend gives it.

The best-known tale tells how suspicious villagers resolved to watch her. For three nights they hid in her garden, but never once saw her come or go; they concluded that she had sensed them, made herself invisible, and slipped away. When at last they broke into her cottage they found only her cats and her broom. Then Kate herself fell upon them, promising to curse the whole pack of them for their trespass. In some tellings the angry mob later burned her cottage and her cats, and she was never seen again.

The legend is preserved in modern Lincolnshire folklore collections, including Polly Howat's *Ghosts and Legends of Lincolnshire and the Fen Country* and the Lincolnshire Folk Tales Project. Crazy Kate is distinct from the older Swineshead legend of Brother Simon, the monk said to have poisoned King John at the nearby abbey.
earliest_record: Polly Howat, Ghosts and Legends of Lincolnshire and the Fen Country (Countryside Books, 1992)

name: The Ghosts of Doddington Hall
summary: Two spirits share the Elizabethan hall: a kindly Brown Lady in a stiff old gown who sits smiling beside new brides, and a screaming girl who falls from the roof each year, killed fleeing a lustful master.
detail:
Doddington Hall, built between 1593 and 1600 by the architect Robert Smythson west of Lincoln, is said to keep two very different ghosts. The gentler is the Brown Lady, who appears to new brides alone in one of the bedrooms, a woman in an old-fashioned, long stiff brown dress who sits smiling at the bride for only a few seconds before fading. Far from frightening, those who have seen her describe feeling soothed, as though she were giving her blessing or recalling the early happy days of her own marriage.

The second haunting is grim. On the anniversary of her death a young woman is said to appear on the roof of the hall and fall from it, screaming, having lost her footing while trying to escape a lustful master. Her cry is said to still be heard as she plunges, a yearly echo of a violent end.

Both traditions are recorded by the University of Lincoln's Haunted History of Lincolnshire project among the county's better-attested house hauntings. Doddington's Brown Lady should not be confused with the far more famous Brown Lady of Raynham Hall in Norfolk; the two are wholly separate spirits who happen to share a colour of dress.
historical_setting: Doddington Hall is a Grade I-listed Elizabethan house built 1595-1600 by Thomas Tailor, registrar to the Bishop of Lincoln, to a design by architect Robert Smythson
cultural_tradition: English country-house ghost lore

name: The Whitwick Giant
summary: The Comyns of Whitwick Castle were remembered as giants; one tried to carry off a lady fleeing to sanctuary, and she was saved only when a monk of the Holy Well revived her with its waters as she collapsed.
detail:
Local Leicestershire tradition remembered the Comyn family, holders of Whitwick Castle, as a line of giants. The best-known tale tells how one of the Comyn giants tried to carry off a lady of Groby Castle, who had fled her home to take sanctuary at the priory of Grace Dieu. Going by a roundabout route to avoid Charley and Whitwick, she was overtaken by nightfall in the Outwoods and would have perished there.

She reached instead the hermitage at the Holy Well, near Garendon by Loughborough, and collapsed at its door. One of the monks of the well used its waters to bring her back to life. The story holds that, in gratitude, the revived lady gave herself to God and became a prioress; some have linked the tale to the historical abduction of Eleanor Ferrers.

The Comyns who lend their name to the legend were real. The motte-and-bailey castle at Whitwick was held by the Earl of Leicester in the mid-twelfth century, passed to royal hands by 1204 under King John (with William de Seneville as keeper), and came at last to John Comyn, Earl of Buchan, by the late thirteenth century, and the folk memory swelled the powerful, half-feared family into giants. The tradition is preserved in East Midlands folklore writing and ties the giant tale to the still-known site of the Holy Well Haw.
period: medieval, 12th-13th century (for the historical castle/Comyn context; the giant legend itself is undated)
historical_setting: Whitwick Castle, Leicestershire, a motte-and-bailey castle held by the Earl of Leicester in the mid-12th century, passing to royal hands by 1204 under King John (keeper William de Seneville) and later to John Comyn, Earl of Buchan, by the late 13th century

name: Furbaide Ferbend
region: Carn Clonhugh (Corn Hill), County Longford, Ireland
summary: A hero of the Ulster Cycle killed Queen Medb with a sling-shot of hard cheese to avenge his mother's murder, then was buried, legend says, beneath the cairn on Longford's highest hill.
detail:
In the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology, Furbaide Ferbend was the son of King Conchobar mac Nessa and Clothru, who was murdered by her own sister, Medb, while pregnant with him, in a struggle for the kingship of Connacht. Furbaide was cut from his dying mother's womb and grew up determined to avenge her death.

Years later, learning that Medb (by then queen of Connacht) bathed every morning in a pool on an island in Lough Ree, on the Shannon, Furbaide practised for months with a sling, stretching a cord between two stakes set at the exact distance to the island and firing stone after stone until he could strike an apple balanced on a post every time. When his aim was perfected, he loaded his sling with a piece of hard cheese and, from the shore, struck Medb in the forehead as she bathed, killing her instantly in payment for his mother's death.

The episode is preserved in the Ulster Cycle text 'Aided Meidbe' ('The Violent Death of Medb'), understood by scholars to depict one of the last events in the Cycle's internal chronology, though the specific earliest manuscript witness for the text is not firmly established. Local tradition holds that Furbaide was afterwards buried in the great passage-tomb cairn atop Carn Clonhugh, now known as Corn Hill or Cairn Hill, the highest point in County Longford, and the dindshenchas (place-name lore) of the hill preserves his name in its older title, Carn Furbaide.
earliest_record: 'Aided Meidbe' ('The Violent Death of Medb'), the Ulster Cycle text in which Furbaide kills Medb, is understood by scholars to depict one of the last events in the Cycle's internal chronology; the specific earliest manuscript witness for this text has not been confirmed
period: Early Medieval Ireland (Ulster Cycle material generally dated to 12th-century manuscript compilation, with older linguistic strata)

name: The Pirates of Dollar Bay
region: Dollar Bay, Hook Peninsula, County Wexford, Ireland
summary: Four mutineers slaughtered Captain Glass, his wife and daughter aboard the Earl of Sandwich in 1765 and buried 250 sacks of Spanish silver on a lonely Wexford beach, giving Dollar Bay its name.
detail:
On the night of 30 November 1765, four crewmen of the merchant ship Earl of Sandwich turned on their captain and passengers as she ran through the English Channel bound for London from Tenerife. Peter McKinley, an Irish boatswain, George Gidley, a Yorkshire-born cook, Richard St Quentin, an Englishman, and Andreas Zekerman, a Dutch seaman, beat Captain John Cochrane to death with a marlinspike and threw him overboard. Among the passengers was Captain George Glass of the Royal Navy, an adventurer returning from the Canary Islands with a fortune in Spanish silver and gold dust; Glass fought back and wounded two of his attackers before he was overpowered, and his wife and young daughter Kathleen were thrown into the sea after him. Only two cabin boys were spared.

The mutineers scuttled the Earl of Sandwich once they were within reach of the Irish coast and rowed inshore in the ship's boat, so heavily loaded with coin that it nearly swamped; they tipped handfuls of silver dollars overboard to keep it afloat. About two miles south of Duncannon Fort they waded ashore on a lonely stretch of the Hook Peninsula and buried some 250 sacks of coin in the dunes, fearing the fort's garrison would search them if they carried it further. Flush with cash they had not troubled to hide, the four spent their way toward New Ross, paying for ale and giving away the drowned family's jewellery to innkeepers along the road; the spending drew notice within the week.

A magistrate's party backed by soldiers from Duncannon Fort recovered the buried treasure from the sand and shipped it under guard to the Custom House. All four mutineers were tried in Dublin and hanged at St Stephen's Green on 3 March 1766; their bodies were caged in chains and displayed as a warning, McKinley and Gidley's on the small rock islet of the Muglins in Dublin Bay.

The beach where the silver was dug from the sand has been called Dollar Bay ever since, and not every coin was recovered. Local tradition holds that some of the Earl of Sandwich's treasure still lies in the dunes, and metal detectorists still search the shore for it. Some tellers of the tale credit it with helping to shape Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island.
earliest_record: Trial records of the four mutineers, Dublin, 3 January 1766 (contemporary judicial record)
period: 18th century (1765-1766)
historical_setting: The merchant ship Earl of Sandwich, en route from Tenerife to London with Spanish silver dollars and gold dust; the murder/mutiny occurred in late November 1765, with the mutineers landing and burying treasure at Dollar Bay near Duncannon Fort, County Wexford
cultural_tradition: Irish coastal pirate/treasure legend, tied directly to a documented criminal trial rather than pure oral folklore

name: Loch nan Dubhrachan Water Horse
summary: A dark loch on Skye's Sleat peninsula was said to be the lair of a vicious each-uisge with a taste for pretty girls, so feared that in 1870 the laird ordered the loch dragged with nets to capture it.
detail:
Loch nan Dubhrachan lies beside the old road between Isle Ornsay and Knock on the Sleat peninsula of Skye, and 19th-century folklorists recorded it as the haunt of an each-uisge, the deadly Highland water-horse. Unlike the more familiar kelpie, the each-uisge could take the form of a fine horse or a handsome young man, and this one was said to have a particular fondness for pretty girls, though, as the old tellers warned, his attentions never ended well for them. Travellers near the loch reported being waylaid by a mysterious 'beast', and the stories grew so persistent that by 1870 the laird ordered a full-scale dragging of the loch to settle the matter once and for all.

A Skye man named MacRae, who as a boy was present at the attempt, recalled that the nets, manned by terrified villagers on both shores, suddenly snagged on something huge and powerful in the depths. Convinced they had hooked the water-horse itself, the men dropped the ropes and fled in panic. When the nets were finally recovered they held nothing but mud and two small pike, but the loch's reputation as a dwelling-place of the each-uisge endured, recorded a generation later in J. A. MacCulloch's 'The Misty Isle of Skye' (1905). A second, independent account of the same 1870 attempt surfaced later still, in Alasdair MacGregor's 'Somewhere in Scotland' (1935), based on a first-hand interview with MacRae himself, giving the incident two separate published witnesses rather than one.
earliest_record: J.A. MacCulloch, 'The Misty Isle of Skye' (1905), describing the water-horse's reputation and the 1870 netting attempt; the 1870 incident was independently retold via an eyewitness account from John MacRae (present as a child on Isle Ornsay), published later in Alasdair MacGregor's 'Somewhere in Scotland' (1935)
period: 19th century (documented incident, 1870; recorded in print 1905)
cultural_tradition: Scottish Highland/Skye each-uisge folklore

name: William Owen, the Smuggler General of Pembrokeshire
summary: Born to a respectable farming family in Nevern in 1717, William Owen ran away to sea as a teenager and became one of Wales's most notorious smugglers, running brandy and salt across Cardigan Bay, leading an armed 'siege' of a Cardiganshire mansion, and surviving one murder trial only to hang after a second.
detail:
William Owen was born in January 1717 in Nevern, Pembrokeshire, the son of a well-to-do farmer who hoped his clever son would become a clergyman. Instead Owen ran away to sea as a teenager and, sailing as far as the Caribbean and trading blows with Spanish vessels along the way, built himself into one of the most successful smugglers on the Welsh coast, running brandy, salt and other contraband across Cardigan Bay between the Isle of Man and the harbours of Pembrokeshire and the Llyn Peninsula.

His most colourful exploit came when he led an armed band of Pembrokeshire and Cardiganshire men, gathered to support a friend, 'Mr Parry', in a dispute with the powerful Johnes family of Aber-mad, in a march on the Johnes' mansion near Aberystwyth. Nominated 'general' of the assembled men, Owen led them to the gates of the great house, but at the sight of its armed and well-manned defences his troops lost their nerve and the siege collapsed without a shot fired. He was also implicated in a corn riot in 1741, part of a wider pattern of coastal disorder that ran alongside his smuggling.

The law caught up with him twice. In spring 1744 a customs officer was killed during a confrontation over contraband in Cardigan Bay, and Owen stood trial for it at Hereford in March 1745. He had, by his own account, 'gained the affection of the country very much', and after twelve hours of proceedings a jury acquitted him outright, though the surviving court record lists his conviction on the lesser charge of manslaughter. His wife died at sea in a storm not long after. Then, in 1746, a fencing master named James Lilly was found shot dead on the road, and witnesses placed Owen at the scene with a pistol in hand. Tried at the Carmarthen Great Sessions in April 1747, he was convicted on circumstantial evidence and hanged on 2 May, aged thirty.

While awaiting execution, Owen dictated or wrote his life story to the Reverend John Davies, rector of Cardigan; the manuscript, some eighteen thousand words on vellum, survives at the National Library of Wales alongside a transcript of his final trial, the only surviving primary account of the case. His exploits were dramatised on stage in towns across Wales within his own lifetime, and his confession remains one of the best-documented smugglers' lives of eighteenth-century Wales.
earliest_record: contemporary 18th-century trial and biographical pamphlet material; The National Archives holds a period record 'Owen, William, (1717-1747), Smuggler'
historical_setting: 18th-century Pembrokeshire/Cardigan Bay smuggling trade; Owen was hanged for murder at Carmarthen, 2 May 1747

name: The Giant Bica of Llangrannog
summary: A giant who lived in the hills above Llangrannog suffered such terrible toothache that he spat the offending tooth onto the beach below, where it still stands today as the rock called Carreg Bica.
detail:
On the beach at Llangrannog in Ceredigion stands a tall, jagged outcrop of rock known as Carreg Bica, 'Bica's Tooth', an Ordovician sea stack that divides the beaches of Traeth Llangrannog and Cilborth. According to local legend it takes its name from Bica, a giant, in some tellings identified as the Devil himself, who lived in the hills overlooking the village and watched over its people as a guardian.

Two versions explain his toothache. In one, Bica's furious stamping and roaring over the pain disturbed a dwarf named Lochtyn, who advised him to head for the coast, where the cold salt water would draw the tooth out; in gratitude for the advice, Lochtyn asked only for a small island of his own where he could live in peace. In the other, Bica was on his way to a village fete when he spotted berries growing on a nearby hill, bent down to bite into them, and instead bit into the bare rock they grew from, then stumbled to the shore to rinse his bleeding mouth in the sea. Either way, the giant's tooth came loose in the cold water and lodged upright in the sand, becoming Carreg Bica.

Whichever telling is followed, Bica kept his side of the bargain with Lochtyn: he ran his finger along the coastline to carve out a peninsula and separate off a small island just for his helper, the rocky promontory and tidal islet still known today as Ynys Lochtyn. Both landmarks remain popular stops on the Ceredigion coast path, where the giant's tooth towers over walkers on the beach below.

name: Bedd Dorti, the Witch's Grave
region: Llyn Tecwyn Uchaf, Meirionnydd, Gwynedd, Wales
summary: A 17th-century woman feared as a witch was hurled in a cask from the cliffs above Llyn Tecwyn Uchaf, and the cairn of stones marking where she landed, Bedd Dorti, is said to bring death within a year to anyone who passes without adding a stone to the pile.
detail:
On the high ground above Llyn Tecwyn Uchaf, on the old road between Llandecwyn and Maentwrog in Meirionnydd, stands a stone-covered mound known as Bedd Dorti, Dorti's Grave, or in fuller Welsh tradition Dorti'r Wrach, Dorti the Witch. Local tradition holds that Dorti was a seventeenth-century woman widely feared as a witch, always seen with a black cat on her shoulder, who was seized by her neighbours, sealed inside a cask and hurled from the rocks above the lake rather than tried under the law. The mound was said to mark the spot where the cask came to rest.

The site carries its own surviving superstition: travellers passing the mound are expected to add a white stone to the heap, on pain of dying within the year if they fail to do so. The antiquarian W. J. Hemp, recording the tradition for the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales, was told in 1943 that the mound had already been disturbed once, moved around 1920 during the construction of a dam at the foot of the lake.

The story took one more turn decades later. When Welsh Water cut into the mound during works around the turn of the twenty-first century, it proved to be not an artificial cairn at all but a natural ridge of rock, no burial and no witch beneath the stones, only the story the white stones themselves had kept alive. Dorti's grave survives today as one of Meirionnydd's best-known pieces of witch-lore regardless of what the ground turned out to hold.
origin_date: 17th century (traditional; the event itself is not precisely dated in any surviving record)
earliest_record: W. J. Hemp's 1943 note to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales, preserved in the RCAHMW/Coflein record (NPRN 800208)
period: 17th century (traditional setting); earliest written record 20th century

name: The Witch of East Somerton
summary: A woman accused of witchcraft was said to have been buried alive in the nave of St Mary's Church at East Somerton, and her wooden leg took root and grew into the great oak that still stands inside the ruined church today.
detail:
In the ruins of St Mary's Church at East Somerton, deep in a Norfolk wood, a massive oak tree now grows where the nave once stood, its trunk rising through walls of knapped flint and ashlar. The tower dates to the 13th century and the nave was rebuilt in the 15th, and the building had fallen out of regular worship by the late 17th century. Local legend says the tree marks the grave of a woman from the village who was accused of witchcraft and buried alive within the church by her neighbours. As she was interred, her wooden leg was said to have been planted with her, and over the centuries it took root and grew into the oak that dominates the ruin today, sometimes called 'the Witch's Leg' or 'the Witch's Finger'.

The ruin is substantial enough to read as a building rather than a scatter of stones. Its three-stage west tower still stands, missing its belfry stage, braced by diagonal buttresses and lit by pointed lancet windows in the ringing chamber below; three tall windows once lined the nave on each side, and the chancel arch survives with roll and sunk hollow mouldings, though no trace of the chancel itself remains. Large holes have been broken through the walls of the two westernmost bays, and Historic England listed the ruin Grade II in September 1962.

The legend carries its own piece of living folk practice: it is said that anyone who walks around the tree three times will release the witch's spirit. The story has become one of the best known pieces of 'Weird Norfolk' folklore, regularly retold by local newspapers and the Norfolk Folklore Society, and the ruin, oak growing through broken flint walls in dense woodland near Winterton-on-Sea, remains a popular, if eerie, walking destination today.
period: medieval church (13th-century tower, 15th-century nave); abandoned in regular use by the late 17th century
historical_setting: the ruined St Mary's Church, East Somerton, Norfolk, between Martham Broad and Winterton-on-Sea; the building fell out of use in the late 17th century and has stood roofless ever since, with an oak tree now growing inside the nave

name: Gill, the Hammer-Throwing Giant of Mount Caburn
summary: Sussex tradition set a giant named Gill on the Iron-Age hillfort of Mount Caburn above Lewes, who amused himself by hurling his great hammer from the summit out across the Downs.
detail:
Mount Caburn, the steep Iron-Age hillfort that rises above the village of Glynde near Lewes, is remembered in Sussex folklore as the seat of a giant named Gill. Like the giants said to have once walked the whole chalk range of the South Downs, he was a hill-dweller of enormous strength, and the tale most often told of him is that he passed the time by flinging his huge hammer from the top of the Caburn far out over the surrounding country.

A related Sussex tradition sets the same giant, sometimes under the same name, on Firle Beacon a few miles to the east, from where he is said to have hurled his hammer clean across the Cuckmere valley at his rival on Windover Hill, the vast chalk-cut figure now known as the Long Man of Wilmington. The tale was collected directly from local tradition by the folklorist John Philipps Emslie, who was told that the giant of Firle Beacon threw his hammer at the giant of Windover Hill and killed him outright, and that the fallen giant's outline is what became the chalk figure still cut into the hillside today. The two hills face each other across open country, and the hammer-throwing rivalry gave Sussex antiquarians a ready explanation for why two such prominent landmarks should stand in sight of one another. Gill of the Caburn belongs to that older imaginative geography, in which the green ramparts above Lewes were not the labour of Iron-Age hands but the home of a being vast enough to throw his hammer across the Downs.

name: Janet Horne
summary: At Dornoch in 1727, an old and confused woman became the last person legally executed for witchcraft in the British Isles, accused of turning her own daughter into a pony shod by the Devil.
detail:
Janet Horne, the name is partly a convention, 'Jenny Horne' being a generic Highland nickname for a witch, was an elderly woman of Dornoch in Sutherland, by all accounts senile, whose daughter had a deformity of the hands and feet. Her neighbours seized on this, accusing the old woman of having used her daughter as a pony to ride to the Devil, who had shod the girl for the journey.

The local sheriff-depute condemned her, and in 1727 Janet Horne was stripped, smeared with tar, paraded through the town in a barrel and burned. Tradition holds that, bewildered to the end, she warmed her hands at the very fire being readied to kill her. Her death is remembered as the last legal execution for witchcraft in the British Isles; the Witchcraft Act was repealed nine years later. A stone in the Littletown district of Dornoch, the Witch's Stone, is said to mark the spot, though even the date is disputed between 1722 and 1727, a measure of how poorly the killing of a confused old woman was recorded.

The historian Lizanne Henderson has shown that most of the details commonly retold today were not set down in print until around ninety-two years after the execution, in the early nineteenth century, and that no contemporary kirk session or presbytery record of the case survives at all, a reminder of how thin the documentary trail behind even Scotland's most infamous witch trial really is.
origin_date: 1727 (traditional date; 1722 also proposed, and the discrepancy is itself well documented rather than a research gap)
earliest_record: Historian Lizanne Henderson has noted that the most commonly retold details of Janet Horne's case were not published in print until 92 years after the execution (i.e. c.1814-1819), with no surviving contemporary kirk session or presbytery records
period: Early 18th-century Scotland (traditional execution date); modern retelling substantially dates from the early 19th century

name: Maggie Wall
summary: A 20-foot cairn near Dunning, topped with a cross and painted 'Maggie Wall burnt here 1657 as a witch', memorialises a woman for whom no historical record exists, a monument to all Scotland's accused.
detail:
On a quiet road outside Dunning in Perthshire stands one of Scotland's strangest monuments: a rough cairn some twenty feet high, crowned by a cross, on which is painted in white letters 'Maggie Wall burnt here 1657 as a witch'. Visitors leave coins, feathers, flowers and candles at its foot, and the inscription is repainted by unknown hands to keep it legible.

The mystery is that no Maggie Wall appears in any record. The exhaustive Survey of Scottish Witchcraft, which lists every documented trial between 1563 and 1736, contains no such woman, and the monument itself seems to date only from the late eighteenth century. Whether she existed, or whether the cairn commemorates some half-remembered local victim under an invented name, has never been resolved. In its very anonymity the monument has become something larger, a memorial to the thousands of mostly poor women accused and killed in Scotland's witch-hunts, a named stone standing in for all the nameless.
origin_date: Late 18th century (the monument's own construction date); 1657 is the date painted on the cairn but is entirely unverified. No such person appears in the Survey of Scottish Witchcraft's comprehensive 1563-1736 trial records
period: The monument itself dates from the late 1700s; the '1657' burning it claims to commemorate has no corroborating historical record of any kind

name: Tamsin Blight
