She is also said to have predicted that two standing stones four miles apart, at Carnduff and Barnish, would eventually be joined, and that Ballycastle would learn of Irish independence when a ship entered the bay with its sails ablaze.

Before her death she asked, as an act of humility, to be buried at the friary's ruined west doorway so that everyone entering would walk over her grave. A holed disc-headed cross still marks the spot today, at the ruins of Bonamargy, which stand on the outskirts of Ballycastle roughly where the McQuillans first raised them five centuries ago. Her story has become a fixture of Antrim's ghost-lore, kept alive by a dedicated local-history site and repeated in regional heritage coverage, with the friary itself still spoken of locally as a place watched over by her spirit.
period: Mid-to-late 17th century
historical_setting: Bonamargy Friary after the Franciscan friars departed, traditionally dated to 1642 during the Irish Confederate Wars
cultural_tradition: Ulster prophecy and ghost-lore tied to the McQuillan clan, who founded the friary c.1500

name: The White Trout of Cong
summary: A noblewoman whose betrothed was murdered and thrown into a Cong lake vanished after him, and reappeared forever after as a white trout that bleeds when cut and heals when returned to the water.
detail:
According to the tale as collected by Samuel Lover from local storytellers and later reprinted by W. B. Yeats in his 1888 anthology of Irish peasant folklore, a beautiful young woman near Cong was promised in marriage to a king's son. When her betrothed was murdered and his body thrown into the lake, grief drove her out of her mind, and she disappeared, swallowed, tradition says, by the fairies who followed him into the water. From that day a white trout appeared in the lake and was never caught, since the people came to believe it was no ordinary fish.

The legend's most vivid episode concerns a soldier who caught the trout regardless and set it in a frying pan to cook. No matter how long he cooked it, the fish would not brown, until he cut into it with a knife, at which point it screamed, leapt from the pan, and became a bleeding woman in white and gold, who rebuked him for the wound before asking to be returned to the water. When he threw the trout back, the lake ran red for a time, and the fish is said to carry the scar of the cut to this day.

The tale is one of the most frequently anthologised pieces of Connacht folklore, distinct from, though sometimes confused with, the region's separate Dobhar-chú legend from County Leitrim.
earliest_record: Samuel Lover, Legends and Stories of Ireland (1831), the earliest print source, collected by Lover from oral tradition in the Cong area
period: Collected in the early 19th century (1831); the underlying oral tradition is likely older
historical_setting: Cong, County Mayo, on the lake shore near Cong Abbey
cultural_tradition: Irish oral folk tradition; widely anthologised afterward, including in W. B. Yeats's Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888)

name: The Hogboon of Helliehow
summary: A mound-dwelling guardian spirit kept Helliehow farm prosperous for generations in exchange for offerings of milk and ale, until a disrespectful new wife let the farm fall to ruin.
detail:
The hogboon (from Old Norse haug-búi, "mound-dweller") is Orkney's name for a family guardian spirit believed to live in an earthen mound beside a farm. At Helliehow, a farm on the island of Sanday, tradition held that the resident hogboon protected the household and ensured good fortune so long as the family shared its produce with him: pouring milk or ale over his mound and leaving butter and bannocks as offerings after a birth or marriage.

The story's turning point comes when a new wife arrives at Helliehow and refuses to keep up the old customs, withholding the hogboon's due. The farm's fortunes collapse soon after and it falls into ruin, told locally as a cautionary demonstration of what happens when the old obligations to the mound-spirit are broken. The tale belongs to a wider Orcadian tradition of named hogboons tied to specific farms (a similar figure is recorded at Maeshowe itself, described in an 1862 antiquarian account as a supernaturally strong "person named Hogboy"), but the Helliehow version is one of the best-preserved individual accounts. It was collected and published by Walter Traill Dennison (1825-1894), a gentleman farmer at West Brough on Sanday itself, whose 'Orcadian Sketch Book' (1880) and later folk-tale collections are now regarded as the single most important surviving record of Orkney's oral tradition, much of it drawn from stories he heard as a child from the island's own crofters and cottars.
period: 19th century (collection/publication); underlying tradition Norse-derived, medieval or earlier
cultural_tradition: Orcadian / Norse-Orkney folklore

name: The Giant Snake of Penhesgyn
summary: A venomous giant viper terrorised a Penmynydd farm until a villager tricked it into striking its own reflection in a polished brass pan, but a fortune-teller's prophecy still claimed a life.
detail:
Tradition tells of a huge, poisonous serpent that took up residence in the wilder corners of Penhesgyn farm, in the parish of Penmynydd on Anglesey, terrorising the local community with its size and venom. A fortune teller warned the farm's owners that the snake would kill their only son, so the family sent him away to England for safety.

A local villager devised a trick to be rid of the creature: he dug a deep pit and set within it a large, shallow brass pan, polished until it shone like a mirror. Mistaking its own reflection for a rival, the viper attacked the pan again and again until it had exhausted itself and spent its venom, at which point the villager killed it with a single blow. The prophecy proved impossible to escape, though: years later the son returned home, visited the burial spot, and contemptuously kicked the serpent's skull, a splinter of which pierced his thin shoe and delivered a final dose of venom that killed him within hours.

The tale is a distinctively local variant of Wales's broader serpent-and-dragon folklore (echoing the Dinas Emrys tradition), and it is recorded independently in both a dedicated Anglesey local-history site and a folklore blog.
earliest_record: Field names 'Parc dragon wen' and 'Part of Parc dragon wen' recorded in Penmynydd parish, Anglesey, in 1841 (RCAHMW Historic Place Names of Wales). This is the earliest documented trace of a dragon/serpent tradition at the site, though this is a landscape/field-name record rather than a telling of the tale itself
period: Dragon tradition attested in local field-naming by 1841 (tithe-era survey); the oral tale itself is almost certainly older but cannot be dated more precisely
cultural_tradition: Anglesey oral dragon/serpent folklore tied to local field-names (a small cluster of 'Dragon' place-names survives around Penmynydd, echoing the red-and-white dragons of Dinas Emrys)

name: St Botolph and the Devil
summary: The Devil, cornered by St Botolph at his new seventh-century chapel, could only huff and puff in fury, and the whirlwind around "Boston Stump" is said never to have entirely subsided since.
detail:
According to an account first printed in Roger Quaint's 1841 Traditions of Lincolnshire, St Botolph, who tradition holds founded a chapel at Boston in 654, though historians now consider Iken in Suffolk the more likely site of his actual monastery, grew briefly proud of his achievement, a weakness the Devil moved to exploit. Botolph recognised the temptation for what it was and confronted Satan directly; the ensuing struggle was so one-sided that "the poor devil puffed and blowed so violently as to raise a whirlwind, which has never since entirely subsided."

The legend survives today as a piece of living folk-explanation: the exposed footpath beside St Botolph's parish church tower, universally known as "Boston Stump," is one of the windiest spots in the churchyard, and locals still attribute the gusts to the Devil's furious, unending exhalation. The Paranormal Database independently records the same tradition under its Lincolnshire devil-lore entries, describing the winds as "the Devil's breath." Quaint himself was already fending off rival explanations in 1841, noting drily that "some vain-glorious philosophers have pretended to explain this phenomenon on what they call scientific principles," a line that shows the supernatural account was competing with weather science even in his own day.

The tale sits alongside a small cluster of Lincolnshire saint-versus-devil stories, including the Lincoln Imp and the curse laid on Crowland Abbey, and follows the same pattern as other English tales in which the Devil is thwarted by a local holy man, such as the story told of Dunstan.
historical_setting: St Botolph's monastery is traditionally said to have been founded in 654; the claim rests on the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and is disputed by modern historians, who consider Iken, Suffolk the more likely site of Botolph's actual foundation.
period: 7th century (historical St Botolph); the devil-and-wind folk tale is undated

name: The Binbrook Bewitched Farm (1905)
summary: Flying sausages, a dead rabbit that kept coming back to its hook, and a wagon six horses couldn't shift. The 1905 "witching" of Walk Farm made national news before the trail went cold.
detail:
In the winter of 1904-1905, foreman Henry White and his wife Sarah Jane, tenants of Walk Farm near Binbrook on the Lincolnshire Wolds, reported an escalating run of inexplicable events: potted plants tilting and righting themselves on the windowsill, a dead rabbit that detached itself from a hook, ran about, and returned to the hook, and brooms that came "dancing" across the floor at dinnertime. The disturbances were widely reported in the local and national press through January and February 1905, and grew steadily more sensational: strings of home-made sausages breaking apart after being re-hung three times, a dozen dinner plates found relocated unbroken from a high shelf, and eventually a loaded wagon that six horses together could not move, while the foreman was reportedly wheeled about the yard at speed in a wheelbarrow by unseen hands.

The household's servant girl, Mabel Sheldrick, was seriously burned when her clothing caught fire while she stood well clear of any hearth, and spent nearly a month recovering in Louth Hospital, an injury that hardened suspicions of witchcraft against her specifically. Offers to "lay the witch" poured in from around the country, and the Whites eventually accepted help from a professional witch-doctor, John Dunn of Grimsby. Mrs White later disputed many of the more fantastical newspaper embellishments, and by March 1905 press interest had faded and the case went cold.

The episode is documented independently in period-newspaper reprints and in local folklore history, and is notable for being investigated as recently as 1905, remarkably late for an English witchcraft scare.
earliest_record: January-February 1905 newspaper reports of the 'Bewitched Farm' at Walk Farm, Binbrook
period: Edwardian era (1905)
historical_setting: A tenant farm on the Lincolnshire Wolds, occupied by foreman White under owner William Drakes
cultural_tradition: English rural witchcraft/poltergeist scare, of the type that regularly attracted national press coverage in this period

name: The Ghost of Hellens Manor
summary: Locked in her room for thirty years after an unsanctioned marriage, Hetty Walwyn scratched her despair into the windowpane with a diamond ring, and is said to haunt the chamber still.
detail:
Hellens Manor at Much Marcle, first recorded in 1180, is home to one of Herefordshire's best-known ghost stories. Mehetabel 'Hetty' Walwyn, the youngest daughter of the 17th-century owner, eloped with a man her family considered beneath her station; by the time she was twenty her husband had died, and she returned home to find her family unforgiving. They locked her in an upstairs bedchamber for the following thirty years as punishment for the disgrace, giving her only a bell to summon servants. She is said to have gone mad in confinement, and to have scratched a mournful verse into the windowpane with her diamond ring: 'it is a part of virtue to abstain from what we love if it should prove our bane.' Tradition holds that she eventually took her own life in the room.

Hetty's ghost is said to still haunt her old bedchamber; the current custodian of Hellens has reported sensing her presence while sleeping in the room above, and a seventeenth-century herbal found in her room is kept by the family as a relic of her confinement. A second, unrelated haunting is attached to the house: an elderly Catholic priest sheltering at Hellens during the Civil War was reportedly cornered and killed by Parliamentarian soldiers in a separate room.

The story is recorded across multiple independent paranormal-history and local-history sources, distinct from Herefordshire's better-known Mordiford dragon and Black Vaughan legends. Hellens remains the Walwyn family's home today and opens its house and garden to visitors, Hetty's room shown among its historic chambers.
period: 17th century (family tradition places Hetty in the generation after Richard Walwyn, who hosted Mary Tudor in the 16th century)
historical_setting: Hellens manor house, Much Marcle, Herefordshire, home of the Walwyn family

name: Cloughmore Stone
summary: A 50-tonne boulder Finn McCool supposedly hurled clean across Carlingford Lough at a rival giant, gouging a 'wishing chair' where it landed above Rostrevor.
detail:
High on the slopes of Slieve Martin, nearly a thousand feet above the County Down village of Rostrevor, sits Cloughmore, from the Irish An Chloch Mhór, 'the big stone'. Geologists identify it as a glacial erratic, a fifty-tonne block of granite carried from an island off the Scottish coast and dropped here some ten thousand years ago as the last ice age retreated. Local tradition tells a different story entirely.

Fionn mac Cumhaill's rival in the tale is named Ruscaire, the Giant of Snow and Ice, sworn enemy of the whole human race. Their feud began, the story goes, when Ruscaire crept up on Fionn as he slept and stole his sword. Furious, Fionn gave chase, and the two fought first with swords, then with clubs, before the battle escalated into a running exchange of boulders hurled across Carlingford Lough that shook the mountains on both sides. Fionn's final throw, the fifty-tonne stone still standing on Slieve Martin today, struck Ruscaire's head and crushed him back into the mountainside, where his body is said to have melted away like the ice he was named for. The effort finished Fionn too: he collapsed where he stood and never woke again, and his own body is said to have turned to stone in turn, its outline still traced today in the profile of Slieve Foy across the water in County Louth, head and face on the peak, body stretching down toward the shore.

The stone's landing on Slieve Martin is said to have carved out a hollow at its base known as Finn's Wishing Chair, and a persistent local custom holds that circling the boulder seven times will bring good luck to the walker who does it. The site now sits within Kilbroney Park and forms part of a National Nature Reserve, drawing hikers up the Cloughmore Stone trail for the view over Carlingford Lough and the Cooley Peninsula as much as for the folklore, a rare case of a scientifically explained landscape feature that has kept its giant's-throw legend fully alive alongside the geology.
origin_date: c. 10,000 years ago (glacial deposit, not a legendary date)
period: The stone's own placement is a natural post-glacial event; the Finn mac Cumhaill throwing-legend has no dateable origin of its own beyond an unconfirmed reference to an '18th-century tale' of a fisherman sheltering at the stone, which has not been traced to a specific written source

name: Daft Eddie and the Merry Hearts of Down
region: Killinchy and Sketrick Island, Strangford Lough, County Down, Northern Ireland
summary: A gang of 18th-century smugglers called the Merry Hearts of Down ran contraband brandy through Strangford Lough's islands, with a simple foundling boy, Daft Eddie, as their unlikely go-between.
detail:
In the eighteenth century, and by some accounts as late as its opening years of the next, a band of smugglers known as the Merry Hearts of Down worked the maze of drumlin islands on Strangford Lough, running brandy, tobacco and other contraband up from the Irish Sea and unloading it at hidden coves along the Ards Peninsula. Their activities went well beyond smuggling into kidnap and extortion, and local memory remembers them running a genuine reign of terror around the lough shore for years. At the centre of the legend that grew up around them is Daft Eddie, said to have been an illegitimate infant left on the doorstep of a family named White on Mahee Island, a simple-minded local boy who came to know every channel and hiding place in the lough. Eddie fell in with the smugglers, meeting their luggers among the islands and helping guide contraband through to Sketrick Island, where the ruins of the fifteenth-century Sketrick Castle still stand. Written accounts differ on exactly when the gang was active and when Eddie himself was born, some placing the smuggling firmly in the eighteenth century and others in its early nineteenth-century tail end, a discrepancy the surviving record has never resolved.

The tale was fixed in local memory by the Bangor journalist W. G. Lyttle, who serialised it in his own newspaper, the North Down Herald and Bangor Gazette, in 1889 as 'Daft Eddie; or, the Smugglers of Strangford Lough: A Tale of Killinchy', publishing it in book form the following year. In Lyttle's telling, Eddie's shadowing of the gang draws him into a plot involving an abducted magistrate and his daughter. The story turned Eddie into a genuine local folk hero, and a restaurant on Sketrick Island, Daft Eddy's, still carries his name today, keeping the smugglers' legend attached to the actual causeway and castle where it is set.
earliest_record: W. G. Lyttle serialised 'Daft Eddie; or, the Smugglers of Strangford Lough: A Tale of Killinchy' in his newspaper the North Down Herald in 1889, publishing it in book form in 1890
period: Story's smuggling setting is the 18th century
historical_setting: 18th-century smuggling economy on Strangford Lough, County Down
cultural_tradition: Ulster-Scots popular literature/serialised local fiction

name: Cribarth, the Sleeping Giant
summary: A mountain silhouette above the Tawe Valley is said to be a giant named Yscydion, lying asleep until Arthur returns and calls him to defend his people.
detail:
Cribarth rises at the southern gateway to the Tawe Valley in the Brecon Beacons, and from the right angle its ridgeline reads unmistakably as a reclining human figure, head to one side, body sloping away down the hill; this has earned the area the local nickname 'the Land of the Sleeping Giant.' Welsh folklore gives the recumbent figure a name, Yscydion, and holds that he lies in enchanted sleep waiting to be roused when his people need him most, echoing the wider Welsh and British tradition of a sleeping hero-defender kept in reserve, the same role played by Arthur himself in numerous Welsh cave legends.

Both this giant and a second name attached to the same hill, Cribwr, trace to the same source: an account of Welsh giants and their dwellings compiled around 1600 and attributed to the Welsh scholar Siôn Dafydd Rhys, one of the earliest attempts to catalogue the country's giant-lore systematically. Rhys's Yscydion Gawr is more properly associated with Moel Yscydion in North Wales, suggesting the name may have travelled south and attached itself to Cribarth's equally giant-shaped silhouette rather than originating there, a reminder that Welsh giant legends were rarely fixed to a single hill for long. The related figure Cribwr, whose name is more directly tied to Cribarth itself, belongs to a separate strand of the tradition connected to Arthur's court, where he answers to the names Hot Pottage, Warm Porridge and Morsel of Bread when summoned by three sisters, a comic variant that shows the sleeping-giant tradition here has been retold and reshaped across several centuries rather than fixed in a single telling.

The mountain sits above one of the most folklore-dense valleys in South Wales: at its foot lies Cerrig Duon, a Bronze Age stone circle and stone row complex sometimes called the most sacred pagan site in Wales, and the surrounding Fforest Fawr has its own scattering of ghost and giant tales tied to the old drovers' roads.
earliest_record: Sion Dafydd Rhys, manuscript treatise on the giants of Wales, Peniarth MS 118 (National Library of Wales), c. 1600. It names 'Cribwr Gawr' directly and states the place was called Cribarth ('Garth Cribwr Gawr') after him
period: Attested in writing by c. 1600; the specific 'Yscydion, sleeping and awaiting Arthur's call' framing found in modern retellings does not appear in the Rhys manuscript (which names the giant Cribwr, not Yscydion, and gives no Arthur-return motif). It looks like a later elaboration or conflation with the separate Yscydion Gawr of Moel Yscydion in Meirionnydd
cultural_tradition: Welsh giant-lore explaining place names (the cyfarwyddiaid storytelling tradition), the same corpus that produced Gogmagog and other Brut-derived giant legends

name: Culver Hole and the Smugglers of Port Eynon
summary: A stone-walled sea cave on the Gower coast was said to be smuggler John Lucas's contraband store, reached by a tunnel wide enough to ride a horse through.
detail:
Culver Hole is a narrow cleft in the cliffs near Port Eynon on the Gower Peninsula, sealed behind a sixty-foot stone wall pierced with irregular window openings. It is usually described as a dovecote, 'culver' being an old English word for pigeon, and the interior still shows roughly thirty rows of what look like nesting boxes. The dovecote explanation has never fully satisfied historians, though. The wall's sheer massiveness, its awkward and barely accessible site, and window openings that look better suited to hoisting goods than housing birds have led some researchers to argue its original purpose was closer to a fortified store or a hideaway invisible from the clifftop above, with the pigeon boxes perhaps a later addition to an older structure. No definite construction date has ever been agreed, with estimates ranging across the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries; Cadw's own scheduled-monument record links the structure to a castle at Port Eynon referenced in a lawsuit dated 1396, giving it at least a firm outer bound independent of anything said about it later.

Local legend attached to the site a far more colourful history. The eighteenth-century smuggler John Lucas, a Gower man reputed to have spent years abroad as a pirate before returning home, was said to have refitted nearby Salthouse as his smuggling headquarters and used Culver Hole itself as a hidden store for contraband brandy and tobacco, connected to Salthouse by a secret tunnel said to be wide enough to ride a horse through.

The legend has a well-documented origin of its own. Research by the National Trust has shown that the Lucas smuggling story was largely invented in the 1830s by the Reverend Dr J. H. Spry, who wrote it up as a family history in connection with a lawsuit over ownership of the property. That the tale is a nineteenth-century fabrication rather than an authentic eighteenth-century tradition does not appear to have dented its staying power. Culver Hole is still presented across Gower tourism and heritage sites today as 'the Smuggler's Cove', and the fictional John Lucas remains the cave's best-known association, making this as much a legend about the manufacture of folklore as a smuggling tale in its own right.
earliest_record: A castle at Port Eynon is referenced in a lawsuit dated 1396, cited in Cadw's Scheduled Monument record (Cadw Source ID 3633 / Legacy ID GM325) as the likely context for the dovecote's construction. The smuggling legend itself is a documented 19th-century fabrication, first written up in the 1830s by Rev. Dr J. H. Spry.
period: Structure: medieval/post-medieval; smuggling legend: fabricated 1830s

name: The Gwybr of Llanrhaeadr
summary: A winged serpent living in the lake above Wales's tallest waterfall swooped down to carry off villagers, until they tricked it into impaling itself on hidden spikes.
detail:
Above Pistyll Rhaeadr, at over 240 feet the tallest waterfall in Wales, near Llanrhaeadr-ym-Mochnant in Powys, local tradition places the lair of a winged serpent called the Gwybr, said to have lived in Llyn Luncaws, the lake feeding the falls. The Gwybr was no shy lake-dweller. It flew down from its pool every few days to seize children, women and livestock from the village below, carrying them back up to the lake to be devoured, terrorising the community for years.

At a loss for how to kill so fearsome a creature, the villagers walked for days over the mountains to consult a wise woman of the hills, who told them how the Gwybr's own aggression could be turned against it. Following her counsel, they built a decoy, a mock dragon set with hidden iron spikes, and needled the real Gwybr into attacking it. The creature threw itself at its rival with such force that it impaled itself on the spikes and died, freeing the village from its reign of terror. A standing stone still marks the spot, an upright monolith over eleven feet tall known locally as Post Coch, the Red Post, or Post-y-Wiber, the Wyvern's Post, set near a possible round barrow a short way from the falls and recorded in the Royal Commission's own inventory of Welsh antiquities. Villagers point to it today as the very spike the Gwybr impaled itself upon, tangible proof of a victory otherwise known only through the spoken tale.

The tale belongs to a small but distinct cluster of North and Mid Wales dragon-and-waterfall legends, sitting alongside the much more famous Dinas Emrys story, but anchored to its own waterfall and its own named creature rather than retelling the red-and-white dragon myth.

name: St Osyth Witches and Ursula Kemp
summary: A cunning woman's falling-out with a neighbour over a nursemaid's job triggered a 1582 witch-hunt that swept up fourteen women from one small Essex village.
detail:
Ursula Kemp worked in the Essex village of St Osyth as a cunning woman, valued by her neighbours for curing illness through charms and folk remedies. Her friendship with a local woman, Grace Thurlow, soured after Ursula, having helped cure Grace's son Davy, hoped to be taken on as nursemaid to Grace's infant daughter Joan and was passed over. When baby Joan later died after falling from her cradle, suspicion fell on the spurned Ursula. A second accuser, Alice Letherdale, added her own charge, claiming Ursula had bewitched her daughter Elizabeth to death after being refused a gift of scouring sand. In February 1582 Ursula was brought before the Chelmsford Assizes, presided over by Brian Darcy, a local magistrate already known as a committed pursuer of witches.

Under questioning, and after promises of leniency that were not kept, Ursula confessed. Her own eight-year-old son, Thomas Rabbet, gave evidence that helped seal the case, describing four familiar spirits his mother kept: a grey cat named Tyffin, a white lamb called Tyttey, a black toad named Pygine and a black cat called Jacke. Ursula went on to name four other women as witches, Elizabeth Bennet, Alice Hunt, Alice Newman and Margery Sammon, who in turn implicated a further nine, dragging a total of fourteen women from the single village of St Osyth into the trial. Only Ursula Kemp and Elizabeth Bennet are known to have been sentenced to hang.

The case remained more than a historical footnote. In 1921 the skeletons of two women were unearthed in a St Osyth garden by Charles Brooker, buried on a north-south axis with iron rivets driven through their joints, a method recalling folk practices for pinning down the restless dead. One skeleton was widely, though never certainly, identified as Ursula Kemp's own. The remains became something of a tourist curiosity: bought by Cecil Williamson for his Museum of Witchcraft and displayed in a purple silk-lined coffin, sold on in 1999 to the artist and collector Robert Lenkiewicz for his private library, then returned to the museum after his death. Their true identity is still disputed, a real body caught up in the same uncertainty that once surrounded the women's guilt.
earliest_record: A True and Just Recorde (1582), a pamphlet attributed to the initials W.W., very probably the prosecuting magistrate Brian Darcy himself, documenting pre-trial examinations and testimony in detail
period: Elizabethan England, reign of Elizabeth I
historical_setting: Witchcraft prosecutions tried at the Chelmsford Assizes, Essex, 1582
cultural_tradition: English witch-hunting and cunning-folk tradition

name: The Killing of Charles Walton
region: Meon Hill, Lower Quinton, Warwickshire, England
summary: A black dog met on nine straight nights, and a headless woman seen the night before an old farmhand's ritualistic murder on Meon Hill, fed Britain's most famous unsolved 'witchcraft' killing.
detail:
On St Valentine's Day 1945, seventy-four-year-old farm labourer Charles Walton was found murdered at The Firs farm on the slopes of Meon Hill near Lower Quinton, Warwickshire, his throat and chest slashed in the shape of a cross with his own billhook, which was left embedded in one of the wounds, and his body pinned to the ground by a hay-fork driven through his neck. Scotland Yard's Chief Inspector Robert Fabian, one of the most celebrated detectives of the era, led the investigation, focusing suspicion on farm manager Alfred Potter, but no charge was ever brought, and the killing remains the oldest unsolved murder in Warwickshire.

What turned a brutal but otherwise unremarkable rural murder into enduring folklore was the local reporting that followed it: the ritualistic staging of the wounds, and a story that a teenage Walton had once claimed to see a phantom black dog on nine consecutive evenings, an animal locally associated with death omens, followed by a headless woman in a silk dress, after which his sister died the next day. The Coventry Telegraph dubbed it a 'whodunnit witchcraft murder,' and the case has been retold ever since as evidence of a folk-magic ritual killing intended to fertilise the soil with a victim's blood, despite Fabian's own contemporary case notes making no mention of witchcraft, black dogs or ritual at all. The gap between the documented police investigation and the folklore that grew up around it makes this one of the clearest modern examples of a real event hardening into a named supernatural legend within living memory.
origin_date: 14 February 1945 (murder); the black-dog/headless-woman legend itself was recorded earlier, in 1929
earliest_record: J. Harvey Bloom, Folklore, Old Customs and Superstitions in Shakespeare Land (1929), recorded the black-dog-on-nine-nights and headless-woman story as told by a plough lad -- who was Charles Walton himself, years before his own 1945 murder
period: 20th century
historical_setting: Rural Warwickshire, England, World War II home front (murder occurred 14 February 1945)

name: Betty's Grave
summary: A lone Gloucestershire crossroads is named for a woman hanged as a witch, gypsy, poisoner or sheep-thief depending who you ask. Villagers left her flowers for two centuries so she wouldn't return.
detail:
A quiet rural crossroads a quarter-mile from the Gloucestershire village of Poulton, near Cirencester, has been marked on maps since at least 1830 as Betty's Grave, named for a woman called Elizabeth Bastre said to have been buried there in 1786. What Elizabeth actually was depends entirely on which version of the story is told: a witch hanged or burned for her craft, a highwaywoman who lured travellers to their doom, a suicide denied burial in consecrated ground, a gypsy, a murderess who poisoned her employer, or a housemaid poisoned by hers, or simply a thief hanged for stealing sheep. Crossroads burial was itself the traditional English punishment for suicides and executed criminals considered unfit for a churchyard, which may explain why so many conflicting explanations have grown up to fill in an anonymous grave's story.

The most vivid version of the tale casts Betty as an outright witch, dancing naked under the moon, reciting spells, and coughing up crows and sharp needles, powers she was said to use to lure and rob travellers on the lonely crossroads. Whatever she was, local custom held that her spirit would return to trouble the village unless her grave was kept decorated with fresh flowers, a practice that persisted, remarkably, until the 1970s, when it stopped as abruptly and inexplicably as it had apparently been observed for nearly two centuries.
earliest_record: Ordnance Survey map, 1830 (first cartographic record of the 'Betty's Grave' name)
period: Georgian era

name: Tavish Dhu (Black Tom), the Pirate of the Skerries
summary: A 14th-century sea raider who plundered the Antrim coast for Robert the Bruce is said to lie buried with his silver on the Skerries off Portrush, his ghost still guarding it.
detail:
In the early 14th century, during the wars of Scottish and Irish independence, a privateer named Tavish Dhu (or Tavish Dubh, "Black Tavish", later anglicised to Black Tom) used the Skerries, a scatter of rocky islets just off Portrush on the north Antrim coast, as his base. Sailing loosely under the banner of Robert the Bruce, he raided English shipping and settlements along the Irish Sea; in 1315 he is said to have delivered captured English supply ships to Edward Bruce's forces up the River Bann, and to have ferried Scottish troops across the water in support of the Bruce invasion of Ireland.

His career ended in 1317, when Edward II dispatched a squadron to hunt him down; after a bloody engagement in which forty of his crew were killed, Tavish was captured and executed, his head reputedly sent to Dublin as a trophy. Local tradition insists his men carried his body back to the Skerries for burial with three bullock-skins of silver, and that his ghost, and those of his crew, still stand guard over the hoard. The easternmost of the islets, Island Dubh, is said to take its name from him, as does the mainland district of Dhuvarren.

The legend has stayed remarkably alive in Portrush: it was recorded in early-20th-century local histories and is retold today by the town's heritage trust, which stages an annual "Pirates Off Portrush" festival built around his story. Whether or not the historical Tavish Dhu ever set foot on the Skerries, the tale binds a documented Bruce-era privateer to a very specific stretch of Antrim coastline, giving Portrush its own outlaw founding myth.
earliest_record: The historical pirate (recorded as 'Thomas Dun', 'Dunn', or 'Dubh' in period and near-period sources) appears in John Barbour's Scots epic poem The Brus (composed c. 1375, within living memory of the events), which calls him 'Scumer of the Se' (scum of the sea). He also appears in Irish annals and English chronicle accounts of Edward Bruce's invasion of Ireland. The specific folk legend of his grave and silver hoard on the Skerries is first found in print in Rev. Hugh Forde's Sketches of Olden Days in Northern Ireland (1926), which states Island Dubh 'is probable that it is named after Tavish Dubh, a pirate, who once frequented the Skerries and died in his ship here, and was buried on the island' (Forde's text does not mention silver -- that detail appears only in later 20th/21st-century retellings).
historical_setting: Edward Bruce's invasion of Ireland, 1315-1318; Thomas Dun/Tavish Dhu ferried Edward Bruce's invasion force from Ayr to Larne in May 1315, raided Holyhead and Anglesey on 12 September 1315, captured four ships of the Earl of Ulster off Portrush, and was captured and killed in a sea battle with John D'Athy in July 1317, after which his head was reportedly sent to Dublin
cultural_tradition: Scots-Irish maritime/pirate folklore of the North Antrim coast

name: Cermand Cestach, the Oracle of Clogher
summary: A gold-sheathed idol once stood on this hill, consulted like a Delphic oracle by pagan Ulster kings, until a devil's voice was said to speak from the stone itself.
detail:
Long before Clogher had a cathedral, tradition holds that a gold-covered cult stone called Cermand Cestach (also recorded as Cermand Celstach or Kermand Kelstach) stood on the hill as the oracle of Ulster, consulted through the druids much as Greek petitioners consulted the oracle at Delphi. The place-name itself preserves the memory: Clogher derives from Cloch-Óir, "the golden stone." The earliest reference to the idol appears in the medieval Life of St Macartan, Clogher's founding bishop (c.430-505 AD), which describes it as a sacred stone given to the saint by an elderly pagan nobleman when the old religion gave way to the new.

An eighth-century gloss on the story is blunter about what the stone represented, recording that "there had once been a stone covered in gold which heathens worshipped: and out of it a devil used to speak", casting the oracle not as a benign wonder but as a mouthpiece for a pre-Christian spirit that Macartan's mission had to silence. According to legend it was consulted by King Conchobar of Ulster himself when he sought guidance on securing his kingship.

What makes the tradition unusually well anchored is that the stone was said to survive as a physical relic long after its oracular days: the Ulster annalist Cathal Óg Mac Maghnusa (Cathal Maguire), who died in 1498, recorded that the idol was still preserved as a curiosity in the porch of Clogher Cathedral in his own lifetime, and a stone answering that description is still kept inside the cathedral today, one of the few places in Ireland where an object from a documented pre-Christian cult is said to have survived, more or less continuously, into the modern church that replaced it.
earliest_record: The Life of St Macartan (Vita S. Macartani), describing the stone's transfer from a pagan nobleman to the saint (fl. c.430-505 AD); an 8th-century gloss on the story is more explicit, recording that a devil once spoke from the gold-covered stone
period: Early Medieval Ireland (earliest textual gloss, 8th century); narrative setting is the 5th-century conversion era of Clogher's founding
historical_setting: Cathal Óg Mac Maghnusa (Cathal Maguire), the Ulster annalist who died in 1498, recorded the stone as still physically preserved in Clogher Cathedral's porch in his own lifetime, giving this legend an unusually continuous physical anchor from the early medieval period into the historical record

name: Saxa and Herman, the Rival Giants of Unst
summary: Two feuding giants hurled boulders at each other across a Shetland inlet until a mermaid lured both to their deaths in a swimming race to the North Pole.
detail:
On Unst, Britain's northernmost inhabited island, local tradition names two giants, Herman and Saxa, as the makers of its wildest headlands. Herman held Hermaness on the island's northwest tip, and Saxa held the opposing headland of Saxa Vord across the narrow inlet of Burrafirth; the two were sworn enemies who spent their days hurling great boulders at one another across the water. The landscape is still read as evidence of the feud. A submerged rock offshore is known as Saxa's Baa, and a flat rock on Herman's side as Herman's Hellyacraig, place names that fossilise the story into the map itself.

According to the tale both giants fell for the same mermaid, a temptress who used their rivalry to destroy them both: she challenged whichever of them could swim fastest to the North Pole to win her heart. Neither Herman nor Saxa could swim a stroke, but pride sent both wading in after her, and both drowned in the attempt, leaving the headlands named for two giants who never got the girl.

The earliest written version comes from Jessie Saxby's The Home of a Naturalist (1888), drawing on her own childhood on Unst; no older record has surfaced, so the tale's true age is unknown beyond the late nineteenth century. Philologists note that Hermaness more likely takes its name from an early Norse landowner than from the giant, a reminder that even the place names the story explains may have older, duller roots of their own. Either way, this Norse-flavoured strand of giant lore sits apart from the Gaelic giant tales of the Hebrides and the Scottish mainland further south.
earliest_record: Earliest known written telling is Jessie Saxby's The Home of a Naturalist (London: Nisbet & Co., 1888), co-written with her brother, drawing on their childhood on Unst.
cultural_tradition: Shetland oral tradition; place-lore explaining the headlands of Hermaness and Saxa Vord

name: The Serpent of Church Island
summary: Beneath a great stone on this Lough Gill island lies a crock of gold guarded by a serpent; legend insists a life must be lost before anyone can take it.
detail:
Church Island, the largest of the wooded islands scattered across Lough Gill outside Sligo town, carries a double legend. Historically it was the site of a monastery founded in the sixth century by St Lomán of Trim, later home to a bardic school run by the O'Cuirnín family and destroyed by fire in 1416, a blaze the Annals of the Four Masters record as having consumed a legendary harp, an ornamental cup, and the manuscript known as the Leabhar Gearr along with the church itself. It is out of the wreck of that lost wealth that the island's folk legend grows.

Local tradition holds that a crock of gold (some say the remnants of the monastery's own treasures) lies hidden beneath a large stone on the island, guarded by a serpent coiled beneath it. The guardianship comes with a grim condition: a life must be lost before the gold can ever be recovered. The story is kept alive by a widely repeated modern anecdote in which two botanists, searching the island for rare mosses, were caught in a sudden thunderstorm and found dead the next day, a tragedy locals folded straight into the old curse as proof it still holds.

Church Island's serpent belongs to a distinctively Irish strand of dragon lore: rather than a fire-breathing beast, it is one of the country's many treasure-guarding "ollphéisteanna", a lake-bound worm whose danger lies less in tooth and claw than in the price it exacts from anyone greedy enough to go looking for what it protects.

name: The Pirates' Ambush at Sark
summary: In 1356 pirates who had seized Sark were tricked and slaughtered by merchants who smuggled swords ashore inside a fake funeral coffin.
detail:
During the depths of the Hundred Years' War, with plague, French raids and Scottish attacks emptying Sark of its population, the island fell into the hands of pirates and wreckers who lit false beacons on stormy nights to lure passing ships onto its rocks. England's garrison amounted to little more than a handful of archers, leaving the pirates effectively in control. In 1356, so the story goes, a party of merchants from the Cinque Ports towns of Rye and Winchelsea decided to take the island back by trickery rather than force.

They sailed to Sark and told the pirates that their captain had died at sea, asking permission to bury him according to Christian rite at St Magloire's chapel. The pirates, promised payment and having searched the newcomers for weapons, allowed them to carry the coffin up the island's 300-foot cliff path into the chapel. Once inside, during what looked like a private funeral service, the merchants broke open the coffin, packed not with a body but with swords and longbows, armed themselves, and burst out to slaughter the pirate garrison. Only one elderly woman is said to have survived, escaping with a loaf of bread to hide in the Convanche Chasm until a passing Guernsey fisherman rescued her.

Historians have long noted how closely the tale echoes the Trojan Horse, and it has been current on Sark for at least four centuries. Sir Walter Raleigh recycled essentially the same coffin-and-weapons trick in his History of the World to describe Flemish corsairs retaking Sark from the French in 1553, suggesting the story had already become a kind of stock local legend for how the tiny island changes hands. The island's vulnerability to exactly this kind of seizure persisted for two more centuries, until Elizabeth I granted Sark by royal patent to Hélier de Carteret in 1565 on condition he settle it permanently with forty armed tenants.
period: mid-16th century (Elizabethan)
historical_setting: Sark, Channel Islands, before and during Hélier de Carteret's 1565 resettlement of the island under a patent from Elizabeth I; French and other pirate raiders had been using the then-uninhabited island as a base

name: Aimee Lake, the Last Witch of Guernsey
summary: As late as January 1914, a Guernsey fortune-teller was convicted of practising witchcraft, three centuries after the island's last burnings, under the same old law.
detail:
On 20 January 1914, Aimée Lake, a fortune-teller living at Robergerie in St Sampson's, was formally charged before the Royal Court of Guernsey with "fortune telling, the explanation of dreams and practising the art of witchcraft" between August 1913 and January 1914, making her the last person tried for witchcraft on the island, and one of the last in the British Isles under a genuinely old statute rather than a modern fraud law.

The complaint came from a farm widow of St Martin's whose cattle had died and who had begun suffering severe headaches. Desperate, she consulted Mrs Lake, who read her tea leaves, told her the deaths were the result of sorcery worked against her, and sold her charmed packets of powder for £3 10s to counter the curse, with a demand for a further £3 when the trouble didn't lift. Frightened, the widow went to the police, who dug up the buried packets from her garden and had them analysed: the "charms" turned out to be nothing more than baking powder, brown starch and cornflour, the everyday ingredients Mrs Lake bought to make blancmange.

Despite the harmlessness of the powders, the Royal Court under Bailiff William Carey convicted her and sentenced her to eight days' imprisonment, the maximum available, with the court reportedly expressing regret it could not impose something harsher. The case is remembered today less as a genuine brush with the supernatural than as a vivid glimpse of how long Guernsey's witchcraft law, and the folk belief that sustained it, survived into the twentieth century.
earliest_record: Royal Court of Guernsey trial records and contemporary press coverage, January 1914
period: Edwardian era

name: Old Mother Digby of East Harting
summary: A Sussex hare-witch could be caught out only by her own wounds. When a hound tore the hare she had become, the injury turned up on her body at home.
detail:
In a cottage on Hog's Lane in East Harting, at the foot of the South Downs, lived a woman remembered as Old Mother Digby (born Mollen), reputed in the 18th century to have the witch's classic gift of turning herself into a hare. Like the goddess Hecate she was said to keep the company of dogs, and the local squire, Squire Russell of Tye Oak, made a habit of hunting a hare that always escaped him at the same spot, a drain by a sink-hole close to the old woman's house.

One day his hounds finally caught the hare by its hindquarters as it fled for the drain, tearing at it before it vanished down the hole. Squire Russell, suspecting what everyone already whispered, went straight to Mother Digby's door and let himself in, to find the old woman nursing a fresh wound on exactly the part of her body where the dog had seized the hare, the classic proof-by-injury that closes so many British witch-hare tales.

The story survives because it was collected and printed by the essayist E. V. Lucas in Highways and Byways in Sussex (1904), one of the standard Edwardian topographical guides to the county, which helped fix a number of otherwise oral South Downs traditions in print before they were lost. It sits alongside other Sussex hare-witch tales (an unnamed witch of Ditchling Common, a witch of Plumpton who could stop carts in the road) as part of a distinctly Wealden and Downland vein of the shapeshifting-witch legend that runs the length of southern England.
earliest_record: E. V. Lucas's 'Highways and Byways in Sussex' (1904)
period: Edwardian topographical-guide tradition (1904); narrative setting is the 18th century

name: Mermaid of Mahee
region: Mahee Island, Strangford Lough, County Down, Northern Ireland
summary: A sea-maiden with a golden harp haunted the monks of Nendrum, luring one beneath the waves, until the sound of the monastery bells called him home to be shut in the round tower for his trouble.
detail:
On Mahee Island, in the sheltered reaches of Strangford Lough, the fifth-century monastery of Nendrum stands on ground sacred long before Christianity arrived in County Down. Local tradition holds that a mermaid haunted the waters below the monastic walls, rising at dusk with a golden harp to sing the fishermen and monks into a trance. Those who heard her music followed her voice into the lough and were never quite themselves again, the story says, living out their days as creatures of the sea in caves beneath the water.

One monk of Nendrum, so the tale goes, dived in after her and lived beneath the waves as her husband, forgetting his old life entirely, until the sound of the monastery's bells carried down through the water and called him back to shore. His brothers, certain he had lost his reason, shut him in the top of Nendrum's round tower, where he spent the rest of his days ringing the very bells that had once saved him.

The legend survives chiefly through the Belfast antiquarian John Vinycomb, MRIA, who set it down as a poem in his pamphlet The Monks of Mahee Island, alongside an account of the site's archaeology and history. Nendrum itself is real and remarkable: founded in the fifth century by St Mochaoi, excavated in the 1920s by H. C. Lawlor, and still ringed by three concentric enclosure walls. The mermaid has since been claimed by Mount Stewart's gardens on the far shore of the lough, where a weathered stone sculpture of her, harp and all, keeps the story visible on the Ards Peninsula.
earliest_record: John Vinycomb (Belfast antiquarian and heraldic artist, 1839-1928) set the legend down in his poem "The Mermaid of Mahee," published alongside "The Monks of Mahee Island" (c. 1903)
period: Written down by a named antiquarian-poet in the early 1900s; the Nendrum monastic site itself was traditionally founded in the 5th century by St Mochaoi (d. 497), giving the setting an early medieval frame even though the mermaid legend's own point of origin is unclear
historical_setting: Nendrum monastic site, Mahee Island, Strangford Lough, County Down
cultural_tradition: Ulster monastic mermaid/otherworldly-temptation legend

name: The Witches Circle of Weelsby Woods
summary: A ring in Grimsby's Weelsby Woods known as the Witches Circle, where covens are said to have met since the woods opened to the public in 1951. Locals still dispute what really happens there.
detail:
Weelsby Woods on the edge of Grimsby is home to a distinctive local legend: a clearing known as the Witches Circle, previously called the Fairy Ring until around the 1950s. According to local tradition, practitioners of witchcraft have gathered there on Friday and Saturday evenings since the woods opened to the public in 1951, performing rituals inside the circle. The tradition took on extra colour once Gerald Gardner's Wicca movement became publicly known in the mid-20th century, with the circle becoming associated with organised modern Pagan witchcraft rather than older cunning-folk practice.

The legend has generated persistent local disputes: rumours of animal sacrifice at the site have circulated for decades, consistently denied by practising Wiccans who point out that sacrifice plays no part in their religion. Some locals instead believe the circle to be an Anglo-Saxon burial mound reused by later visitors, though no archaeological evidence has been found to confirm this, and the site's true origin remains disputed among local historians. Ghost-hunting groups have also investigated the location, reporting unexplained EVP responses, adding a paranormal layer to the folklore.

Whatever its true origin, the Witches Circle has become a well-known piece of Grimsby's local identity, straddling the line between genuine folk memory and a modern urban legend that grew up around a patch of woodland after it was opened to the public.
period: mid-20th century onward (after 1951)
historical_setting: Weelsby Woods, Grimsby, Lincolnshire, formerly part of the Weelsby Old Hall Estate, used as a prisoner-of-war camp during and after the Second World War before Fred Parkes (of the Boston Deep Sea Fishing and Ice Company) donated roughly 150 acres of woodland, which opened to the public in 1951; the clearing known as the Witches Circle was called the Fairy Ring before the 1950s
earliest_record: No written record of the name 'Witches Circle' predates 2010s local newspaper coverage. Before that, the site was known locally as the Fairy Ring.

name: Maeve Roe, the Banshee of Dunluce Castle
region: Dunluce Castle, County Antrim, Northern Ireland
summary: Locked in Dunluce Castle's tower for refusing an arranged marriage, Maeve Roe drowned fleeing by boat with her lover, and her wails are still said to echo from the tower on stormy nights.
detail:
According to Ulster legend, Maeve Roe was the only daughter of Lord MacQuillan, ruling lord of Dunluce Castle on the County Antrim coast. Her father demanded she marry a suitor of his choosing, but Maeve had already given her heart to Reginald O'Cahan (in some tellings, a MacDonnell), the son of a rival clan. When she refused the arranged match, MacQuillan had her locked in the castle's northeastern tower overlooking the sea.

On a stormy night, Reginald came to rescue her, and the couple fled down through the sea cave beneath the castle known today as Mermaid's Cave, launching a small boat to cross to the safety of Portrush. The crossing proved fatal: the boat was overwhelmed by the rough waters, and the couple drowned together, Maeve's body never recovered from the sea. Her grieving spirit is said to remain at Dunluce, and visitors and staff have long reported wailing cries and screams from the northeastern tower, particularly during storms, the origin of the site's popular name, the Banshee's Tower.

The legend has been retold in numerous popular collections of Ulster folklore and ghost stories over the past century, including a dedicated modern retelling, Maeve Roe of Dunluce: The Banshee of Dunluce Castle, but its print history goes back further. The Vicomte d'Arlincourt's travel account The Three Kingdoms: England, Scotland, Ireland (1844) already mentions 'Mava, the sweeper of Dunluce, and the Banshee of the Macquillans', the earliest identified written trace of the story. It appears alongside other Ulster tales of the MacQuillan and MacDonnell clans who successively held Dunluce, and while no contemporary medieval record confirms Maeve Roe's historical existence, the story is consistently associated with the specific architectural features of the castle, the North Tower and Mermaid's Cave, giving it an unusually concrete physical anchor for a legend of this kind.
earliest_record: Referenced in print by 1844 in Vicomte d'Arlincourt's The Three Kingdoms: England, Scotland, Ireland, which mentions 'Mava, the sweeper of Dunluce, and the Banshee of the Macquillans'
period: First substantial written record mid-19th century (1844); underlying oral tradition likely older and undated
historical_setting: Dunluce Castle under the MacQuillan family, prior to its passing to the MacDonnells in the mid-16th century
cultural_tradition: Ulster banshee / doomed-lovers legend

name: Feolagan of Kebock Head
region: Kebock Head, Isle of Lewis, Outer Hebrides, Scotland
summary: A mouse-sized fairy at Kebock Head paralysed grazing sheep by walking across their backs, curable only by making it retrace its steps, or trapping it in a jar of salt.
detail:
Hebridean sheep-herding tradition, particularly the crofting townships around Kebock Head on the east coast of the Isle of Lewis, told of a small, mouse-sized fairy creature called the feolagan. To cross a sheep's back was enough for the feolagan to leave the animal paralysed, unable to eat or drink, so that without intervention it would die where it lay.

Two remedies were said to work. The feolagan itself could be caught and forced to retrace its steps back across the same sheep in the opposite direction, undoing whatever harm its first crossing had done. Where many animals fell ill at once and catching the creature was impractical, shepherds instead trapped it inside a jar of salt, then used grains from that jar to treat the whole flock.

The tale is recorded consistently across more than one folklore reference dealing with the Outer Hebrides, but its trail runs cold before reaching an older printed or academic collection, leaving its age and original source unclear.
earliest_record: Otta F. Swire recorded the Feolagan in 'The Outer Hebrides and Their Legends', published in 1966 by Oliver and Boyd. Swire drew the tale from stories she had heard from her mother and grandmother, so the oral tradition likely predates the book, though no earlier written account has been found.
cultural_tradition: Sheep-herding folklore of the Isle of Lewis, Outer Hebrides.

name: The Witch of Ditchling Common
summary: A Sussex witch who turned into a hare by night was unmasked when the hare, bitten while fleeing hunters' dogs, showed the same wound as an old woman's leg the next morning.
detail:
Ditchling Common in East Sussex carries a pair of linked witch legends recorded by local heritage bodies. In the best-known version, a hare seen bounding across the common at night was long suspected by locals of being an old woman from the area in disguise. When men hunting with dogs cornered and bit the hare on the leg one night, they let it escape, and the following day an old woman in the village was seen limping home nursing an injured ankle, confirming what everyone had already believed. The shapeshifting-witch-as-hare motif recurs across Sussex folklore, but the Ditchling Common telling is distinguished by its specific, verifiable injury as proof, a common device in English witch legend used to convert suspicion into supposed evidence.

A second, related tradition ties an unnamed witch, said to have lived in a cottage on the common called Jack o'Spades, to a different power entirely: the ability to stop carts and wagons dead in the road. According to the story, however hard the horses pulled, a cart could not be made to move past a certain point on the common until the witch's spell was lifted, a variant on the widespread English 'stayed cart' legend, in which a witch demonstrates her power over travellers passing through her territory rather than over animals or the weather. Together the two tales place Ditchling Common within the broader documented tradition of South Downs witch-lore that the South Downs National Park Authority has actively catalogued in recent years.
period: 19th-20th century Sussex witch-lore, within the widespread British 'witch-hare' shapeshifting folk motif
historical_setting: Ditchling Common, East Sussex. The witch is said to have lived in a cottage called 'Jack o'Spades' on the Common
cultural_tradition: English witch-hare shapeshifting legend, a recurring British folk motif (the unmasking of a hare-witch by a matching wound)

name: Lowri and Siân Owen, the Witches of Llanarmon
summary: Two women near Pwllheli, said to run a cottage "school," cast out unclean spirits by ceremony and were reputed to read the sea's ebb and flow before it turned.
detail:
In Llanarmon, a small parish near Pwllheli on the Llŷn Peninsula, local memory preserves two women named Lowri and Siân Owen as figures of both fear and use. They were said to run a kind of school from a cottage in the village, holding ceremonies that could cast out unclean spirits and demons from those who came to them for help.

Their other reputed gift was reading the sea itself. Villagers believed the two women could sense the turn of the tide in advance, anticipating its ebb and flow before it happened, a skill valued in a fishing community where the sea set the rhythm of daily life.

Little else survives about them individually, no firm dates and no account of how their reputation began or ended, but their story fits a pattern found across Wales. The artist Efa Lois has traced around sixty such women through her Gwrachod Cymru (Welsh Witches) project, and found that most functioned less as villains than as healers, using herbal remedies, rituals and chants to treat neighbours for ailments no one else could explain, then taking the blame when something went wrong. Wales prosecuted its accused witches far more rarely than continental Europe did: only five were executed between 1482 and 1782, against tens of thousands killed across Europe in the same period. Lowri and Siân Owen's story today rests mainly on oral tradition gathered by recent Welsh folklore projects rather than any older written record, one small entry in a much larger, and much less bloody, tradition than the word "witch" usually suggests.
earliest_record: Efa Lois's 'Gwrachod Cymru / Welsh Witches' (Seren, 2023), with an introduction by the folklorist Dr Juliette Wood, is the fullest published account of Lowri and Siân Owen found. No earlier written record of the pair has been located.
cultural_tradition: Llŷn Peninsula folk-witch tradition, North Wales.

name: Madame's Blow-well
summary: Circular ponds on the Lincolnshire coast were said to be bottomless, and one is still called Madame's Blow-well for the great lady whose coach and four vanished into it and were never seen again.
detail:
Tetney, on the Lincolnshire coast near the Humber, sits above a cluster of natural artesian springs known as the Blow Wells, where fresh water forces itself up through the clay in circular pools. Local tradition long held these ponds to be bottomless: one 19th-century account records that a local landowner had some of them sounded and found no bottom, and that they were popularly said to run clean through to the Antipodes. Charles Hope's 'Legendary Lore of Holy Wells' (1893) independently describes the site in the same terms, as popularly believed bottomless.

One well in particular carries its own name and its own story. Rev. J. Wild's 1901 account of Tetney parish records that a great lady, travelling with her coach and four horses, was swallowed bodily into one of the ponds and never seen again, and that the pool has been called Madame's Blow-well ever since. The tale was collected alongside other Lincolnshire ghost and water lore by Eliza Gutch and Mabel Peacock for the Folk-Lore Society's County Folk-Lore series in 1908, one of the more rigorous county-by-county folklore surveys of its era. Related accounts describe the wider blow-hole ponds in this corner of the county as haunted by a phantom coach and four and a grey lady, suggesting Madame's Blow-well anchors a broader local tradition of a vanished noblewoman still abroad on the marsh.

The wells themselves are real and still flowing: the site is now a Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust nature reserve southeast of Tetney church, its four spring-fed pools and surrounding wetland protected for the plant and bird life the constant flow of water supports, a quietly persistent landscape for a story about something that never stops disappearing into it.
earliest_record: Rev. John Wild's 1901 account of Tetney parish records the legend of a great lady, coach and four swallowed by the blow-well; Charles Hope's Legendary Lore of Holy Wells (1893) independently describes the site as popularly believed bottomless
period: Documented in print by the late Victorian/Edwardian era (1893, 1901); underlying oral tradition likely older and undated
cultural_tradition: Lincolnshire holy/healing well folklore

name: Baron Kitter and the Witch Ada
region: Calf of Man, Isle of Man
summary: A Norwegian tyrant hunted the Isle of Man's wildlife to extinction until the witch Ada burned his castle behind his back. His drowned crew gave their name to the islet of Kitterland forever after.
detail:
Manx tradition holds that, generations before recorded history, a Norwegian baron named Kitter ruled the Isle of Man from a castle on the mountain of Barrule. Kitter was an obsessive hunter, and in time he wiped out the island's native bison and elk entirely. The Manx people, fearing he would turn next to their livestock and to the wild creatures of the hills, went to the wisest of the island's witches for help.

When Kitter crossed to the Calf of Man to hunt red deer, he left his castle in the care of his cook, Eaoch. While Eaoch slept, the witch Ada worked a spell on the cooking pot left over the fire, so that the fat boiled over and set the castle alight. Eaoch's cries carried across the water to Kitter on the Calf, and he and his companions launched a small currach to race back and save it. Partway across the sound, the currach struck a rock in the treacherous currents and everyone aboard was drowned. The rock has been called Kitterland ever since.

The story was collected by Sophia Morrison in her 1911 Manx Fairy Tales, itself drawing on folklore already circulating in earlier nineteenth-century collections of Manx tradition. It remains attached to a real, named place. Kitterland is a small islet in the Calf Sound between the Isle of Man and the Calf of Man, now in the care of the Manx National Trust and known today chiefly as a haven for seabirds rather than the site of a drowned baron's ambition.
earliest_record: Sophia Morrison, 'Manx Fairy Tales' (1911), which draws on earlier 19th-century Manx folklore collection; the tale is set in an unspecified pre-historical Norse period ('generations before recorded history').
period: Recorded in the early-20th-century Manx folklore revival; narrative setting is the Norse era of Manx history, though this is legendary rather than historically anchored dating

name: Scota Bess
summary: A storm-witch ruled the Mermaid's Chair on Stronsay's shore, cursing fishermen with endless gales, until islanders beat her to death and still couldn't keep her in the ground.
detail:
On the Orkney island of Stronsay, tradition holds that a witch called Scota Bess once occupied a rock seat on the shore of Mill Bay, known as the Mermaid's Chair. From there she was said to order up storms, keeping the island's fishing boats trapped in harbour through weeks of unbroken January gales. When the islanders had endured enough, they drove her from her chair and beat her to death in a barn at Huip, one of Stronsay's farming settlements near the loch of Meikle Water.

The story does not end with her death. Each time the islanders buried Scota Bess, her body was found lying disinterred beside the grave the following morning, as though the ground itself refused her. Unable to keep her under, the men finally carried her body to Meikle Water and threw it in; a mound of earth is said to have grown up in the loch afterwards, later used as a nesting site by swans, read by some as a sign of the witch's uneasy rest, by others as evidence she was still scheming beneath the water.

No historical record of an actual woman behind the name survives, and Scota Bess reads as much like a Norse-inflected storm-hag or minor local deity as a remembered individual, of a piece with Orkney's wider tradition of weather-witches blamed for wrecking boats and ruining harvests. The Mermaid's Chair itself carries a second, gentler strand of folklore alongside hers: local tradition holds that a girl who sits in it will come to understand the mysteries of life and be able to foretell the future, folding the site's fearsome history into a piece of everyday island courting-lore.
earliest_record: Ernest W. Marwick, The Folklore of Orkney and Shetland (Batsford, 1975), which gathers the Stronsay material
historical_setting: The Mill Bay coast of Stronsay, at the rock seat known as the Mermaid's Chair, in a fishing community that feared weather witchcraft
cultural_tradition: Orkney storm witch tradition, with the figure carrying traces of an older creation or hag figure as well as a witch

name: Kitty Kilroy, the Witch of Huntsfield
summary: A priest's horse was said to collapse paralysed on the Huntsfield road, and the villagers who watched dared suggest fetching the local witch to cure it.
detail:
In the townland of Huntsfield near Kilkelly, County Mayo, local memory preserved the story of a woman named Kitty Kilroy who was reputed to practise witchcraft, roughly a generation before the account was written down. What marked her out as much as any spell was her absence from the parish's religious life: she was said never to attend Mass or take the Sacraments, a defiance that drew open hostility from the local priests.

The one incident remembered in detail concerns a priest travelling the Huntsfield road on horseback, whose horse suddenly "got paralized" and collapsed beneath him. As villagers gathered to help, someone in the crowd suggested sending for the witch, since her reputed power might be the only thing able to undo whatever had struck the animal down. The suggestion itself was recorded as a scandal, "a great insult to the priest," caught between the parish's official religious authority and an informal, grudging belief in Kitty Kilroy's own power that the priest's own flock could not quite shake off.

The account comes from the National Folklore Collection's Schools' Collection, gathered in the 1930s when Irish schoolchildren were sent to record local tradition from older relatives and neighbours. This version was collected by Annie M. Dunleavy from Mrs Patrick Boyle of nearby Urlaur. Like most Schools' Collection witch stories, it preserves a community's reputation and rumour about a named local figure rather than any court record or formal accusation, and should be read as a piece of living oral folklore rather than documented history.
earliest_record: The Irish Folklore Commission's Schools' Collection (Bailiúchán na Scol, 1930s), collected by Annie M. Dunleavy from Mrs Patrick Boyle of Urlaur, already the entry's own existing primary source
period: Recorded in the 1930s; narrative setting is 'roughly a generation before the account was written down', placing the events themselves around the 1900s-1910s
cultural_tradition: A community reputation-and-rumour account rather than a documented court case

name: Burial Place of the Big Women
region: Hynish, Isle of Tiree, Inner Hebrides, Scotland
summary: A farm shed built from the robbed stones of an ancient women's graveyard on Tiree left a servant hearing faint voices repeat: "This is the stone that was at my head."
detail:
At Hynish on the Isle of Tiree stood a disused burial ground known in Gaelic as Cladh nam Ban Mòra, the Burial Place of the Big Women, likely once linked to a chapel and, by local tradition, associated with a community of religious women. By the nineteenth century the graveyard had long fallen out of use, and its stones were considered fair game for building material: some were taken to construct an outbuilding on the Hynish farm.

The ghost story attached to that reuse was recorded by the folklorist Rev. John Gregorson Campbell in his 1902 collection Witchcraft and Second Sight in the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. A servant from the neighbouring island of Mull, sent to sleep in the newly built shed, found his dog would not settle, repeatedly leaping onto the bed and snarling at something unseen in the dark. Through the night the servant heard faint voices around the building, each repeating the same complaint: "This is the stone that was at my head." He refused ever to sleep there again, convinced the graveyard's disturbed dead had followed their headstones into the new building.

Gregorson Campbell's account allows that the servant may have been the victim of a hoax, but records the story as it was told and believed locally. The scholar Ronald Black later discussed the tale in his annotated edition The Gaelic Otherworld, situating it within a wider Hebridean tradition of "big women" place-names, which range from this specific haunted graveyard at Hynish to a broader, older strand of legend on the nearby Isle of Eigg (whose Gaelic name likewise translates as the Island of the Big Women) about a vanished race of giant women. The Hynish story is the more concrete and place-anchored of the two: a named graveyard, a named building, and a specific, quotable haunting rather than a general legendary ancestry.
origin_date: Ghost story documented by 1902; the underlying disused graveyard is of unknown but clearly earlier date
earliest_record: Rev. John Gregorson Campbell, Witchcraft and Second Sight in the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1902); a related but separate documentation of the adjacent Hynish 'Cladh beag' burial ground appears in Sands, 1881-82
period: Recorded in Highland folklore scholarship, 1881-1902
cultural_tradition: Hebridean 'big women' place-name tradition (Cladh nam Ban Mòra); discussed further, alongside the distinct but similarly-named Eigg legend, in Ronald Black's annotated edition The Gaelic Otherworld

name: Rose Cullender and Amy Duny, the Lowestoft Witches
summary: A refused herring sale and children vomiting pins hanged two Lowestoft widows in 1662; Sir Thomas Browne's testimony helped convict them, and Salem's judges later cited the trial as precedent.
detail:
In March 1662 the Suffolk fishing town of Lowestoft accused two elderly widows, Amy Duny and Rose Cullender, of witchcraft after the merchant Samuel Pacy refused to sell them herring and his daughters Elizabeth and Deborah began suffering violent fits, vomiting pins and complaining of biting and pinching by invisible hands. Neighbours added further charges: that a toad had fallen hissing from a child's blanket and vanished into the fire, that a cart had jammed at Duny's gate, and that livestock, chimneys and other household mishaps across the town could be traced back to the two women.

The case went to trial at the Bury St Edmunds assizes on 10 March 1662 before Sir Matthew Hale, later Lord Chief Baron of the Exchequer, who told the jury they need only decide whether the children were genuinely bewitched and whether the two women were responsible. Crucially, the physician and author Sir Thomas Browne, then living in Norwich, was called as an expert witness and testified that the children's fits were consistent with witchcraft, drawing a comparison to reported cases in Denmark. The jury convicted Duny and Cullender within half an hour; they were hanged at Bury St Edmunds on 17 March 1662.

The trial's afterlife proved longer than the women's lives. An anonymous account, A Tryal of Witches (1682), circulated in New England and was read closely by Cotton Mather, who cited it in The Wonders of the Invisible World (1692) as a case 'much considered by the judges of New England,' while Increase Mather referenced it that same autumn. Because Sir Matthew Hale was among the most respected jurists in England, his willingness to accept spectral evidence at Lowestoft gave the Salem magistrates a precedent to lean on three decades later, tying a Suffolk fishing town directly into the most notorious witch trials in American history.
earliest_record: First recorded in A Tryal of Witches, at the Assizes Held at Bury St. Edmunds for the County of Suffolk, on the Tenth Day of March, 1664, printed in London in 1682 (a first-hand account written by an anonymous attendee of the court, published 18 years after the trial); reprinted in 1716, with a copy held at Moyse's Hall Museum, Bury St Edmunds.
period: 17th century (Restoration-era England)
historical_setting: Trial held at the Suffolk assizes in Bury St Edmunds, presided over by Sir Matthew Hale (later Lord Chief Justice), under the Witchcraft Act of 1603. Sir Thomas Browne, author of Religio Medici, testified as a medical expert witness.
cultural_tradition: English witch-trial / Restoration-era legal and religious tradition; the trial record was later cited as a legal precedent by Salem, Massachusetts magistrates in 1692

name: John Walsh, the Cunning Man of Netherbury
summary: Examined by the Bishop of Exeter's court in 1566, Dorset wise-man John Walsh met fairies on the hills at noon and midnight, and kept a familiar that turned into a grey dog or a man with cloven feet.
detail:
In August 1566 the church courts of the diocese of Exeter examined John Walsh, a cunning man from the Dorset village of Netherbury, on suspicion of witchcraft and sorcery. Questioned by Thomas Williams, commissary to the Bishop of Exeter, in front of an audience of local gentlemen, Walsh described a working life spent diagnosing bewitchment, tracing stolen goods, and consulting a familiar spirit, all recorded and printed that same year as The Examination of John Walsh, the earliest surviving pamphlet account of an English church court's interrogation of a cunning-folk practitioner.

Walsh told his questioners that he met with fairies on certain hills between twelve and one at noon, or at midnight, and that he could sort them into three kinds by colour: white, green and black, the black fairies being the most dangerous to deal with. His familiar spirit, he said, appeared to him variously as a grey dog, a dove, or a man in every respect ordinary except for cloven feet, and it was this spirit that told him which of his neighbours were bewitched and helped him recover stolen property, including, he claimed, several missing horses. He also owned what the pamphlet calls a book of circles, used in his consultations.

The pamphlet, printed in London by John Awdely, survives in a single known copy and gives no account of what became of Walsh after his examination: no verdict, sentence or acquittal is recorded, only the interrogation itself. That silence has left him a genuinely open case in the history of English witchcraft prosecution, and modern scholars, including Marion Gibson in her sourcebook Early Modern Witches, treat his testimony as a rare direct record of what a working Tudor cunning-man actually believed and practised, rather than what his accusers assumed about him.
earliest_record: 'The examination of John Walsh...', a pamphlet printed in London in 1566 recording his examination before the Bishop of Exeter's commissary
period: Elizabethan England
cultural_tradition: English cunning-folk / fairy-belief tradition

name: King Bladud
summary: Exiled with leprosy, a prince turned swineherd watched his pigs cure themselves in Bath's hot mud. He founded the city on the spot, then, legend says, strapped on feathered wings and fell to his death trying to fly.
detail:
According to Geoffrey of Monmouth's twelfth-century Historia Regum Britanniae, Bladud was the ninth king of the Britons, a prince who studied in Athens, contracted leprosy, and was driven from court and disinherited. Disguised and destitute, he found work as a swineherd near Swainswick, a couple of miles from the later site of Bath.
