He noticed his pigs would wallow in a warm, black mud fed by a hot spring in a nearby alder-moor, and that the ones that did so were free of the skin disease that plagued the rest of the herd. He tried the mud himself, was cured, and went on to found the city of Bath at the spring, later dedicated to the goddess Sulis.

Geoffrey was the first writer to name Bladud as Bath's founder, claiming to translate from "a very ancient book written in the British language," though he is now thought to have drawn on a much older Roman-era description of Aquae Sulis and grafted the Greek myth of Daedalus and Icarus onto Bladud's death: later in life the king took up magical experiments, fashioned wings, and leaped from a tall building, sometimes placed at a temple of Apollo in London, plunging to his death. The leprous-swineherd episode itself is a later medieval addition, absent from Geoffrey's original text, and some historians trace the figure's root to an earlier Welsh prince, Bleiddudd of Dyfed, praised in a ninth-century poem.

Bath still keeps Bladud close: a statue of him overlooks the King's Bath in the Pump Room precinct, and a trail of painted pig sculptures, King Bladud's Pigs, has run through the city's streets in his honour. In Geoffrey's line of legendary kings descended from Brutus of Troy, Bladud is the father of Leir, whose story of a divided kingdom and a favourite daughter later became the basis for Shakespeare's King Lear.
earliest_record: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, c. 1136
period: Legendary pre-Roman Britain. Geoffrey places Bladud as the 10th king in descent from Brutus, reigning roughly in the 9th century BC
cultural_tradition: Later absorbed into Bath's civic founding-myth tradition, tied to the city's Roman-era hot springs

name: King Lud
summary: London's legendary pre-Roman king rebuilt the city and gave Ludgate its name. His own statue, beheaded during the Reformation and rebuilt twice, still stands in a Fleet Street churchyard.
detail:
In Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae, Lud was the son of King Heli and, by Geoffrey's legendary chronology, ruled Britain around 66 BC, late in the line of kings descended from Brutus of Troy. He is credited with rebuilding and fortifying London, renaming it Caer Lud, Lud's fortress, a name later writers connected to both "London" itself and to Ludgate, the westernmost of the City's ancient gates, where Lud was said to have been buried. When he died, his sons Androgeus and Tenvantius were judged too young to rule, so the throne passed to his brother Cassibelanus; both sons later distinguished themselves under their uncle, Androgeus as ruler of London and Tenvantius of Cornwall, in the defence of Britain against Julius Caesar.

The legend gained an unusually durable physical form. In 1260 Henry III commissioned stone figures of Lud and his two sons for Ludgate itself; the statues were beheaded during Edward VI's Reformation-era iconoclasm, repaired under Mary I, and rebuilt entirely in 1586 under Elizabeth I. When Ludgate was finally demolished in 1760, following damage in the Great Fire of London a century earlier, the statues survived: Sir Francis Gosling donated them to the City, the Marquess of Hertford later acquired them, and they now stand in the courtyard of St Dunstan-in-the-West on Fleet Street, close to their original site.

Even contemporaries were sceptical of the story; nineteenth-century antiquarians preferred a more prosaic origin for Ludgate, from an Old English term for "flood-gate" or "Fleet-gate," after the River Fleet that once ran past the spot. Geoffrey's Lud, like the rest of his Brutus-descended king-list, is treated by modern historians as literary invention rather than history. What makes the legend unusual within that tradition is the survival of a genuine monument: few of Geoffrey's early British kings can be visited in stone form on a London street corner today.
earliest_record: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae is the source for Lud's legendary reign (c.66 BC in Geoffrey's own internal chronology); the physical statues have their own independently dated history: commissioned 1260, damaged during the Reformation, rebuilt 1586, moved 1760
period: High Medieval Britain (literary composition, 1135-39); physical monument history spans 1260-1760

name: Elspeth Reoch
summary: A Caithness girl said fairies taught her second sight at a lochside meeting when she was twelve. Decades later in Orkney, her confession of a dead kinsman's nightly visits sent her to the gallows within a single day.
detail:
Elspeth Reoch was born in Caithness, the daughter of a piper to the Earl of Caithness, and spent part of her childhood with relatives on an island in Lochaber before eventually settling on Orkney's mainland. She told her interrogators that at around twelve years old, while staying in Lochaber, she met two men by a loch, one dressed in black and one in green tartan. The man in green told her he could teach her to know "anything she wanted," and instructed her to boil an egg and rub its steam over her eyes and hands, unwashed, to gain the power of second sight.

Years later, after Reoch had settled in Orkney and borne an illegitimate child, she said the man in black returned, this time identified as a dead relative named Johne Stewart, who visited her bedside on three successive nights and became her lover. He told her he was "neither dead nor alive but was forever trapped between heaven and earth," and commanded her to remain silent about their meetings to preserve her powers. Brought before the court at Kirkwall in March 1616, she confessed to these encounters, to curing illness with the herb melefour (yarrow) while reciting the Trinity formula, and to feigning muteness to protect her gift. She was found guilty, executed by strangulation, and her body burned that same afternoon.

Reoch's case is preserved in the University of Edinburgh's Survey of Scottish Witchcraft database, drawn from the original Lawting Court records of Orkney and Shetland. Scholars who have studied the case, including Diane Purkiss, have noted that Orkney's court clerks, following Bishop James Law's 1614 reforms, routinely rewrote references to "fairies" in testimony as "the devil" or "a demon." That editorial habit means Reoch's own account of a fairy initiation survives only filtered through the language of a demonic pact, making her one of the clearest documented instances of fairy-belief testimony absorbed into a Scottish witch trial.
earliest_record: Original Lawting Court records of Orkney and Shetland, March 1616, preserved via the University of Edinburgh's Survey of Scottish Witchcraft database (the entry's own existing source)
period: Early modern Scotland (Orkney/Shetland witch trials, post-1614 under Bishop James Law's judicial reforms)

name: Shane Bernagh
region: Cappagh and Altmore, County Tyrone, Northern Ireland
summary: A dispossessed Tyrone landowner turned mountain outlaw, robbing coaches on the Dublin road and sharing his takings with the poor like an Ulster Robin Hood, from a hideout still called his Chair.
detail:
Shane Bernagh Donnelly, according to local tradition, was dispossessed of his family's land at Ballydonnelly, now Castlecaulfield, and retreated into the Altmore mountains above Cappagh, County Tyrone, where he lived in a cave and turned highwayman, holding up coaches on the main Dublin-to-Derry road. He is remembered as targeting the Protestant Ascendancy in particular and sharing his takings with poorer neighbours, earning him a reputation, still current in the area, as a local Robin Hood.

The authorities took him seriously enough to build Altmore Barracks in 1700 specifically to counter his activities, garrisoning soldiers within sight of the cave still known locally as Shane Bearnach's Sentry Box. Nearby Bernish Glen is said to mark a horseback leap he made to escape pursuing soldiers, and a rock outcrop on the edge of Cappagh and Altmore, shaped like a chair, is still known as Shane Bernagh's Chair. He was eventually captured and executed by the Dublin Castle administration, his body reportedly cast into a lough at the summit of Slieve Beagh, the mountain where the counties of Tyrone, Fermanagh and Monaghan meet.

A related but distinct tradition survives on the Monaghan side of the same mountain: fieldwork gathered for the Irish Folklore Commission's Schools' Collection in the Tydavnet area recorded a "Shane Bearna," active there "about 1840," who drove stolen cattle across Slieve Beagh to hidden stables reached by swimming the animals across a lake, and who reputedly had his horses shod backwards to confuse pursuers. Whether this is the same figure remembered with a different, later date, or a separate cattle-raider whose story merged with the earlier rapparee's, the Schools' Collection account does not resolve, and it is presented here as a second, place-anchored strand of the same regional legend. Bernagh's memory was later carried into print by George Sigerson's ballad "The Mountains of Pomeroy" and John Montague's poem "A Lost Tradition."
period: Late 17th century into the early 18th century. The Donnelly clan of Tyrone was dispossessed of lands during the reign of Charles II (1660s-1680s), given as the trigger for Shane's turn to outlaw life; a military barracks was established at Altmore specifically to capture him by 1703, and was not closed until 1749, implying his activity or notoriety persisted into the early 1700s.
historical_setting: Ulster land confiscations affecting the Donnelly clan of County Tyrone. An ancestor, Donnell O'Donnelly, fought at the Battle of Kinsale (1601/1603) with Hugh O'Neill; Shane's father Patrick Donnelly fought with Sir Phelim O'Neill's forces in the 1641 Rebellion, during which Castle Caulfield (built 1611-1619 on former Donnelly lands) was burned
cultural_tradition: Irish rapparee/outlaw tradition, Ulster

name: Bincombe Bumps
summary: Six Bronze Age round barrows crown the down above the hamlet of Bincombe, known locally as the Bincombe Bumps. One of them is the Music Barrow, where country people said that anyone who laid an ear to the top of the mound at midday would hear the sweetest melody playing inside. The players were the fairies, whose halls were held to lie under the turf.
detail:
The Bincombe Bumps sit on the crest of the South Dorset Ridgeway, between Dorchester and Weymouth and directly above the hamlet of Bincombe. Six round barrows run in a line that shrinks from west to east, the largest on the top of the hill and the rest stepping downhill from it. They were raised in the Bronze Age, and the group is a scheduled monument, listed as 'Six round barrows on Bincombe Down'.

The folklore attaches to one mound rather than to all six. Charles Warne set it down in 'The Celtic Tumuli of Dorset' in 1866: on Bincombe Down there is a 'Music Barrow' of which the rustics say that if the ear be laid close to the apex at midday the sweetest melody will be heard within. J. S. Udal quoted the passage in 'Dorsetshire Folk-Lore' in 1922, which is how it reached the standard county collection and, through that, most retellings since.

The conditions are as particular as the claim. One barrow and not the group, the ear against the apex, and the hour exactly noon. Dorset holds more than one such mound. Warne recorded the same belief at Culliford Tree a few miles east, and Leslie Grinsell, who catalogued the county's barrows before writing on the folklore of prehistoric sites across Britain, went and tried the test there himself in May 1954. He reported hearing the cuckoo and some jet aircraft.

Music is the usual way these mounds announce who is inside them. Across Britain and Ireland the old burial mounds are treated as inhabited, and what reaches the living from within is far more often heard than seen. Much barrow lore warns against digging or ploughing them. The Bincombe tradition asks only that you listen, and only at the right hour.

The story now told about the hill is a modern one. For a Dorset National Landscape myths and legends project, the storyteller Martin Maudsley wrote a tale of a fairy queen who forbids music on the hill and a warrior who breaks the ban and dies for it, his heart turning to stone and his body rising as a skylark whose song lifts the silence. It is credited to him openly, and it is a composition of recent years rather than a tradition collected from the down. The older belief is narrower. It names one barrow, one hour of the day, and one way of listening.
earliest_record: Charles Warne, 'The Celtic Tumuli of Dorset' (1866), which records that on Bincombe Down there is a 'Music Barrow' of which the rustics say that if the ear be laid close to the apex at midday the sweetest melody will be heard within. J. S. Udal quoted the passage in 'Dorsetshire Folk-Lore' (1922). No earlier written account of the Bincombe tradition was found.
period: Bronze Age barrows; the fairy-music belief is recorded from the 19th century
origin_date: Barrows c. 2000-1500 BC. The listening tradition is first recorded in 1866 and was probably in oral currency well before that.
historical_setting: Bincombe Down, on the South Dorset Ridgeway between Dorchester and Weymouth. Six round barrows, scheduled as 'Six round barrows on Bincombe Down', list entry 1002744.
cultural_tradition: English barrow folklore and fairy belief, in the Dorset 'music barrow' group alongside Culliford Tree

name: The Liver Birds
summary: Two copper birds stand on the clock towers of the Royal Liver Building, one turned to the city and one to the sea, and pointedly not to each other. Local tradition holds that they are chained in place, because if they ever broke free and flew off the Mersey would burst its banks and drown Liverpool. They are kept facing apart for a second reason. Were the pair to mate and leave together, the city would cease to exist.
detail:
The birds were designed by the German sculptor Carl Bernard Bartels and went up when the Royal Liver Building opened in 1911. Each is eighteen feet tall with a wingspan of twenty four, and each is fixed down hard against the weather coming up the estuary, which is the mundane origin of the chains the legend makes so much of.

The liver bird itself is far older than the building and has served as the town's emblem since the medieval seal, but the superstition belongs to the twentieth century. It grew up around the statues once they were tall enough to be seen from every part of the waterfront, and it works the way a city's protective myths usually do, by making the survival of the place depend on something anyone can look up and check.

The two versions sit oddly together and are usually told as though they were one. In the first the birds are shackled against flight and the danger is flood. In the second they are turned away from one another and the danger is courtship. Both agree that Liverpool stands only as long as the birds stay where they are.
period: The statues were installed in 1911 and the superstition is first recorded after that. No earlier form of the flight legend has been traced

name: William Mackenzie's Pyramid
summary: A granite pyramid fifteen feet high stands in the churchyard of St Andrew's on Rodney Street, over the grave of the railway contractor William Mackenzie. The story told about it is that Mackenzie gambled with the Devil, lost his soul on the turn of a card, and arranged to be entombed sitting upright at a table with the winning hand still in his fingers, so the debt could never be collected while the game stayed unfinished. Having cheated hell he was refused heaven, and his figure is said to walk Rodney Street as the light goes.
detail:
Mackenzie was a real and substantial man. Born in 1794, he became one of the leading contractors in Europe during the 1840s, building railways and canals across Britain and the Continent, and he died in 1851 having made a great deal of money.

The pyramid was not his idea. It was raised in 1868 by his brother Edward, seventeen years after the burial, and the bronze plaque on its blind door settles the question the legend depends on. It records that the remains lie in the vault beneath, along with both of Mackenzie's wives. Nobody is sitting up inside it holding cards.

The story appears to be modern and owes its wide currency to the Liverpool writer Tom Slemen, who put it in front of a large readership in the late twentieth century. That does not make it worthless. A blank stone pyramid in a Georgian street is strange enough that it was always going to attract an explanation, and the one the city settled on assumes that a fortune of that size was got by dealing with somebody.
period: Mackenzie died in 1851 and the pyramid was erected in 1868. The Devil legend has no traced source earlier than its popularisation by Tom Slemen in the late twentieth century

name: Thor's Stone
summary: A rib of red sandstone stands clear of the heather on Thurstaston Common, and Victorian antiquaries made it an altar where Norse settlers cut throats in honour of Thor. The Wirral really was Scandinavian ground, with an assembly site at Thingwall a few miles off, which is what gave the story its footing. An older and quieter local name for the rock was Fair Maiden's Hall, and children were remembered dancing round it once a year.
detail:
The sacrificial reading was established by the nineteenth century and has proved almost impossible to shift. Geologists and historians now agree that the outcrop is natural, a small tor left by periglacial weathering of the sandstone and afterwards cut about by quarrymen in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The straight faces that look worked are worked, but by men taking building stone rather than by anyone preparing an altar.

The Fair Maiden's Hall tradition is the more interesting half and the less often repeated. It was noted in 1888 by the Reverend A. E. P. Gray, who recorded both the name and the annual dance, and it has the ordinary shape of genuine local usage rather than the shape of an antiquarian theory.

A Norse district, a red rock and a nineteenth century appetite for Viking blood were enough between them to produce a legend that now has to be argued down every time the site is written about.
period: The Thor and sacrifice attribution is nineteenth century antiquarian invention rather than Norse survival. The Fair Maiden's Hall name and the annual dance were recorded in 1888
earliest_record: The sacrificial-altar interpretation was first proposed in 1877 by the antiquarian J. A. Picton, part of a wider Victorian enthusiasm for Old Norse paganism on the Wirral. No archaeological evidence of early medieval activity on the site has been found

name: The Monk's Well
summary: A sandstone well on Mill Lane in Wavertree carries a Latin line cut in 1414. Qui non dat quod habet, daemon infra ridet, which runs roughly as he who gives not what he has, the Devil below laughs at him. Travellers who drank at the spring were expected to leave alms for the monks, and the inscription tells them exactly who is listening when they walk on without paying.
detail:
The well is Grade II listed and was built in the early fifteenth century. Steps once went down to the spring itself and a cross stood over the structure carrying a second and gentler inscription, Deus dedit, homo bibit, God gives and man drinks. An iron pump was fitted in 1835 to save people the descent.

By 1893, when Robert Charles Hope gathered it into his Legendary Lore of the Holy Wells of England, the cross had already gone. It was replaced later. The well no longer runs and the basin is planted as a flower bed, so the threat is now addressed to people waiting at a bus stop.

What makes it unusual among British holy wells is that the folklore was never recovered from oral tradition at all. It is cut into the stone, in the fifteenth century, in the voice of the institution that wanted the money. Most wells had a story attached to them afterwards by somebody else. This one arrived with its own.
period: Dated by its own inscription to 1414. The tradition was recorded by Robert Charles Hope in 1893

name: The Bidston Hill Carvings
summary: A long figure with her arms spread is cut into the flat sandstone north east of Bidston Observatory, set so that she faces the midsummer sunrise. She is known locally as the sun goddess and is credited to the Norse Irish who settled the Wirral around the year 1000. A worn horse lies carved nearby, stamped at some later date with the Latin word EQUINO by a hand nobody has identified.
detail:
The figure is about four and a half feet long. The midsummer alignment is the strongest argument for taking her seriously, since an alignment like that is either deliberate or chance, with very little room in between.

The dating is the weak point and should be held loosely. Open rock carving is close to undateable by ordinary means, the sandstone here weathers quickly, and the Norse attribution rests on the district's known Scandinavian settlement rather than on anything in the carving itself. The year 1000 is the best available guess rather than a finding.

The hill has gathered a good deal else. Witches were said to meet on it, and the windmill on the ridge carries stories of a murdered miller and of something that will not settle. Those belong to a much later stratum than the carvings and mostly to the last century or so of ghost writing. The windmill standing today replaced one burnt down in 1791 and ground wheat until steam took the trade in 1875.
period: The carvings are attributed to Norse Irish settlers around 1000 AD, but open rock carving resists dating and the attribution rests on the district's settlement history rather than on the carvings themselves
historical_setting: Attribution rests on three competing theories: Norse Irish settlement of the Wirral in the ninth or tenth century, an alternative Gallo-Roman origin in the second century AD, and a minority view that the carvings are no older than the eighteenth century. Open-air sandstone carving cannot be scientifically dated, so none of the three can be confirmed

name: The Bloody Acre
summary: A field beside All Saints' Church in Childwall has been called the Bloody Acre for as long as anyone has written the name down. It is usually traced to fighting in the 1640s between the parish and the new owners of land taken from the church, and cannonballs are said to have come up when houses went in along Score Lane. The ground has a reputation for refusing what is done to it, and schemes for building on it have a habit of falling through.
detail:
All Saints' is the oldest church in Liverpool and the only medieval one left in the borough, founded in the fourteenth century and Grade I listed. The field sits immediately beside it and has served as overspill for the churchyard, which is enough on its own to give a patch of grass a certain atmosphere.

The historical kernel is reasonably solid. Land seized from the church under Henry VIII passed to new owners, and the quarrel between those owners and the parish turned violent in the 1640s, in the same years the Civil War was being fought across Lancashire. A name meaning the field where blood was shed needs no curse to explain it.

The curse is the later reading and it is the sort that grows backwards from the name. A parish hall was proposed for the site within living memory and did not happen, which the story absorbed as further proof. Whether the ground is unlucky or merely awkward to build on beside a Grade I listed church and a graveyard is not a question the tradition takes any interest in.
period: The name is traced to fighting in the 1640s over land taken from the church. The cursed ground reading is later and is not attested in any early source
historical_setting: The ground beside All Saints, Childwall, the only surviving medieval church in Liverpool, in the years of religious and tenurial conflict before the Civil War
origin_date: The name is attributed to a skirmish of about 1640 between new landowners and defenders of the church

name: The Queensway Tunnel Hitchhiker
region: Queensway Tunnel, Liverpool and Birkenhead, Merseyside
summary: A figure stands out in the carriageway inside the Mersey road tunnel with a hand raised for a lift. Drivers who stop and carry the hitchhiker under the river find the seat beside them empty before they reach daylight at the far end. Swerving to miss the figure has caused wrecks of its own, which is the part of the story that gets repeated most.
detail:
The tunnel was dug between 1925 and 1934 and seventeen men were killed building it. Two miles of tiled roadway under a tidal river, with no daylight and nowhere to stop, is close to ideal ground for a story of this kind, and the tunnel has attracted several.

There are two hitchhikers and they are told interchangeably. In one, a man killed in the tunnel in the middle of the last century gets in, talks to the driver and is gone before the exit. In the other, told more often on the Wirral side, a young woman came off the back of a motorbike in the 1960s and died of her injuries, and was afterwards seen standing in the road by a run of motorists and by the tunnel police.

The vanishing hitchhiker is one of the most widely travelled legends in the world and turns up wherever there is a stretch of road people are frightened of. The Queensway version is worth recording for how firmly it has fastened to one particular tunnel, complete with a named decade and an accident specific enough to sound checkable.
period: The tunnel opened in 1934 and the accounts place the deaths in the mid twentieth century, the motorbike version specifically in the 1960s. No contemporary record of either death has been tied to the legend
historical_setting: An account from a Mersey Tunnels employee of thirty years, until 2013, describes police reports of the same phantom hitchhiker in the later Kingsway Tunnel at Wallasey, suggesting the story circulates across both Mersey road tunnels rather than being fixed to one

name: The Grey Lady of Speke Hall
summary: A woman in grey crosses the Tapestry Room at Speke Hall and leaves through the wall. The story fastened to her is that Mary Norris, married to a husband who gambled the estate away, threw her infant son from a window into the moat and went down after him. Crying is reported in the north wing, near the oldest part of the house.
detail:
Speke Hall is a timber framed manor begun in 1530 under Sir William Norris, with two priest holes built into the east wing and a priest recorded hidden there in 1586. It is a house with a genuine history of concealment, which has probably helped the ghost along.

Mary Norris existed. She married Lord Sidney Beauclerk in 1736, and his reputation was bad enough that he was known as Worthless Sidney. That much is real and it is the seed the legend grew from.

The rest does not survive checking. The couple are not recorded as having lived at Speke, and their son Topham reached adulthood and outlived his mother. Neither the National Trust's own account of the house nor the standard published history mentions the Grey Lady at all, and the tale is carried entirely by ghost writing of the last few decades.

The story is best read as the afterlife of Sidney Beauclerk's reputation. It was bad enough in his own lifetime that it was still circulating in Liverpool two hundred years later, by which point it had acquired a drowned child and a window.
period: Mary Norris married Sidney Beauclerk in 1736, which fixes the story's claimed setting. The events are contradicted by the record, since the couple are not recorded at Speke and their son lived to adulthood
earliest_record: Some historians trace the story's rise to prominence to the tenure of Adelaide Watt, the last private occupant of Speke Hall from 1878 until her death in 1921, though no printed record earlier than the twentieth century has been found

name: Mother Redcap's
summary: A low house stood on the Wallasey shore behind walls nearly three feet thick, with a five inch oak door and a trapdoor inside the entrance that dropped an unwelcome caller some nine feet into a cellar. It was built in 1595 and kept, by tradition, by a red hooded woman who sheltered smugglers, held privateers' money for them and hid sailors from the press gang. Tunnels were said to run inland towards Bidston and out to the caves at the Red Noses.
detail:
The house went by several names over the years, among them the Halfway House, the White House and Seabank Nook, but the one that stuck came from the red hood or cap its keeper was said to wear. She is remembered as a Cheshire woman of pleasant manner and formidable competence, trusted with the earnings of men who had nowhere safe to put them.

The hiding places were not invented. When the building was worked on in 1888 the owner found a large cellar under the yard, reached through flagstones and screened by heaps of coal and manure, along with smaller cavities in the walls, one of them just big enough to take a small man. The defences were built into the fabric by someone who expected to need them.

The press gang side of it is grounded too. Men rowed ashore near the Red Noses and lay up in the sandhills until their ships had sailed, and the parish register records the ones who drowned trying, among them William Evans in 1762.

The tunnels are the part that belongs to legend. They are always said to reach somewhere satisfying and have never been traced. The house came down in the 1960s and a nursing home was put up on the ground in 1999.
period: The building dates from 1595 and the smuggling and press gang traditions belong to the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The hiding places are documented from 1888. The tunnels are not
earliest_record: The smugglers' caves and tunnels of the Red and White Noses are described from firsthand visits by the Liverpool antiquarian James Stonehouse in the mid nineteenth century, well before the 1927 newspaper article that supplies the innkeeper's name
historical_setting: Wallasey's reputation as a smuggling and wrecking coast in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, with the tavern said to stand on what is now Egremont Promenade

name: Poldies
summary: Poldies are the fairies of the Wirral woods and their business is keeping people out of them. Anyone who breaks a branch can expect an accident shortly afterwards, and children were sent home before dusk because dusk is when the poldies come out. They are never seen, and are known only by what happens to people who take liberties with the trees.
detail:
The belief belongs to the Wirral and the country along the Cheshire and Lancashire border, and it is recorded in the Oxford Dictionary of English Folklore. Poldies are woodland guardians rather than household or water fairies, and what they do to people is proportionate to what those people have done to the wood.

Two anecdotes carry the tradition. In one, a boy twisted small branches off a tree and threw them away, then sprained his ankle badly a few minutes later, which his cousin put down to the poldies. In the other, a building contractor abandoned plans to clear a Wirral wood after a run of flooding and machinery breakdowns, and local people said the poldies were defending their homes.

The date is the unusual part. The tradition reaches print through the folklorist Jacqueline Simpson, who had it from a friend recalling childhood visits to the Wirral in the 1950s. Most English fairy belief comes down through nineteenth century collectors describing something they thought was ending. This was current within living memory, in a commuter county across the water from Liverpool, and it passed from parents to children as a practical instruction about getting home.

No single wood is named in the record. The warning covers woodland in general, which is why the poldies have no shrine, no stone and no one hill to be attached to. They are a rule about how to behave among trees, given a name and a habit of coming out at dusk.
period: Attested as living belief in the Wirral in the 1950s and recorded by Jacqueline Simpson in the Oxford Dictionary of English Folklore. No earlier record has been traced, so the age of the tradition is unknown

name: The Ravens of the Tower of London
summary: Ravens are kept at the Tower of London under the care of a Yeoman Warder titled the Ravenmaster, and tradition holds that if they ever leave, the Crown will fall and Britain with it. The custom is popularly credited to Charles II. The written record tells a different story. No reference to ravens at the Tower has been found before 1883, and the prophecy itself is first attested in 1944.
detail:
The Tower of London keeps a flock of ravens on the South Lawn, tended by a Yeoman Warder who holds the title of Ravenmaster. The tradition attached to them is one of the best known superstitions in Britain. If the ravens ever leave the Tower, it is said, the Crown will fall and the kingdom with it. Six birds are the working minimum, usually with a spare, and their wing feathers are trimmed so that they stay.

The story most often told credits Charles II. In one version his astronomer John Flamsteed complained that the birds were fouling his observations from the White Tower, and the king, warned of what would follow if they were destroyed, ordered instead that six be kept for ever. A separate and far older strand connects the site to Bran the Blessed of the Mabinogi, whose name means raven and whose head was buried beneath the White Hill to guard Britain against invasion.

The documentary record supports neither connection. Geoffrey Parnell, the Tower's official historian, and the independent scholar Boria Sax both searched for early references and found none at all. The earliest known evidence of ravens living at the Tower is an illustration of 1883, and the birds appear to have been introduced in the Victorian period as living props for the fortress's grim reputation. The prophecy that the kingdom would fall with them is first recorded in the summer of 1944, when Londoners watched the birds through the Blitz. That makes it one of the youngest national legends in Britain, and one of the most thoroughly believed.
period: Popularly set in the reign of Charles II (1660 to 1685), but no ravens are recorded at the Tower before 1883 and the prophecy is first attested in 1944

name: The Screaming Skull of Wardley Hall
summary: A human skull kept in a niche on the staircase at Wardley Hall is said to answer with storms and uproar whenever anyone tries to remove or bury it. Lancashire tradition long named it as the head of the Restoration rake Roger Downes, an identification the opening of his coffin in 1779 destroyed. It is now accepted as the head of Ambrose Barlow, a Benedictine priest executed at Lancaster in 1641.
detail:
Wardley Hall is a moated timber framed manor house of about 1500 near Worsley in Salford, Grade I listed and, since 1930, the residence of the Roman Catholic Bishop of Salford. Set into a niche at the head of the main staircase is a human skull, and around it has grown one of the best documented of the English screaming skull traditions. Move the skull, bury it, throw it into the moat or carry it from the house, and the hall is said to answer with storms, crashing noises and misfortune until it is put back.

The tradition as the Lancashire antiquaries received it named the skull as that of Roger Downes, the last male heir of his family and remembered as one of the more dissolute courtiers of Charles II. In that telling he killed a tailor in a drunken London brawl, was beheaded by a watchman on London Bridge, and his head was boxed up and sent home to his sister at Wardley. John Roby printed a version in his Traditions of Lancashire in 1829, and Harland and Wilkinson gave it again in Lancashire Legends in 1867. The story failed its first real test. When the Downes coffin was opened in 1779 the head was still on the body.

The identification now accepted is a different one altogether. Ambrose Barlow, a Benedictine priest who had ministered secretly in the district for years, was seized while preaching on Easter Sunday 1641 and hanged, drawn and quartered at Lancaster on 10 September of that year. His head was set on a spike in Manchester, and a Catholic kinsman, Francis Downes, is said to have taken it down by night and hidden it at Wardley. A forensic examination in 1960 found the skull of a man of about fifty to sixty years, pierced by a sharp object, which fits Barlow closely. He was canonised in 1970 among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales, and the skull is now treated at the hall as a relic rather than a curiosity.
period: The execution behind the relic took place in 1641. The skull legend is in print by 1829

name: Gef the Talking Mongoose
summary: From 1931 the Irving family of Doarlish Cashen, a lonely farm above Dalby on the Isle of Man, said they shared their house with a talking mongoose who called himself Gef. He scratched behind the panelling, sang, swore, ran errands and reported back what the neighbours were saying. The case drew the psychical researcher Harry Price and became the strangest British newspaper sensation of the 1930s.
detail:
Doarlish Cashen was a stone farmhouse high on the slope above Dalby, exposed, remote and without electricity, where James Irving farmed with his wife Margaret and their daughter Voirrey. In the autumn of 1931 the family began to hear scratching and rustling behind the matchboard panelling of the walls. Within months the noises had become a voice, and the voice had a name and a biography. He was Gef, born in India in 1852, a mongoose, and by his own account an extra clever mongoose.

What made the case famous was how domestic it became. Gef stayed for years. He killed rabbits and left them for the family, rode the bus to Peel to gather gossip and reported it back, screamed abuse at visitors he disliked and sang hymns. James Irving kept a detailed diary of all of it. The Manx press took the story up, then the London papers, and Gef became known across the island as the Dalby Spook.

The investigators arrived in 1935. Harry Price, the best known psychical researcher in Britain, came with Richard Lambert, editor of the BBC magazine The Listener, and the two published The Haunting of Cashen's Gap in 1936. Neither of them heard Gef. Hair said to be his went to Julian Huxley and then to the naturalist F. Martin Duncan, who identified it as dog hair, probably from the family sheepdog Mona. Voirrey Irving, a shy girl of thirteen when it began, was widely suspected of ventriloquism and denied it for the rest of her life. The farmhouse was pulled down in the early 1970s and nothing of it stands above ground, so the location shown here is the farm's recorded position on the slope above Dalby rather than a surveyed footprint. The case has never been satisfactorily explained and has never quite gone away.
period: The reported events run from autumn 1931 to about 1937, with the Price and Lambert investigation in 1935
